detail.title: Regulating Drip Pricing in Platform Markets: Consumer Behavioral Responses and Host Strategic Adaptation under California's SB 478
detail.abstract: Drip pricing-the incremental disclosure of mandatory fees at checkout — distorts consumer choice and has prompted regulatory intervention in digital markets. This study evaluates the behavioral and strategic consequences of California's SB 478, a mandatory price transparency regulation, in peer-to-peer accommodation markets. Applying a continuous difference-in-differences design to listing-level Airbnb data from Los Angeles (July 2023–July 2025), I identify three findings. First, pre-policy cleaning fee ratios positively predicted occupancy, confirming drip pricing bias in consumer decision-making. Second, following enactment, high-fee hosts strategically recomposed fees into base nightly rates, partially offsetting consumer welfare gains. Third, Superhost certification attenuated the resulting occupancy penalty by approximately 39%. These findings indicate that mandatory disclosure effectively corrects informational asymmetry but remains vulnerable to strategic circumvention, underscoring the need for complementary enforcement mechanisms and adaptive platform governance.

To prevent double-counting, losses are evaluated across a two-tiered structure: Tier 1 Direct Institutional Exposure (synthesizing civil payouts, regulatory penalties, mandatory tech remediation, and net brand impairment) and Tier 2 Total Macroeconomic Exposure incorporating real-economy wealth multipliers driven by supply-chain network contagion.

detail.title: AI-Driven Adaptive User Experience and Impulse Buying in Digital Payment Platforms: A Stimulus–Organism–Response Framework
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming digital payment platforms by enabling adaptive interfaces and personalised experiences that influence consumer purchase decisions. Despite AI's growing role in payment technology, little research has examined how adaptive design affects impulse buying within a single behavioural framework. This study addresses the gap by developing and empirically testing a Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model to explain how AI-driven payment features lead to impulsive purchasing.Data from 375 Generation Z users of digital payment apps were analysed using structural equation modelling (SEM) to examine links between AI personalisation, adaptive design, payment friction, enjoyment, trust, user experience, and impulse buying.Results show AI-powered personalisation and adaptive interfaces make shopping more enjoyable and increase impulse buying. Payment friction reduces user experience and impulse purchases, while demographics and trust have less impact than adaptive design.This study advances digital commerce and fintech research by integrating AI-based adaptive design with consumer behaviour theory for payment platforms. It offers guidance for providers, highlighting the need to balance smart personalisation with responsible design to promote positive user experience and ethical engagement

title: Digital Sovereignty as Double-Edged Sword
affiliations: Georgetown University Law Center and The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Digital Sovereignty as Double-Edged Sword

publicationDetails.detailsText: Published in Data Sovereignty: From the Digital Silk Road to the Return of the State, by Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780197582794.003.0004
Georgetown University Law Center Research Paper

detail.abstract: Digital sovereignty is simultaneously a necessary incident of democratic governance and democracy’s dreaded antagonist. Governments need to control the Internet’s impact on their people. Yet, at the same time, control over the Internet offers governments enormous power over their residents’ lives. In a sense, this is simply a 21st-century version of the insight of international law scholar Louis Henkin: sovereignty can insulate a government’s worst ills from foreign intrusion. Assertions of digital sovereignty thus carry a double edge—useful both to protect citizens and to control them. Digital sovereignty can magnify the government’s powers by making legible behaviors that were previously invisible to the state. Thus, the same rule can be used to safeguard or repress—a feature that legislators across the Global North and South should anticipate through careful checks and balances.

title: "The Impact of Website Characteristics on Online Impulse Buying Behavior in Algeria The Mediating Role of Consumer Impulsivity"

detail.title: "The Impact of Website Characteristics on Online Impulse Buying Behavior in Algeria The Mediating Role of Consumer Impulsivity"
detail.abstract: This study seeks to explore the main factors of impulse buying behavior online in Algeria because of the rapid digital transformation and the increasing role of e-commerce platforms. The majority of earlier literature has focused on traditional retail environments and there is a gap in research on emerging markets where consumers’ online behavior is subject to profound changes.This study investigates the influence of website features on impulse buying through impulse mediation using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM).The results show that website features do have a direct and significant effect on impulse buying behavior, and they influence it indirectly through the impulse variable as a mediator, which is one of the most important drivers of impulse buying behavior in the Algerian context.This study broadens the support to e-commerce practitioners by incorporating external triggers in the emerging markets environment. It highlights the importance of improving website quality and providing value-added digital products so as to improve the user experience for stimulating consumer engagement and impulse buying.

title: From NLP to LLMs to Agentic AI: The Evolution of Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: Rutgers University, New Brunswick, William Paterson University, Columbia University, The College of New Jersey, Rowan University, Stevens Institute of Technology and Hofstra University

detail.title: From NLP to LLMs to Agentic AI: The Evolution of Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has undergone a remarkable evolution, progressing from rule-based natural language processing (NLP) systems to large language models (LLMs) and, more recently, to agentic AI (AAI). This editorial examines this technological progression and argues that agentic AI represents a paradigm shift from reactive language generation to autonomous, goal-oriented intelligence capable of planning, reasoning, memory, and tool integration. While LLMs have significantly advanced natural language understanding and generation, their reactive nature limits their ability to execute complex, multistep workflows and deliver sustained organizational value. Agentic AI addresses these limitations by enabling proactive decision-making, persistent context management, and autonomous task execution across diverse domains. The editorial reviews the historical development of NLP, statistical machine learning, deep learning, transformer-based architectures, and generative AI, highlighting how each stage laid the foundation for modern agentic systems. It also discusses emerging enterprise applications, economic opportunities, and the growing ecosystem of agentic frameworks, while emphasizing the accompanying challenges related to governance, accountability, security, alignment, interpretability, and systemic risk. The article concludes that the future of AI lies in combining linguistic intelligence with responsible autonomous action through robust sociotechnical governance, ensuring that increasingly capable AI systems augment human judgment, create sustainable value, and operate ethically in complex real-world environments.

detail.abstract: United States trade enforcement has intensified sharply while the compliance capacity of the businesses that bear it has not. In Fiscal Year 2025, U.S. Customs and Border Protection issued 2,432 trade penalties, liquidated-damages cases rose 136.8 percent to 53,052, and 465 audits recovered $235.5 million. The Office of Foreign Assets Control enforces economic sanctions on a strict-liability basis, and the U.S. Government Accountability Office has identified trade based money laundering as one of the primary mechanisms criminal organizations use to launder illicit proceeds, exploiting vulnerabilities in international trade documentation. Large corporations answer these obligations with dedicated compliance departments; the typical small importer, exporter, logistics intermediary, or cross-border nonprofit has none. This toolkit is intended to help address that gap by providing practical compliance frameworks. It converts the governing federal obligations, the importer's reasonable-care duty under 19 U.S.C. § 1484, sanctions screening under the regulations administered by OFAC, and trade-related anti-money-laundering vigilance, into four operational modules with checklists, a model screening log, a red-flag reference, and a thirty-day implementation roadmap that a small organization can adopt without specialist staff. A dedicated section addresses the responsible use of artificial intelligence in compliance work: where AI tools genuinely accelerate screening, classification, and document review, where human judgment must remain, and the governance rules that keep liability, which never transfers to software, under control. It is written for business owners and nonprofit managers, not for lawyers, and it is offered for free distribution by trade associations, chambers of commerce, small-business development organizations, and community networks.

title: When Pricing Agents Meet Buying Agents: Personalized Pricing and Verifiable Trust

detail.title: When Pricing Agents Meet Buying Agents: Personalized Pricing and Verifiable Trust
detail.abstract: Same fairness rule, different posterior, no trade. We study personalized pricing when a pricing agent and a buying agent act for different principals, receive different signals of latent value, and execute machine-enforced mandates. Equal nominal surplus-sharing rules can be incompatible because each rule is evaluated against its agent's posterior. We solve the buyer's acceptance and costly-inspection problem, the seller's coverage-pricing problem, and the principals' mandateselection game. Verification can recover trades and soften both principals' policies, but only when its evidence boundary covers the disputed rule and inputs. In repeated transactions, attributable offers above the buyer's reference cap depreciate relationship capital; the seller then follows a state-dependent Markov policy with a reference-respecting region. Verification is privately underprovided when the seller does not internalize avoided buyer inspection and relationship spillovers, although evidence that legitimizes extraction can instead produce overadoption. The model turns AI measurement, algorithmic extraction, and verifiable restraint into one bilateral equilibrium and yields protocol-level records that identify posterior disagreement, trust depreciation, and the verification premium.

title: When the Student Becomes the Rival: Distillation vs. Thin Wrapping in AI Service Markets
affiliations: ,  and City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Information Systems

detail.title: When the Student Becomes the Rival: Distillation vs. Thin Wrapping in AI Service Markets
detail.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping digital service markets. While foundation models provide general-purpose intelligence, domain-specific adaptation is often undertaken by downstream developers. Traditionally, many developers operate as thin wrappers, serving users through real-time API calls to foundation models. Recently, model distillation has emerged as an alternative: developers use foundation-model outputs to train smaller, domain-specific student models that can operate independently after training. This shift creates a fundamental tension in the AI value chain. On the one hand, distillation offers developers a pathway to escape perpetual API dependence; on the other, foundation-model providers fiercely criticize it as a substitution threat that transfers model value to future rivals. Despite its growing prevalence and controversy, the economic consequences of distillation remain underexplored. We develop a game-theoretic model in which a foundation-model provider competes with a downstream developer while selling API access to the developer. We compare thin wrapping with distillation and characterize equilibrium API pricing, subscription pricing, training investment, positioning, and profits. Our analysis shows that distillation is not universally beneficial to developers. Instead, it disproportionately benefits developers with strong domain-specific capabilities, challenging the popular expectation that distillation democratizes the AI market by empowering marginal entrants. More importantly, when developers can endogenously position their services, distillation induces high-capability developers to differentiate more strongly from the foundation model. This strategic repositioning softens downstream subscription competition and can even allow the foundation-model provider to benefit from distillation, creating a win-win outcome for both the provider and the developer. Finally, by comparing several market outcomes under these two scenarios, we identify how distillation reshapes the balance between API monetization and competition. Our findings offer actionable implications for foundation-model providers, downstream AI developers, and policymakers seeking to govern the evolving AI value chain.

title: Artificial Intelligence in it Auditing: Risk, Reliability, and Auditor Judgment
affiliations: Bowie State University

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in it Auditing: Risk, Reliability, and Auditor Judgment
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping IT auditing, raising urgent questions about automation bias, explainability, and the preservation of professional skepticism in auditor judgment. This study examines how AI affects audit risk, reliability, and auditor judgment through a multi-method design combining a systematic review of 42 carefully selected articles, a controlled behavioral experiment, and a survey of IT audit professionals. The results show that AI plays a crucial role in improving anomaly detection, expanding audit coverage, and prioritizing risks, especially in environments with large volumes of digital data. However, the findings also reveal that automation bias (particularly among less experienced auditors), black-box explainability challenges, and weaknesses in AI governance can undermine the defensibility of audit evidence. To address these risks, the study proposes an AI audit risk framework grounded in COSO Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) principles, spanning five dimensions: model, data, explainability, operational, and behavioral risk. Ultimately, the advantages of AI in IT auditing hinge on maintaining high data quality, using transparent and explainable models, and ensuring robust governance oversight to achieve reliable, defensible audit results.

title: The Auditability of Identity and Access Management (IAM) in Zero Trust Architectures: A Systematic Review
affiliations: Bowie State University

detail.title: The Auditability of Identity and Access Management (IAM) in Zero Trust Architectures: A Systematic Review
detail.abstract: Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) replaces perimeter-based security with continuous verification, creating a fundamental gap between how Identity and Access Management (IAM) controls operate and how traditional periodic audits validate them. This systematic review examines the auditability of IAM within ZTA environments, employing a qualitative meta-synthesis approach following PRISMA guidelines. The study identifies reliable audit evidence for validating IAM controls, including authentication logs, policy engine decisions, continuous monitoring outputs, and micro-segmentation records. Three major themes emerge from the analysis: IAM Control Validity, Algorithm-based Access Control, and Legacy Compatibility. The findings reveal significant gaps between ZTA's continuous verification paradigm and traditional periodic audit methodologies, highlighting challenges in algorithmic transparency and auditor competency as AI and machine learning increasingly drive trust evaluation. This research provides actionable guidance for IT auditors transitioning from perimeter-based control validation to identity-centric security assessment frameworks.

title: Process Discipline as the Isolating Variable in AI-Assisted Enterprise Software Development: A Natural Experiment

detail.title: Process Discipline as the Isolating Variable in AI-Assisted Enterprise Software Development: A Natural Experiment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper reports a natural experiment conducted on the author's own AI-assisted software development practice. The author directed the team studied and has a professional and financial interest in the software produced under the study conditions.

detail.abstract:
Over 12 months (March 2025-March 2026), a two-person team using AI coding assistants produced 2.6 million lines of code across 2,929 commits and retained approximately 250,000 lines: a 90% elimination rate. Every line that survived was reviewed, evaluated against enterprise requirements, and kept or discarded by a human architect. GitClear (2025, 211M lines across Google, Microsoft, and Meta) reports that industry cleanup activity collapsed from 25% to under 10% after AI adoption. This team sustained 90%. The dataset spans two process conditions applied to the same team using the same tools.
Under a structured AI-specific SDLC: 1,484,038 lines produced, 811,684 lines eliminated (55% cleanup ratio), 3,977 function points delivered, 18 of 18 enterprise audit dimensions satisfied, 68 test files, 13 CI/CD pipelines. Without it: 1,153,069 lines produced, 483,991 lines eliminated (42% cleanup ratio), 428 functional FP delivered (working demo with live prospect accounts), 2 of 18 dimensions satisfied (including plain text password storage), zero test files, zero pipelines, four repositories abandoned. The unstructured condition generated code 4.2x faster by volume (360,334 lines/month vs. 84,802) and produced working software that cannot be sold to a regulated customer and must be discarded rather than remediated: zero enterprise-ready function points. The structured condition produced at 9–11x the published elite productivity benchmark (227 FP/FTE-month vs. 20–26 for best-in-class manual teams; Capers Jones/SPR, 26,000+ projects).

title: B2B eWOM on Alibaba: Signaling Through Online Reviews in Platform-based Social Exchange

detail.title: B2B eWOM on Alibaba: Signaling Through Online Reviews in Platform-based Social Exchange
detail.abstract:
This study investigates the contemporary role of electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) in business exchanges through buyers' signaling of observable and unobservable supplier characteristics on the Alibaba e-commerce platform. Utilizing a qualitative pre-study of 20 interviews (five buyer-supplier dyads with two interviews per firm) and more than 8,000 buyer reviews on Alibaba, we identify characteristic patterns of this type of B2B eWOM. 

Signaling Theory and Social Exchange Theory underpin the empirical investigation. To enable further conceptualization, the study distinguishes between online B2B reviews based on the extent to which they are controlled by organizational partners. Unlike some other forms of B2B reviews, reviews on Alibaba are uncontrolled and comprise a form of eWOM. 

Findings indicate that the relational patterns of B2B eWOM shared on Alibaba can be aggregated into three categories: human touch, responsiveness, and resilience. Besides these new categories, the importance of product/service quality has been confirmed. Through Alibaba reviews, buyers' signals are sent not only to suppliers as feedback, but also to other prospective buyers to influence their purchase decisions. 

Our study aims to contribute to the B2B literature on eWOM and signaling in business relationships. By showing that human touch occurs even in online-only buyer-supplier relationships, the study provides evidence that bonding, the development of mutuality, and relationship intimacy in buyer-supplier relationships does not always require in-person contact. Managerial implications are offered with a focus on the signaling of unobservable qualities, such as human touch, with the help of B2B eWOM.

detail.abstract:
This study investigates how international environmental regulation influences South Africa’s environmental policy development, corporate emissions performance, and capital market dynamics, with a particular focus on the gold mining sector. The sector remains economically significant but highly carbon-intensive due to its reliance on coal-based electricity. Against the backdrop of intensifying global climate governance, frameworks such as the Paris Agreement, the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and international disclosure standards are increasingly shaping domestic policy frameworks and firm-level strategies.

The research is guided by two central questions: (RQ1) How do international environmental regulations influence environmental policy and regulatory development in South Africa? and (RQ2) To what extent do international regulatory frameworks drive carbon emission reductions in South African gold mining companies?

Drawing on Institutional Theory, Signalling Theory, and Multi-Level Governance, the study combines policy analysis with a quantitative assessment of carbon intensity trends across five JSE-listed gold mining firms between 2018 and 2024.

The findings demonstrate that international regulatory frameworks have been a decisive driver of South Africa’s climate policy trajectory, consistent with institutional theory perspectives on regulatory diffusion and isomorphic pressures. The Carbon Tax Act (2019) reflects alignment with South Africa’s Paris Agreement commitments while anticipating emerging trade-related carbon constraints such as CBAM. The Johannesburg Stock Exchange’s Sustainability and Climate Disclosure Guidance further illustrates convergence with global reporting standards, reinforcing the institutionalisation of ESG disclosure practices within capital markets.

Firm-level analysis reveals a 47% reduction in aggregate carbon intensity between 2018 and 2024, with the most significant declines occurring between 2019 and 2021 following the implementation of the Carbon Tax Act and the announcement of CBAM. Thereafter, reductions moderated and were sustained primarily through disclosure-driven normative pressures. The findings further indicate that global climate regulation increasingly influences investor behaviour, capital allocation, and market competitiveness, with firms demonstrating credible ESG disclosure and decarbonisation strategies better positioned to maintain investor confidence and access international markets. The study concludes that international regulatory mechanisms have catalysed significant, though uneven, decarbonisation, while highlighting that long-term progress remains constrained by South Africa’s structural dependence on coal-based energy.

title: The Perceptual Enterprise A Unified Systems Architecture of the Business Enterprise

detail.title: The Perceptual Enterprise A Unified Systems Architecture of the Business Enterprise

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: Organizational theory is more than a century old and has produced frameworks of genuine power — resource theory, dynamic capabilities, open systems theory, organizational learning, institutional theory, competitive strategy. Each illuminates something real about how enterprises function and fail. What the field has not yet produced is a consolidating architecture: a prior ontological answer to what kind of thing the enterprise constitutively is, such that all of these traditions describe aspects of it. This theoretical monograph provides that architecture. Its foundational claim is that the business enterprise is a perceptual entity — a meaning system that sustains itself by engaging its environment through governing premises so foundational they do not appear as premises. They appear as reality itself. This is not a metaphor. It is the constitutive feature of organizational life that prior traditions have each partially illuminated without naming: the reason enterprises develop the resources they develop, form the capabilities they form, learn what they learn, and fail as they fail. Establishing the enterprise as a perceptual entity makes integration possible because it identifies the cross-cutting mechanism — the interpretive architecture — through which every organizational domain operates. The architecture is developed across eight sections. The perceptual entity construct specifies the enterprise’s constitutive nature and addresses the persistent tension between objective and interpretive views of organization. A fully specified open systems architecture grounds six subsystems, three feedback loops, and core constructs — the success syndrome, the coherence horizon, structural gravity, reconstruction potential — as genuine instantiations of formal properties from physics and cybernetics rather than organizational metaphors. A resource architecture specifies the two classes of inputs, the recognition mechanism governing what gets built, and why accumulated resource positions both sustain viability and eventually mask its erosion. The value event — a first-order theoretical construct prior organizational theory has not specified — operationalizes the enterprise as a purposeful energetic system whose viability is measured by the continuous generation of exchanges the environment recognizes as worth sustaining. A six-subsystem architecture develops each subsystem in full, mapping the theoretical traditions that addressed each domain, specifying what each contributed, and showing where each stopped. A feedback architecture specifies the success syndrome as a positive feedback loop without internal limit that systematically degrades its own balancing mechanisms. A unified theoretical map shows how seven theoretical regions developed independently were always partial specifications of a single architectural reality.  The monograph’s most consequential contribution is the demonstration that organizational theory’s fragmentation into competing traditions reflects not the actual structure of organizational reality but the limits of what any single tradition could see from within its own domain. The perceptual enterprise architecture shows what those traditions collectively imply — and provides the unified framework through which they can be understood in relation to each other and to the enterprise whose operation they have always been jointly describing.

title: Human AI Cognitive Synergy

detail.title: Human AI Cognitive Synergy
detail.abstract: Contemporary scholarship on human-AI collaboration evaluates how artificial intelligence improves performance within discrete episodes of interaction, diagnostic accuracy, decision quality, task completion, but leaves largely unexamined whether sustained, recursive interaction with conversational AI changes the cognitive capabilities of the human participant over time. This paper introduces Human-AI Cognitive Synergy (HACS), a conceptual and formal framework proposing that recursive collaboration with AI can constitute a distinct mechanism of human cognitive development, one that is contingent on the structure and quality of the collaboration rather than a fixed consequence of AI use itself. Synthesizing scholarship from intelligence augmentation, distributed cognition, human-AI teaming, the learning sciences, and metacognition alongside a growing empirical literature on cognitive offloading, the paper develops a dynamic model in which capability growth is bounded by a context dependent capacity ceiling and can be offset by a loss mechanism tied specifically to AI reliance unaccompanied by reflection. The model generates falsifiable predictions, including a crowding out hypothesis under which AI assistance without active reflection is predicted to reduce unassisted capability even as AI assisted performance improves. Applications to education, professional judgment, and software engineering are developed against existing controlled evidence, including randomized experiments showing that AI assistance can either substantially accelerate or measurably slow performance depending on a practitioner's proximity to the frontier of their own expertise. The paper concludes that whether recursive AI collaboration strengthens or erodes human cognitive capability is an open empirical question the framework is built to test rather than assume, and it outlines a research agenda for doing so.

title: Tourism and Social-Ecological Change in North America's Gateway and Natural Amenity Regions

detail.title: Tourism and Social-Ecological Change in North America's Gateway and Natural Amenity Regions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflict of interest to disclose.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the Institute of Outdoor Recreation and Tourism at Utah State University.

detail.abstract: Tourism growth is associated with substantial landscape and social-ecological change in gateway and natural amenity regions (GNARs), yet individual studies often focus on select social, environmental, and economic outcomes. We conducted a hybrid systematic--integrative review of 37 peer-reviewed studies examining tourism-related change in North American GNARs. The review identified 18 recurring primary effects across social, environmental, and economic dimensions and synthesized the reported pathways connecting those effects to wider regional consequences. Tourism was commonly associated with employment growth, entrepreneurship, public revenue, and infrastructure investment. However, it was also associated with housing unaffordability, congestion, environmental degradation, inequality, and governance challenges. Environmental effects were less frequently and less consistently measured than social and economic effects. The review documents how the primary effects of tourism often propagate across social, environmental, and economic dimensions rather than remaining confined to one part of the regional system. The synthesis also indicates that tourism pressures are mediated by five regional systems: infrastructure, governance, local value capture, housing and land use, and mobility. These domains constitute potential leverage points for sustainable tourism and land use planning. The review provides a regional and landscape-scale approach for understanding tourism-related change and identifies priorities for more spatially explicit, longitudinal, and intervention-oriented research.

title: Distributed Accountability and the Production of Institutional Trust: A General Theory of Governance Architecture

detail.title: Distributed Accountability and the Production of Institutional Trust: A General Theory of Governance Architecture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no financial, commercial, or personal relationships that could have inappropriately influenced the work reported in this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This manuscript is a conceptual and theoretical study. It did not involve human participants, identifiable personal data, animals, or biological materials. Institutional Review Board approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external grant funding. The study was independently conducted by the authors as part of the Governance Accountability Architecture Research Program at the IAM of America Policy Center.

detail.abstract: Complex public institutions increasingly operate through governance systems in which monitoring, investigative, adjudicative, and enforcement responsibilities are distributed across multiple autonomous organizations. Although such arrangements frequently preserve constitutional checks and balances, professional specialization, and institutional independence, they may also create accountability failures when authority, information, and coordination become insufficiently integrated. Existing governance scholarship has examined institutional capacity, implementation, and trust extensively, yet relatively little attention has been given to how governance architecture itself conditions the production of institutional trust through accountability processes. This paper develops a general governance framework explaining the relationship among institutional design, governance architecture, accountability operations, trust production, and organizational resilience. The framework introduces Governance Authority Configuration (GAC) as the structural allocation of accountability authority; the Governance Authority Integration Index (GAII) as a multidimensional diagnostic profile across five dimensions—authority resolution, functional connectivity, information continuity, coordination formalization, and review and constraint; and Distributed Accountability Failure (DAF) as a conditional governance failure arising when distributed accountability systems lack sufficient integration, capacity, or safeguards for the complexity of their accountability tasks. The framework’s central contribution is the proposition that institutional trust is partially produced through governance behaviors that are enabled—or constrained—by accountability architecture. Governance architecture influences accountability-process performance, which shapes procedural legitimacy and contributes to trust production. Institutional trust is interpreted as an accumulated stock—Trust Capital when strengthened and Trust Debt when depleted—that conditions organizational resilience during exogenous institutional shocks. The paper therefore distinguishes governance architecture from governance behavior, organizational capability from observed performance, procedural legitimacy from institutional trust, and trust from institutional resilience. The framework does not assume that distributed governance is inherently deficient. Rather, it proposes that Distributed Accountability Failure emerges only when distributed institutional arrangements are unable to maintain timely, consistent, transparent, and enforceable accountability given the complexity, urgency, and jurisdictional dispersion of the accountability task. The theory generates explicit boundary conditions, identifies competing explanations, proposes falsifiable theoretical propositions, and establishes an empirical research agenda. The framework is designed for comparative application across constitutional institutions, universities, professional licensing systems, regulatory agencies, nonprofit governance, international organizations, healthcare systems, and other complex public institutions. This framework contributes to the emerging field of governance science by positioning institutional trust as a measurable organizational capability and by offering an implementation-oriented model that bridges governance theory and institutional practice.

title: Continuous it Auditing in Hybrid Cloud Environments: Effectiveness, Maturity, and Risk Coverage
affiliations: Bowie State University

detail.title: Continuous it Auditing in Hybrid Cloud Environments: Effectiveness, Maturity, and Risk Coverage
detail.abstract: Continuous IT auditing is rapidly displacing periodic, point-in-time audits in hybrid cloud environments, where configuration drift, identity compromise, and data residency risks evolve faster than traditional assurance cycles can detect. This study synthesizes scholarly evidence on cybersecurity auditing, tool integration, and governance practices in cloud-centric environments, validates continuous auditing models through empirical evidence, and proposes a maturity framework designed for hybrid cloud governance. The research examines how security tools such as SIEM, CSPM, and SOAR can be integrated to enable automated monitoring and incident management; explores dynamic access controls paired with load balancing in hybrid and multicloud setups; and assesses maturity methodologies such as PLS-PM and multi-case analysis, alongside compliance-driven risk mitigation strategies aligned with established frameworks including NIST, COBIT, ISO 27001, SOC 2, and FedRAMP. The key findings reveal that automation plays a crucial role in reducing response times, minimizing human error, and facilitating real-time threat detection and remediation across distributed infrastructures, while maturity progression is shaped by organizational, technological, and governance factors that shift auditing practices from manual, reactive approaches to proactive, continuous assurance. The proposed maturity framework serves as a structured guide for practitioners to evaluate and enhance their auditing capabilities, while also aiding regulators in enforcing adaptive standards. This positions continuous auditing as a vital component of sustainable risk management and organizational resilience in today's cloud governance landscape.

title: Generative Closure in Generative Relational Being: A Preliminary Reflection on Turbulence Models

detail.title: Generative Closure in Generative Relational Being: A Preliminary Reflection on Turbulence Models
detail.abstract: Research on culture, norms, trust, and institutions routinely writes the macro-level as a system with dynamics of its own-an equation in which the future of a collective variable is a function of that variable alone. This paper argues that the self-containedness such writing presupposes is an assumption rather than a finding, and that a mature physical case, fully developed turbulence, shows how and why the assumption fails. The failure has a precise name in statistical physics: the closure problem. When a system with exact microscopic dynamics is projected onto the coarse variables one wishes to study, the projected dynamics are in general not closed-each order depends on a higher one, and the coarse variable is not by itself a sufficient description of its own future. The Mori-Zwanzig formalism gives the projected evolution exactly: alongside its drift it carries a memory kernel and a noise, and reduces to a self-contained macroscopic equation only when a separation of scales lets the memory decay and the noise whiten. Turbulence is the case in which that separation is absent across the range that matters, and it serves here as a calibration rather than a metaphor: it exhibits the closure problem on a fixed state space under the simultaneous loss of every feature that ordinarily rescues it, and thereby marks what a relational difficulty of merely this kind would amount to. The renormalization group, the second instrument for the passage across scales, sharpens the caution from the other side: where it succeeds, universality forbids reading a closed macroscopic law back to its microscopic mechanism; where it fails, as on the anomalous scaling of turbulence, it shows that a scaling law is no warrant for a universal macroscopic theory. The paper carries these into the study of relational emergence as a methodological caution-that a macro-level's autonomy is to be established, not assumed-and distinguishes the closure it warns about, a closure of dynamics, from the notion the framework will require, a closure of generation. The latter is named and delimited, not established: what would ground it, an invariant of generation not underwritten by any conservation law, is set down as the open problem the reflection leaves standing.

title: Equity and Inclusion as Unifying Principles
affiliations: Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge - Paul M. Hebert Law Center

detail.title: Equity and Inclusion as Unifying Principles
detail.abstract: As the country grows more polarized politically, culture wars in higher education are widely reported across myriad news outlets. Diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) have been maligned and linked to “wokeness.” This alleged link precipitated politicians, especially in red states, to push for legislation curtailing DEI efforts across campuses in spheres ranging from human resources to the classroom. Since January of 2023, forty bills have been introduced that target DEI efforts in higher education. Since 2020, 750 anti-Critical Race Theory (CRT) bills have been introduced across the country.

title: Observation, Indeterminacy, and Discontinuous Explanation: A Quantum-continuity Model for the Philosophy of Social Science

detail.title: Observation, Indeterminacy, and Discontinuous Explanation: A Quantum-continuity Model for the Philosophy of Social Science
detail.abstract:
The philosophy of social science faces a persistent explanatory gap in reflexive systems: when modeling alters what is being modeled, predictive frameworks become unstable at the moments they are most needed. Complexity theory and reflexivity each address part of this problemnonlinearity, feedback, recursive expectation-but each leaves comparatively underspecified the moment at which structured indeterminacy resolves into a realized social outcome. 

This article proposes Potentialism and the Quantum-Continuity Model (QCM) as a candidate epistemological framework. Rather than claiming social systems are literally quantum, QCM treats quantum theory as a source for disciplined structural analogy, transferring the bare structure by which multiple live possibilities resolve into a definite outcome-while explicitly bounding what does and does not carry over. From this it generates three concepts: Transition Zones, Quantum Thresholds, and Quantum Measurement Events. The framework positions itself among existing accounts of constitutive observation-self-fulfilling prophecy, performativity, and second-order systems theory-specifying what it adds to them. 

The Arab Spring serves as illustration, with briefer extensions to the 2008 financial crisis and #MeToo. QCM offers a vocabulary for discontinuous social resolution, reorienting inquiry from prediction toward the navigation of structured indeterminacy.

title: Merchant Incentive Optimization in Digital Payment Ecosystems

detail.title: Merchant Incentive Optimization in Digital Payment Ecosystems
detail.abstract: Digital payment networks rely on a delicate two-sided equilibrium: consumers use a payment rail when enough merchants accept it, while merchants accept and actively promote the rail when enough consumers bring transactions, liquidity, and ancillary financial opportunities. Incentives such as merchant commissions, onboarding subsidies, fee holidays, settlement acceleration, working-capital hooks, advertising credits, and consumer coupons can accelerate this equilibrium, but blunt incentive programs waste budget on merchants who would have digitized anyway, underfund merchants whose constraints are structural, and obscure the causal effect of the platform intervention. This paper synthesizes platform economics, merchant payment acceptance research, graph-based incentive optimization, uplift modeling, and contextual bandit methods into a deployment-oriented strategy for merchant incentive optimization. The proposed operating model separates adoption, activation, retention, and expansion outcomes; treats merchant incentives as multi-treatment causal interventions; uses randomized holdouts alongside graph, uplift, and high-cardinality merchant representations; and solves budget allocation under profitability, fairness, risk, and operational constraints. An illustrative simulation shows why allocation should rank merchants by expected incremental value rather than raw transaction volume or predicted response alone. The central conclusion is that payment platforms should optimize incentives as a governed learning system, not as a campaign discount engine: the winning policy is the one that buys incremental, durable, and compliant merchant-side network growth at the lowest opportunity cost.

title: Public Grant Theory - Revisiting Incorporation, Reclaiming the Public Space
affiliations: University of Ottawa - Common Law Section

detail.title: Public Grant Theory - Revisiting Incorporation, Reclaiming the Public Space
detail.abstract:
The Public Grant theory stresses the legislative origin of business corporations. The theory rests on the factual position that the core corporate attributes – entity status, organizational continuity and protection for corporate actors (directors, executives, shareholders) – are unattainable without legislative rules. Contractual methods are simply inadequate.

In granting incorporation, legislation also places corporate enterprises under a normative governance framework. This includes voting rights for shareholders (as contributors of risk capital) to elect directors (custodians of the capital), a clear organizational structure and protection for creditors (recognized as relatively vulnerable financial stakeholders).

Countering neoliberal interpretations, the Public Grant theory reclaims the public space in incorporation. Informed by a constitutional/democratic perspective, the theory postulates utilitarianism and advancing the larger public interest represent normative legislative goals. These metrics can legitimate meaningful regulation, to assure corporate responsibility and accountability. The method can aid efforts to address inequality in which the current structure of corporate law is instrumental. Specifically, this can facilitate a legislative statement that corporations represent communities of interests and thereby, promote inclusive governance.

title: Why Communities Fight Data Centers: Evidence from Moratoria, Litigation, and Public Opinion
affiliations: 273 Ventures

detail.title: Why Communities Fight Data Centers: Evidence from Moratoria, Litigation, and Public Opinion
detail.abstract: Opposition to data center development in the United States has, in roughly two years, grown from scattered local complaints into an organized national movement that blocked or delayed roughly $130 billion in projects in the first quarter of 2026 alone. This paper argues that the opposition is neither irrational nor merely parochial, and that the common "NIMBY" label obscures more than it explains. The opposition rests on a structural asymmetry: the benefits of a data center flow broadly, while its costs concentrate locally. A siting logic in which the binding constraint is electric power, not community consent, compounds the problem. I offer a framework for making sense of the resulting grievances along three axes: their remediability (whether any condition of approval could satisfy them), their scale (parcel, community, or societal), and the project phase at which they appear (announcement, construction, operation, or enforcement). The framework organizes the complaints and predicts how each is likely to be resolved: negotiated conditions for remediable grievances, moratoria and referenda for intrinsic ones. It also clarifies why the disputes that residents actually win in court are overwhelmingly procedural. I ground the framework in the current empirical record, test its central prediction descriptively against a national inventory of local moratoria, and close with its implications for developers, policymakers, and the communities themselves.

title: Non-Monotonic Entry Dynamics in Oligopoly with Common Ownership
affiliations: Aarhus University - School of Business and Social Sciences, Università degli Studi della Calabria, EM Lyon (Ecole de Management de Lyon) and University of Macedonia - Department of Economics

detail.title: Non-Monotonic Entry Dynamics in Oligopoly with Common Ownership

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare.

detail.abstract: We show how common ownership fundamentally transforms entry in an uncertain market from sequential preemption into a regime of coordination with contest-like dynamics. We do this by studying an industry with three firms facing a stochastically evolving demand that internalize the effect of their entry and output decisions on rivals. Equilibrium exhibits an accordion effect with respect to internalization: common ownership softens the last entry, intensifies competition at the duopoly stage, and ultimately slows down first market entry, reducing overall dynamism. But unlike in two-firm industries, a coordination equilibrium emerges at the duopoly stage if option value is high enough. The contest-like dynamics in this equilibrium accelerate first entry and raise welfare.

title: From Reactive Alerts to Predictive Whale Avoidance: Integrating Live AIS, Environmental Indicators, and Whale Reports into a Real-Time Collision-risk System

detail.title: From Reactive Alerts to Predictive Whale Avoidance: Integrating Live AIS, Environmental Indicators, and Whale Reports into a Real-Time Collision-risk System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: My father recommended that I do and look into this as a project as it is something I am interested in.

detail.abstract: Whale-vessel collisions remain a major conservation concern where shipping routes overlap with whale feeding, migration, and resting habitat. Existing protection systems often depend on observations made after whales have already entered areas of vessel traffic, while ecological forecasts and vessel-monitoring tools are frequently managed separately. This study presents AI Marine Sentinel, a deployed decision-support prototype that combines live Automatic Identification System (AIS) vessel data, NOAA sea-surface temperature retrieved through Google Earth Engine, NOAA buoy observations when available, bathymetric habitat context, historical whale records, and recent user reports. A transparent heuristic model calculates environmental suitability, relative whale likelihood, and relative collision risk. Geodesic distance calculations generate advisory zones, recommend speeds of 10 knots in high-risk areas, and evaluate compliance among eligible live vessels. Missing inputs are excluded and remaining weights are renormalized when sufficient data remain. Calculations, source states, effective weights, zone geometry, and compliance counts are logged to BigQuery for reproducibility. Production testing confirmed live AIS synchronization across backend records, frontend state, and map markers, successful Earth Engine retrieval of NOAA OISST values, and dynamic riskzone generation. The system is operational as a real-time prototype, but its manually selected weights have not yet been calibrated against an independent set of confirmed whale observations. Its outputs should therefore be interpreted as transparent prioritization indices rather than validated probabilities.

detail.abstract:
This concept note introduces ImpactAlign, a policy visualization framework designed to strengthen reproducibility and transparency in Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) benchmarking. The framework responds to a persistent challenge in global research governance: the fragmentation between policy directives and methodological execution. By embedding governance schematics into a reproducible flowchart, ImpactAlign bridges this gap, offering institutions a clear pathway from strategic intent to measurable outcomes. 

Concept Note 2 emphasizes the visualization dimension, presenting a governance-oriented flowchart (Figure 1) that integrates national directives, institutional policies, and methodological pathways. The sequential mapping illustrates how directives are operationalized through data collection, normalization, and benchmarking, culminating in outputs that are transparent, auditable, and globally comparable. This visualization responds directly to SSRN reviewers' emphasis on clarity, governance diagrams, and reproducibility.

 The framework's expected outcomes include enhanced reproducibility through schema-driven workflows, transparent benchmarking supported by reviewer-friendly templates and dashboards, and increased institutional recognition in international forums. By aligning outputs with UN SDG Academy guidelines and open science standards, ImpactAlign strengthens institutional accountability while advancing visibility within the global SDG ecosystem. 

Ultimately, ImpactAlign contributes to the standardization of SDG benchmarking by offering a reproducible, policy-driven visualization tool. Its adoption enables institutions to move beyond fragmented reporting toward coherent, transparent, and globally recognized contributions to sustainable development.

title: Empirical Predictability Limits of Financial Markets via Correlated-Decorrelated Structure Function Decomposition: A Departure from Atmospheric Turbulence Theory Draft preprint -CPE research series
affiliations: Independent Quantitative Researcher

detail.title: Empirical Predictability Limits of Financial Markets via Correlated-Decorrelated Structure Function Decomposition: A Departure from Atmospheric Turbulence Theory Draft preprint -CPE research series
detail.abstract: Theoretical predictability limits of the atmosphere have been derived, in prior work by the author and others, from a multifractal cascade formalism in which the correlated and decorrelated components of a turbulent field’s polyspectrum are tracked as a function of lead time, with the predictability limit defined as the time at which correlated energy falls to a fixed fraction of total energy (Ramanathan et al., 2019; Ramanathan & Satyanarayana, 2019, 2021). This paper investig‐ ates whether the same formalism transfers to financial markets. We show that it does not transfer directly: financial return/price-increment fields are empirically conservative (Hurst-type nonconservation exponent H ≈ 0), which collapses the moment-scaling relationship (ξ(q) = qH − K(qη) + qK(η)) that the atmospheric derivation depends on, and removes the spatial dimension (and with it, the entire generalized-scale-invariance anisotropy apparatus — sphero-scale, aspect ratio, vertical stratification exponent) that the atmospheric formula’s lead-time dependence is built on. We therefore abandon the parametric route and construct the correlated and decorrel‐ ated structure functions directly and empirically, defining the predictability limit operationally as the lag at which they are equal, and — going further — treating the full gap between them as a function of lag as the object of interest rather than a single crossing time. Applied to a raw (untransformed) multi-asset universe spanning equities, commodities, crypto, rates, FX, and volatility, this reveals that the correlated fraction of the moment budget is bounded within an instrument-specific range across the entire 300-trading-day lag window tested — never reaching full correlation or full decorrelation, unlike the atmospheric picture’s terminal state. But the shape of that boundedness is not uniform, and is not uniformly unlike the atmosphere either: classifying instruments by how many times their correlated and decorrelated components swap dominance reveals three distinct regimes. A minority of instruments (Treasury bonds and a few sector ETFs) remain correlation-dominant for the entire year tested, never crossing into decorrel‐ ation at all. One instrument (VIX) shows, at typical (q=2) moment order, a single clean transition that closely resembles the atmospheric formalism’s own monotonic picture, just plateauing at a bound rather than reaching zero — though this resemblance disappears at higher moment order (q=4), where VIX’s extreme fluctuations show the same repeated-crossing behavior as everything else. The majority of equities and Bitcoin show that repeated-crossing behavior throughout: pre‐ dictability that comes and goes in discrete, recurring “pockets” at specific lags rather than decaying once and staying gone. A pocket at approximately 21–24 trading days recurs across most equities tested; a second pocket near 252 trading days (one calendar year) is prominent for SPY specifically, and coincides with the strongest validated-signal concentration independently found for SPY by the authors’ unrelated Conditional Probability of Exceedance (CPE) framework — a nonparametric methodology sharing no assumptions with the structure-function approach used here. We argue this cross-method convergence, together with the observed asset-class and moment-order-dependent heterogeneity in crossing behavior, supports treating the pocket struc‐ ture as a genuine, economically meaningful feature of market structure for the instruments that show it, rather than an artifact of either method or a universal law applying uniformly across all instruments.

title:
Allocative Gains, Welfare Losses? 
Polarizing Effects of Disclosing Greenness
affiliations: University of Rochester - Simon Business School, University of Rochester - Simon Business School and The Chinese University of Hong Kong Business School

detail.title:
Allocative Gains, Welfare Losses? 
Polarizing Effects of Disclosing Greenness
detail.abstract: We study how green disclosure shapes portfolios and green investment. Disclosure polarizes shareholders and greenness outcomes: green investors concentrate in green firms and push them to become greener, while brown firms are held by less-green investors and reduce greenness. Because brown firms typically have cheaper opportunities to increase greenness, this sorting reduces aggregate greenness and imposes an externality cost despite improving allocative efficiency. Disclosure alone is not always welfare-improving and is complementary to externality-correcting policies such as carbon pricing. Welfare-maximizing managers overdisclose because they internalize disclosure's allocative gain but not its externality cost; price-maximizing managers can deliver higher welfare.

title: Compression of the Variance Risk Premium: Demand Pressure or a Repricing of Variance Carry?
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Charlotte and University of North Carolina at Charlotte

detail.title: Compression of the Variance Risk Premium: Demand Pressure or a Repricing of Variance Carry?
detail.abstract: Systematic call-overwriting through option-based ETFs has grown into a large one-sided supply of short volatility, inviting a demand-pressure interpretation in which dealer inventory constraints compress compensation where the flow lands. We test this reading with an exact discrete-time decomposition of covered-call returns into passive equity, active equity, and delta-hedged short-call components, with the short call split further into gamma, vega, and residual channels and with explicit treatment of ETF cash distributions. The gamma channel is variance carry in realized form, and dividing it by ex-ante implied variance prices the carry in each market, at each strike, at each date. Across fifty strategies on SPY, QQQ, IWM, GLD, and TLT over 2010 through 2026, the price declines significantly on four of the five underlyings, spread across strikes and as strong on IWM, outside the overwrite footprint, as on the index leaders. Offsetting drift in the residual channel masks the decline in aggregate covered-call returns. A single level factor carries each surface, the five prices share a common component of half to three-fifths of their variation that survives detrending, and Treasury carry decouples and reprices upward in the 2022 through 2024 rates regime. The evidence rejects a strike-local demand-pressure channel and supports a broad repricing of variance carry, without excluding declining intermediation frictions within the equity complex.

title: The Architecture of Liquidity: Certainty and Immediacy in European Electronic Bond Markets
affiliations: Heriot-Watt University - Edinburgh Business School, Erasmus Research Institute of Management (ERIM), Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, School of Business and Economics, University of Oxford - Said Business School and Heriot-Watt University

detail.abstract: In electronic request-for-quote (RFQ) markets, liquidity is observed through both execution probability and time-to-trade, each shaped by market design. We show theoretically that price conditions these two margins jointly, but also that market architecture is fundamental to liquidity. Empirically, using MarketAxess data for European corporate bonds, we estimate a mixed cure model with residual inclusion to address endogenous price formation. Our findings indicate that price is an endogenous liquidity attribute and that RFQ design choices materially affect both execution likelihood and speed, with clear implications for structuring trades to achieve faster and more certain outcomes.

title: How Immigration Shapes Politics: Populism, Labor Movements, and Political Preferences in Brazil
affiliations: , Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) - Sao Paulo School of Economics and Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV)

detail.title: How Immigration Shapes Politics: Populism, Labor Movements, and Political Preferences in Brazil
detail.abstract: This paper examines how European immigration during the Age of Mass Migration (1886-1920) shaped long-run political preferences in Brazil. While existing research links the emergence of labor-based politics in Latin America to industrialization and urban working-class growth, we argue that earlier demographic changes induced by mass migration also played an important role. Using an instrumental-variable strategy that exploits the interaction between aggregate immigration inflows and the expansion of São Paulo's railway network, we show that municipalities with a larger share of European immigrants were more likely to support labor-oriented candidates during Brazil's democratic interregnum (1945-1964). We also show suggestive evidence that the political effects of immigration persisted after Brazil's return to democracy in 1985. The findings suggest that the consequences of mass migration extended beyond economic development and contributed to the long-run formation of local political preferences.

title: Wage Advantage and Selection of Indian Immigrants in the US
affiliations: Rutgers University, New Brunswick - Department of Economics

detail.title: Wage Advantage and Selection of Indian Immigrants in the US
detail.abstract: I study the wage gap between Indian immigrants in the United States and residents of India. Using data from the 2011 and 2021 American Community Surveys and India's Employment-Unemployment Survey (2011-12) and Periodic Labour Force Survey (2020-21), I adjust the wage density of residents of India to reflect the observable characteristics of Indian immigrants in the US applying the DiNardo, Fortin, and Lemieux (1995) reweighting method. I find that differences in skills explain 24 to 36 percent of the wage gap for males and 37 to 48 percent for females. This indicates a difference in skills selection between male and female migrants or selection into labor force participation.

title: Negotiating Clean Energy: Women’s Bargaining Power and the impact of energy transition subsidy
affiliations: ETH Zürich and ETH Zürich - CER-ETH - Center of Economic Research at ETH Zurich

detail.title: Negotiating Clean Energy: Women’s Bargaining Power and the impact of energy transition subsidy
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates India’s Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY), the world’s largest LPG subsidy program. Using a difference-in-difference approach with propensity score matching, we examine how intra-household decision-making and local fuel availability modulate policy effectiveness. Results show that PMUY increased LPG adoption, with impacts notably amplified in households where women have greater bargaining power but subdued in households with local fuel availability. These findings highlight that successful energy transitions depend on addressing intra-household decision-making and economic barriers. Our study provides critical insights for designing effective clean cooking interventions in developing countries.

title: Telework Adoption and Mobility-Related Carbon Emissions: Causal Evidence from France
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Savoie Mont Blanc, University of Savoy and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Telework Adoption and Mobility-Related Carbon Emissions: Causal Evidence from France
detail.abstract: Demand-side measures are increasingly recognized as an essential component of climate mitigation, yet credible causal evidence on their effectiveness remains limited. Teleworking is widely viewed as a promising ``Avoid'' strategy because it reduces the need for commuting, but its net environmental impact remains uncertain due to behavioural rebound effects and the non-random adoption of remote work. Using a unique two-period panel survey of 3,530 French workers observed before and after the widespread diffusion of teleworking, we estimate the causal effect of telework adoption on annual mobility-related greenhouse gas emissions. Identification relies on a doubly robust difference-in-differences estimator that combines outcome regression and propensity-score weighting to account for selective treatment adoption. We find that teleworking reduces annual mobility-related emissions by approximately 270-300 kgCO2e per treated worker. These reductions are driven almost entirely by lower commuting emissions, while additional non-work travel offsets only a small share of the initial gains. The estimated effects remain stable across alternative estimators and robustness checks. Our results provide causal evidence that teleworking constitutes an effective demand-side mitigation strategy for workers able to adopt it. At the same time, because teleworkable jobs remain concentrated among highly skilled occupations, the aggregate mitigation potential and distributional consequences of teleworking depend critically on its unequal feasibility across sectors of the labour market.

title: Cash Transfers and Local Prices

detail.title: Cash Transfers and Local Prices

keywords: cash transfers; local prices; inflation; general equilibrium; multilevel meta-analysis; robust variance estimation; publication bias. JEL codes: C12

detail.abstract: Cash transfers increase household purchasing power, but their effect on local prices depends on productive capacity, market integration, tradability, program saturation, and the speed at which supply can respond. This study presents a harmonized causal meta-analysis of 49 goods-price estimates nested within nine independent programs or experiments. The confirmatory estimand aggregates dependent outcomes within each program, incorporates an assumed within-study correlation, and applies restricted maximum likelihood with a modified Knapp-Hartung correction. The estimated average change in goods prices is 0.101 %, with a 95 % confidence interval from-0.030 % to 0.233 %. The result is nearly invariant to within-study correlations between 0 and 0.90. A three-level model that retains all 49 outcomes, estimates between-program and within-program heterogeneity, and uses CR2 small-sample inference yields a point estimate of-0.585 % and a 95 % interval from-2.274 % to 1.134 %. The wider interval shows that the precision of the aggregated estimate depends on an exceptionally informative price index and on compressing product-level heterogeneity. Egger, Begg, PET, PEESE, trim-and-fill, excess-significance tests, and selection models do not identify a systematic publication-bias pattern, although statistical power is limited with only nine independent clusters. A Bayesian model that jointly addresses dependence, heterogeneity, and outcome selection yields a median effect of 0.080 % and a 95 % credible interval from-0.645 % to 0.713 %. The evidence does not support generalized goodsprice inflation following cash transfers, but it remains compatible with larger responses in non-tradable services, perishable products, highly saturated interventions, and markets facing binding supply constraints.

title: Evidentiary Design and Cross-Border Monitoring in Frontier-AI Safety

detail.title: Evidentiary Design and Cross-Border Monitoring in Frontier-AI Safety
detail.abstract: This paper studies how evidentiary design mediates enforcement of minimum safety requirements in a two-country frontier-AI contest. Monitoring changes both the probability of an actionable evaluation and the precision of the resulting evidence. We show that cross-border information sharing can affect domestic AI safety non-monotonically, but the familiar single-test hump is not a robust policy prediction. Its shape depends on the legal rule used to aggregate adverse findings. Under an any-of-three-tests rule, independent and moderately correlated evaluations place domestic safety on a strictly declining path as foreign monitoring capacity expands. Under highly correlated testing, the smooth compliance continuation collapses: the developer problem becomes non-concave and fails global best-response validation, consistent with discrete or "bang-bang" adjustment rather than stable interior compliance. The central result is therefore institutional dependence. Pooling international evaluation capacity changes safety incentives only through the evidentiary rule, the dependence structure among tests, and the legal treatment of adverse findings. Full-dimensional equilibrium searches, unilateral-deviation checks, and appendix diagnostics support the reported monitoring equilibria. The quantitative exercises remain normalized and partially identified rather than predictive.

detail.abstract: This brief note presents a street-level translation of certain ideas in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) return decomposition and the biological dilution test applied to dynastic wealth transmission. By analyzing the multi-generational compounding of an average billionaire fortune held by an entirely passive beneficiary-modeled here as an ethically bred poodle-we demonstrate that the compound interest engine of the capital commons effortlessly outruns human reproduction and natural biological fragmentation. We argue that passive market returns (Beta in the sense of the return on the total stock market) represent a participation dividend generated by the nation's collective infrastructure, thus requiring a generational benchmark settlement to preserve a meritocratic republic, while active outperformance over a broad-based index of all the common stocks available ("Practical Alpha") should remain entirely exempt.

title: Optimal Dividend Policy under Global Warming
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Université de Rennes I and CREM

detail.title: Optimal Dividend Policy under Global Warming
detail.abstract: Global warming affects the payout policy of heat-sensitive firms by shortening their economic lifetime, thereby reducing the option value of retained cash and inducing earlier dividend distributions. A firm-specific heat-tolerance threshold determines when business activity ceases, translating the projected temperature trajectory into a finite operating horizon, and yielding a finite-horizon, time-inhomogeneous version of the classical De Finetti dividend problem. We characterize the optimal dividend policy analytically and complement the analysis with numerical solutions of the associated HJB quasi-variational inequality. The optimal dividend barrier declines over time and converges to zero as climate-induced business termination approaches, reflecting the progressive loss of the option value of retained cash. The barrier increases with business risk and decreases with the discount rate, while its response to expected cash-flow growth is non-monotonic. We also analyze a one-time irreversible adaptation investment, showing that adaptation may be value-enhancing and that an optimal adaptation effort exists under mild cost conditions. Finally, extending the model to stochastic temperature dynamics shows that the declining dividend barrier is not an artifact of deterministic warming trajectories. Unlike in the deterministic model, firms may optimally retain positive cash reserves for distribution at climate-induced business termination.

title: The Intent Gap: Artificial Intelligence, Prediction Markets, and the Collapse of Federal Manipulation Doctrine

detail.title: The Intent Gap: Artificial Intelligence, Prediction Markets, and the Collapse of Federal Manipulation Doctrine
detail.abstract: Prediction markets are now public infrastructure. Their prices are quoted in political analysis, cited by institutional investors, and used by policymakers as real-time probability signals for elections, economic events, and geopolitical crises. Documented wash trading exceeds twentyfive percent of volume on major platforms. AI trading systems-reinforcement learning agents, LLM-powered probability models, autonomous arbitrage bots-are proliferating in these markets. And the federal enforcement framework designed to protect market integrity cannot reach them, because every manipulation provision under the Commodity Exchange Act and federal securities laws requires proof of human intent that AI systems do not possess. This Article addresses that structural enforcement vacuum. It develops the first systematic taxonomy of AI manipulation risks specific to prediction markets-coordinated trading without communication, information asymmetry exploitation, and emergent manipulative behavior-and demonstrates that each defeats every existing doctrine at the intent element. It proposes upstream scienter: a liability framework that relocates the legally relevant intent inquiry from the moment of manipulation to the design and deployment decisions that made manipulation foreseeable. The framework includes a three-part liability test, a tiered safeguard structure calibrated to AI system risk, a compliance safe harbor, and a complete model rule suitable for CFTC adoption. It operates coherently across the SEC/CFTC jurisdictional divide. The analysis also identifies a problem that extends far beyond financial regulation: every intent-based legal doctrine-criminal mens rea, antitrust conspiracy, tort negligence-faces the same structural failure when AI agents replace human actors. Prediction market manipulation is the leading edge.

title: A Composite Multi-Dimensional Risk-Scoring Framework for Aerospace Supply Chains: Evidence from the Boeing 787 Program

detail.title: A Composite Multi-Dimensional Risk-Scoring Framework for Aerospace Supply Chains: Evidence from the Boeing 787 Program
detail.abstract: Commercial aerospace supply chains exhibit a distinctive risk structure: a small number of sole-source suppliers, often geographically concentrated, produce structurally critical components whose replacement requires multi-year regulatory re-certification. Existing supply chain risk-management tools assess these exposures in organizational silos: geophysical hazard, supplier financial health, export-control exposure, and logistics disruption are each analyzed by different functions using incommensurable metrics. This paper develops a composite, multi-dimensional risk-scoring framework that integrates nine risk dimensions into a single program-level index, and applies it to the Boeing 787 Dreamliner. Using a hand-constructed dataset of 28 suppliers, 31 geocoded production sites, 19 program dependencies, and 8 documented disruption events assembled from primary sources (SEC filings, FAA airworthiness directives, USGS and Japan Cabinet Office seismic hazard assessments, and OFAC sanctions data), the framework produces a Q1 2026 composite score of 65/100 (high risk) for the 787 program. The analysis surfaces two findings not visible to single-dimension methods: (1) five sole-source Tier 1 suppliers operate primary facilities within a single probabilistic seismic rupture zone (Nankai Trough, 70-80% probability of a M8+ event within 30 years), creating a correlated failure mode with an estimated 2-3 year recovery horizon; and (2) the aircraft's bleedless electrical architecture embeds a rare-earth-element processing dependency on a single country (China, 85-98% of relevant Nd/Dy processing) across more than 100 permanent-magnet motor systems, a dependency invisible at the commodity-tariff level of analysis. The framework demonstrates that cross-referencing geophysical, regulatory, financial, and material-chain data at the program level reveals concentrated, correlated exposures that sole-source registries and supplier self-reporting structurally understate. Implications for aerospace industrial-base policy and program-level risk monitoring are discussed.

detail.abstract: This article examines how legal and historical categories determine whose claims become visible in Palestine and Israel. It focuses on a recurrent argumentative move in which a limited fact, such as historical attachment, refuge, land purchase, military victory, or the conduct of political leaders, is treated as if it resolved the separate questions of sovereignty, property, return, or civilian rights. Drawing on Mandate records, legal instruments, Palestinian and Israeli or Jewish historiography, minority-community studies, and structured testing of counter-arguments, the article develops the Broken Kinship and Exclusive Sovereignty framework. Broken Kinship describes the transformation of overlapping local relations and sacred geographies into inherited civilisational opposition. Exclusive Sovereignty describes the institutional process through which one community’s memory, vulnerability, sacred attachment, or demographic project acquires superior constitutional and territorial priority. The article examines asymmetrical recognition under the Balfour Declaration and the Mandate, the displacement and non-return regime formed around 1948, post-1948 property and nationality laws, and later constitutional arrangements. It also develops the concepts of transferred cost, collective forfeiture, and presumed counterfactual complicity. The central normative claim is that Jewish security and Palestinian freedom must be made institutionally compatible rather than one being achieved through the erasure of the other.

detail.title: Consensus Change Standards: A Legal and Technical Framework for Bitcoin Protocol Governance
