detail.abstract:
Bitcoin has no formal process for evaluating proposed changes to its consensus rules. The Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP) system provides a way to propose changes, but sets no minimum standards a proposal must meet before the community considers activation. There are no required review periods, no mandatory code audit standards, no agreed-upon activation thresholds, no chain split risk assessment methodology, and no framework for evaluating the legal and economic consequences of a failed activation.

This absence of standards has produced predictable results. The block size wars of 2015-2017 consumed years of developer time, fractured the community, and produced a contentious hard fork. The SegWit activation is widely credited to the threat of a novel User Activated Soft Fork (UASF) - BIP-148 - breaking the deadlock that had persisted after BIP-9 signaling failed to reach its 95% threshold over the preceding eight months. More recently, BIP-110 - a proposed temporary soft fork to restrict arbitrary data in Bitcoin transactions - was released with an activation client that multiple developers reported contained significant bugs. Its deployment paired that client with a 55% activation threshold far below any successful modern deployment and a six-week timeline from initial proposal to activation client - shorter than the review period of every modern successful soft fork, for SegWit and Taproot by more than an order of magnitude. The activation client was first distributed alongside stable Knots releases on node management platforms with no risk disclosure or visual differentiation, then bundled into the default release stream itself - so that the routine upgrade ladder terminates in a confirmation dialog that presents consensus alteration as the path forward.

This paper proposes a framework for evaluating Bitcoin consensus change proposals, and it begins from a claim these debates rarely confront: the catastrophic failure mode of a consensus change - a persistent chain split - has a computable risk profile, and that risk depends almost entirely on one variable, the share of hashrate that will enforce the new rules at activation. Section 3 models it and shows it is not a smooth function of that share but a cliff: at 55% enforcement the chance of a six-block reorganization during activation is roughly thirty percent; by 90% or above it is effectively zero, five to seven orders of magnitude lower. Much of the governance argument turns out to be a fight over a number - one the standard mathematics of chain-race security already supplies, but that the activation debate has almost never computed. The framework builds on that quantification, on the history of Bitcoin's prior consensus changes, on the maturity-gate principles the open-standards tradition has applied to protocol governance for thirty years, and on a legal analysis of the liabilities an inadequately reviewed activation creates. It is practical, concrete, and immediately applicable. It proposes no changes to Bitcoin's code; it proposes standards for the process by which such changes are evaluated, debated, and either adopted or rejected.

The author is a practicing litigator, solo Bitcoin miner, full node operator, and computer scientist - roles that carry their own operational stake in how block space is used. This framework is written from the intersection of those disciplines, and is deliberately limited to procedural standards so that its conclusions do not turn on the author's view of the underlying inscription debate. The problems it addresses - governance, liability, technical risk, and economic consequence - cannot be fully analyzed from any single perspective.

detail.abstract: Why do incumbent hegemons sometimes revise the very international orders they created? Classical theories of hegemonic stability and power transition typically attribute revisionism to dissatisfied rising powers or to shifts in ideology and preferences. Yet even while remaining system leaders, incumbent hegemons have sometimes revised the institutional and normative foundations of their own orders. This paper develops a formal theory of hegemonic revisionism grounded in variation in global dependence. We model international order as an institutional arrangement whose orientation can be strategically adjusted by competing superpowers. Non-superpower states affiliate based on both institutional compatibility and material dependence. When dependence on a superpower is high, the superpower can sustain participation while reproducing its historically embedded mode of authority. As dependence declines, however, maintaining coalition support requires reorienting the institutional terms of order provision. Revisionism thus emerges endogenously as a structural response to weakening leverage. The model identifies five equilibrium phases, partitioned by dependence thresholds, from unipolar dominance through bipolar rivalry to hegemonic reversal. It shows that challengers are most accommodating when their leverage is weakest, while incumbents revise the authoritative content of their orders only after dependence falls below a critical level-even if they remain materially dominant. By deriving the conditions for order revision within a formal framework, the paper advances hegemonic-order theory and reframes revisionism as structural phases in superpower competition life cycle.

detail.abstract: I examine whether investors perceive higher-priced stocks as riskier despite identical percentage price changes. Using survey evidence, the study investigates whether nominal stock prices influence decisions to sell during market downturns.  The findings suggest that investors exhibit non-proportional reasoning, attributing significance to nominal price movements rather than proportional changes.

title: A SPOT in the dark: using AI to assess financial stability risks
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB), European Central Bank (ECB), University of Marburg and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: A SPOT in the dark: using AI to assess financial stability risks
detail.abstract: Financial stability risks consist of two distinct components: vulnerabilities and possible trigger events. While there has been considerable progress regarding the measurement of vulnerabilities, the assessment of possible trigger events remains largely qualitative. To fill this gap, we employ Large Language Models to extract information about the Severity and Probability Of potential Trigger events (SPOT) from a large dataset of financial news articles over the period2005 – 2026. The SPOT indicator increases ahead of major historical trigger events, correctly identifies trigger sources, and helps to improve forward looking model estimates of downside risks to the economy. The results indicate that the use of AI-based signal extraction from text can be a promising avenue to improve the monitoring of financial stability risks.

detail.abstract: The Western Ghats, a UNESCO World Heritage biodiversity hotspot spanning roughly 1,600 km across six Indian states, has experienced a marked escalation in landslide frequency and severity over the past decade, culminating in high casualty events such as the 2024 Mundakkai-Chooralmala landslide in Wayanad, Kerala. Yet disaster governance in the region remains fragmented across state jurisdictions, each operating distinct hazard mapping protocols, regulatory regimes, and response mechanisms. This paper applies a systemic risk framework, integrating natural hazard drivers, socio-ecological vulnerability, and human exposure, to conduct a qualitative comparative policy analysis of landslide governance in Kerala, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu, the three Western Ghats states with the most developed institutional frameworks and the highest documented landslide incidence. Drawing on national hazard atlases, state disaster management authority reports, peer-reviewed geomorphological studies, and the National Disaster Management Authority's guidelines, the analysis identifies distinct state level vulnerability profiles: Kerala's high density settlement saturation on deeply weathered lateritic slopes, Karnataka's linear infrastructure stress along transit corridors compounded by an unresolved ecological zoning dispute, and Tamil Nadu's seasonal mass tourism exposure in the Nilgiris and Kodaikanal belts. An institutional assessment reveals structural enforcement deficits, cartographic resolution failures, and temporal gaps in bio-engineering interventions common across all three states despite their differing operational models. The paper concludes with targeted, scalable policy prescriptions, including statutory liability and independent geotechnical audit frameworks, blended finance vehicles for eco-relocation, LiDAR assisted micro zonation, and hybrid biostructural stabilization protocols, and argues for a unified pan regional governance model that treats the Western Ghats as a single ecological unit rather than a set of fragmented administrative territories.

title: Behavioural Risk in Governance: The Missing Link Between Governance Structures and Governance Outcomes

detail.title: Behavioural Risk in Governance: The Missing Link Between Governance Structures and Governance Outcomes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract:
This paper argues that behavioural risk — the risk that governance judgement is systematically influenced by psychological, social, and organisational conditions in ways inconsistent with an organisation's purpose, responsibilities, or objectives — is the most significant unnamed risk category in contemporary governance. Conventional governance frameworks focus on structures, policies and compliance, but structurally sound governance systems continue to produce poor outcomes because the behavioural conditions shaping judgement inside them are neither identified nor governed. The paper identifies nine behavioural drivers — pressure, incentives, power, fear, fatigue, loyalty, ego, cognitive bias, and identity–purpose inversion — and two governing mechanisms, behavioural capture and moral licensing, through which behavioural risk becomes embedded and normalised within governance systems. It introduces Behavioural Information Distortion to explain how organisational reality becomes filtered before it reaches the board, and the Decision Integrity Model to demonstrate precisely where behavioural risk interferes with governance — from organisational purpose, through judgement, decision and action, to organisational outcomes.

These concepts are examined against five major governance failures — the NASA Challenger disaster, the Volkswagen emissions scandal, the Boeing 737 MAX crashes, the Robodebt scheme, and the PwC Australia tax leaks — before setting out practical governance actions by role (boards, chairs, CEOs, executive teams, people leaders, internal audit and risk committees) and a call for systemic recognition of behavioural risk by regulators, governance codes, professional bodies, risk standards and academia.

title: The Market After God: Adam Smith and the Forgotten Problem of Evil

detail.title: The Market After God: Adam Smith and the Forgotten Problem of Evil
detail.abstract: The Adam Smith Problem has been misdescribed. The familiar question asks whether the sympathy of The Theory of Moral Sentiments can be reconciled with the self-interest of The Wealth of Nations; the consensus has answered that it can. This paper argues that the reconciliation answered the wrong question. The Moral Sentiments poses and answers a theodicy: fortune’s sway over merit, the deception that drives industry and the emptiness of greatness are justified as instruments of a benevolent systemic design. The Wealth of Nations presupposes the harmony conclusion without reopening the question that licensed it. The discontinuity between the books is therefore not a contradiction of motives but the seam of an asymmetric survival: a providential structure of harmony persisted in economic thought after the problem of evil ceased to be asked within the genre. The paper defends this redescription against Blumenberg’s objection to secularization theses and traces the structure’s afterlife from Mandeville to welfare economics.

detail.abstract: In Guilbeau v. BEPCO, L.P., a landowner filed suit seeking remediation of contamination arising from oil and gas activities prior to his purchase of the property. The landowner previously had filed a suit seeking a clean-up based on the defendants’ obligations under the Louisiana Mineral Code. That earlier suit was dismissed based on the subsequent purchaser doctrine. The subsequent purchaser doctrine states that private claims for damages to property belong to the person who owned the property at the time of the damages and absent that person’s assignment of his claims to a subsequent purchaser of the property, the subsequent purchaser does not have a claim against the person who caused the damages. In the current suit, the landowner seeks injunctive relief—in particular, an order requiring a remediation—in a citizen suit brought pursuant to Louisiana Revised Statutes 30:14 and 30:16.

title: Compensated to Completion, Stalled at Initiation: Fiscal Capacity, Depopulation, and Bridge Maintenance Across Japan’s Two National Inspection Rounds

detail.abstract: Japan inspects every road bridge on a five-year cycle, and the resulting grades feed a policy narrative in which poor, shrinking municipalities let their bridges decay. The evidence behind that narrative is cross-sectional, and it points support at the wrong margin. We link records across the first (FY2014-2018) and second (FY2019-2023) statutory inspection rounds into a condition transition panel of 655,353 bridges. Money is not the binding constraint. Within prefectures, repair completion shows no municipal fiscal gradient (+0.003, s.e. 0.032), consistent with a subsidy formula that raises the national cost share as fiscal capacity falls. Initiation is the binding margin. A flagged bridge in a one-standard-deviation poorer municipality carries about 15% higher odds of having no work started. That estimate strengthens under inspection-cohort controls and vanishes for nationally managed bridges in the same areas. The familiar raw gradient (47.3% of flagged bridges unrestored in the poorest municipal quartile against 36.7% in the richest) is a between-prefecture composition. Within prefectures, poorer municipalities keep pace on completing repairs and on removals. The shortfall is confined to starting work, and measured staffing and contractor densities do not explain it. Unrestored bridges cluster regionally, but neighborhood fiscal terms fail a placebo test and should not be read as spillovers. The panel reproduces official aggregates at three points, two of them independent of our outcome measures, including the government's 4% untreateddeterioration figure (ours: 4.12%). Equalizing money does not equalize the capacity to begin: maintenance support should target project initiation, not cost shares.

title: Exploring Pathways and Modelling for Net-zero Energy Transitions: A Case Study in the City of Winterthur

detail.title: Exploring Pathways and Modelling for Net-zero Energy Transitions: A Case Study in the City of Winterthur
detail.abstract: This study applies a participatory Dynamic Bayesian Network to support urban energy transition planning in Winterthur, Switzerland, with the objective of reaching net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2040. The model compares three policy pathways: Business-as-Usual, Klima Cockpit Portal, and Klima Cockpit Portal ++, the latter representing a "bend the curve harder" pathway with enhanced co-created mobility interventions. Results reveal substantial differences between the pathways, with the KCP++ scenario increasing the probability of achieving low-emission outcomes to 61%. Additionally, the DBN evolves structurally over time, capturing increasing interdependencies among behavioural, infrastructural, and technological nodes. Behavioural drivers also vary temporally: Information Facilities are most influential in the short term, Perceived Viability dominates the mid-term, and Environmental Norms prevail in the long term. Finally, the model functions not only as a predictive tool but as a belief-based representation of stakeholder perspectives, embedding local knowledge into dynamic, policy-relevant analysis

title: Assessing the Risk of Commercial Bank Disintermediation in a Retail CBDC Ecosystem

detail.title: Assessing the Risk of Commercial Bank Disintermediation in a Retail CBDC Ecosystem
detail.abstract:
The introduction of Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) represents a profound paradigm shift in sovereign monetary architecture. By providing retail consumers with a direct, risk-free digital alternative to private commercial bank deposits, central banks introduce a powerful vector of competition into the financial sector. This paper examines the structural mechanics of bank disintermediation resulting from retail CBDC adoption. Through the lens of the Disintermediation Hypothesis and the Monopsony Discipline Hypothesis, we model how the migration of core retail deposits to central bank digital wallets alters the funding mix of commercial banking institutions. 

Our findings indicate that during macroeconomic expansions, the operational conveniences and rewards offered by commercial institutions may stabilize deposit bases. However, during systemic macroeconomic shocks, a rapid, rational "flight to safety" toward zero-credit-risk sovereign liabilities threatens commercial bank liquidity. This contraction in low-cost funding drives up the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) for banks, structurally elevating interest rates on private credit instruments such as mortgages and commercial loans. Ultimately, this paper argues that structural guardrails, such as tiered interest rates and quantitative holding caps, are essential to mitigating systemic disintermediation and preserving the credit-generation capacity of the fractional-reserve banking system.

title: The CFA Franc Zone: Euro Peg and Nominal Effective Exchange Rate Volatility in WAEMU and CEMAC

detail.title: The CFA Franc Zone: Euro Peg and Nominal Effective Exchange Rate Volatility in WAEMU and CEMAC
detail.abstract: The CFA franc arrangements are routinely described as stable because the two CFA francs maintain a fixed parity against the euro. This paper asks what exactly is stabilized once the evolving external exposure of WAEMU and CEMAC is taken into account. It distinguishes bilateral nominal stability, domestic price stability, nominal and real effective exchange-rate stability, financial stability, and institutional credibility, while empirically focusing on one dimension: nominal effective exchange-rate (NEER) volatility. Ngouana (2012) showed for WAEMU that the NEER was roughly twice as volatile under the euro peg as under a counterfactual Special Drawing Rights (SDR) peg between 2001 and 2010. This paper conducts an audited replication using a harmonized month-end exchange-rate convention, extends the analysis through 2024, and applies the same framework to CEMAC. The expanded partner universe is selected empirically and confidence intervals are obtained from a paired circular moving-block bootstrap. Over 2001-2024, the euro/SDR standard-deviation ratio equals 2.00 for WAEMU and 3.05 for CEMAC. A dual-convention exercise shows that switching from monthly averages to month-end observations changes the magnitude of the ratio by up to 23 percent across zones and windows, without ever pushing it below one. The result also survives stress tests for dominant-dollar invoicing and for lagged, predetermined, and fixed trade weights. These exercises remain partial-equilibrium accounting counterfactuals; they do not identify the equilibrium consequences of adopting another regime. The findings therefore do not identify an optimal anchor. They establish that the conventional description of the CFA franc as "stable" refers primarily to bilateral nominal stability against the euro and cannot, without qualification, be extended to the currency's multilateral external position. » renvoie d'abord à sa stabilité nominale bilatérale contre l'euro et ne peut, sans qualification, être étendue à sa position extérieure multilatérale. title: Threshold endogeneity in vector autoregressions: reassessing monetary state dependence
affiliations: Athens University of Economics and Business, European Central Bank (ECB) and Athens University of Economics and Business - Department of Economics

detail.title: Threshold endogeneity in vector autoregressions: reassessing monetary state dependence
detail.abstract: We develop an endogenous threshold VAR that addresses contemporaneous dependence between the threshold variable and reduced-form innovations— a pervasive issue when regime indicators are jointly determined with system dynamics. A regime-specific copula-based control function removes this dependence instrument-free, without parametric assumptions on the threshold’s marginal distribution, while preserving the linear regime-wise least-squares structure. We characterize the resulting misspecification through excess sensitivity and excess propagation errors in impulse responses, clarify structural and proxy-SVAR identification under endogenous regimes, and establish conditions under which Chan-type threshold asymptotics remain valid with generated controls. A Hermite sieve extension accommodates tail-dependent and asymmetric dependence. Monte Carlo evidence documents large distortions from ignoring endogeneity. Applied to monetary transmission, the framework avoids the price and persistence puzzles displayed by the linear VAR, delivers regime-dependent sacrifice ratios, and aligns estimated regimes with historical inflation episodes.

title: Credit Scoring Using Machine Learning Techniques: A Comparative and Explainable Evaluation of Five Classifiers on Imbalanced Credit-Card Data
affiliations: University of Johannesburg, Tshwane University of Technology - Digital Transformation Portfolio and University of Johannesburg

detail.title: Credit Scoring Using Machine Learning Techniques: A Comparative and Explainable Evaluation of Five Classifiers on Imbalanced Credit-Card Data
detail.abstract: Credit scoring underpins risk management at banks and other lenders, yet credit datasets are highly imbalanced, and the most accurate machine learning models are often the least transparent. This paper systematically compares five supervised classifiers — logistic regression (LR), decision tree (DT), random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM) and k-nearest neighbours (KNN) — for default prediction on a public credit-card dataset of 30,000 accounts (22% defaulters), evaluated on a held-out test set using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC/AUC and the Gini coefficient. Random forest achieved the strongest discrimination (accuracy 81%, AUC 0.74, Gini 0.50); SVM attained the highest accuracy (82%) but detected only 29% of defaulters; and the single decision tree was weakest (AUC 0.59) despite the highest defaulter recall. A Friedman test confirmed that the differences are statistically significant at the 95% level. Feature-importance analysis consistently identified recent repayment status, credit limit and age as the dominant predictors, with demographic attributes contributing little, and LIME rendered individual predictions transparent. A fully seeded, reproducible extension then adds an XGBoost benchmark — statistically indistinguishable from the random forest (paired bootstrap p = 0.20), with both significantly exceeding logistic regression (ΔAUC ≈ 0.05, p < 0.001) — bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for all AUCs, probability-calibration assessment (XGBoost best calibrated, Brier 0.145), and cost-sensitive threshold optimisation, which at a 5:1 false-negative-to-false-positive cost ratio raises random-forest defaulter recall from 54% to 78% while reducing expected misclassification cost by 8%. The findings quantify the trade-offs among predictive power, minority-class sensitivity, calibration and interpretability, and offer lenders — including in African credit markets governed by responsible-lending regulation — practical guidance on aligning model selection and threshold policy with institutional risk appetite.

title: Deconstructing the Risk-free Rate in Emerging Markets: Methodologies and Viability for Cost of Equity Calculations

detail.title: Deconstructing the Risk-free Rate in Emerging Markets: Methodologies and Viability for Cost of Equity Calculations
detail.abstract: In corporate finance and valuation, we often operate under the presumption that the risk-free rate is a given, easily observable input, focusing the bulk of our attention on estimating firm-specific risk parameters and equity risk premiums. But is the risk-free rate truly that simple to obtain? While standard practice defaults to utilizing local 10-year government bond yields, this foundational assumption completely breaks down in emerging markets due to embedded sovereign default risk. This paper deconstructs the risk-free rate by evaluating three practical methodologies designed to isolate the zero-default baseline: the Sovereign Credit Rating approach, the Net Credit Default Swap (CDS) framework, and the Dollar-Denominated bond spread method. Our analysis reveals that relying on raw, unadjusted local yields introduces a structural upward bias that severely distorts the Cost of Equity (𝑲𝒆), whereas systematically stripping out the sovereign default spread yields a stable, mathematically consistent baseline. We conclude that executing currency-consistent, default-adjusted refinements is non-negotiable for preserving structural integrity and preventing critical valuation errors in developing economies.

detail.title: Mercury exposure and antioxidant gene expression in Neotropical invertivorous birds from a gold-mining region in Chocó, Colombia
detail.abstract: The Chocó Department in Colombia contains the country's highest concentration of on-land alluvial gold mining, approximately 78% of which is illegal, and relies on mercury (Hg) amalgamation. Much of this activity occurs within remote tropical forests of the Chocó biogeographic region, a global biodiversity hotspot with exceptional levels of avian endemism. Although Hg contamination poses a recognized threat to wildlife, its molecular effects on free-living tropical birds remain poorly understood. Here, we evaluated the relationship between feather total mercury (THg) concentrations and the relative expression of four oxidative stress-related genes (GPX1, GPX3, GSTM3, and TrxR1) in invertivorous birds from the families Hirundinidae, Thamnophilidae, and Troglodytidae inhabiting a gold-mining area of the Chocó tropical forest. Among the genes analyzed, TrxR1 was the only whose expression was significantly associated with feather THg concentration, and its expression differed significantly among avian families. These findings provide the first evidence that environmental Hg exposure is associated with altered antioxidant gene expression in wild Neotropical birds and identify TrxR1 as a promising non-lethal biomarker of Hg exposure and early biological effects. Future studies integrating gene expression, Hg toxicokinetic, selenium status, and oxidative damage biomarkers will improve our understanding of species-specific susceptibility and strengthen biomonitoring and conservation efforts in Hg-contamined tropical ecosystems.

title: Predictive Modeling of Asset Growth and Liquidity Risk in Umurenge SACCOs Using Machine Learning Techniques
affiliations: University of Rwanda - Kigali Campus, University of Rwanda - African Centre of Excellence in Internet of Things and University of Rwanda - Department of Economics

detail.title: Predictive Modeling of Asset Growth and Liquidity Risk in Umurenge SACCOs Using Machine Learning Techniques

keywords.keywords: Machine learningAsset growth predictionLiquidity risk assessmentUmurenge SACCOsFinancial inclusionPredictive analyticsEnsemble learningRwanda

detail.abstract: This study examines the application of machine learning techniques to predict asset growth patterns and evaluate liquidity risk in Umurenge Savings and Credit Cooperatives (SACCOs) in Rwanda. Given the pivotal role of SACCOs in fostering financial in-clusion and local economic development, understanding the interaction between asset expansion and liquidity stability is essential for sustainable financial management. Using historical financial and operational data, multiple predictive models are developed and comparatively assessed to classify asset growth behaviors and associated liquidity risk levels. A range of supervised learning algorithms, including tree based models, ensemble approaches, and neural networks, is applied to key financial indicators such as deposits, loan portfolios, repayment performance, and liquidity reserves. Model performance is evaluated using standard metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC, G-mean, balanced accuracy, and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC). The results demonstrate that ensemble based models outperform conventional approaches, with the Extra Trees classifier achieving the highest performance (98.75 % accuracy, AUC = 0.9993, MCC = 0.9813). Confusion matrix analysis indicates high classifica-tion accuracy, with minor misclassifications concentrated in the controlled growth category due to its intermediate characteristics. Overall, the findings highlight the effectiveness of machine learning in capturing complex financial dynamics and supporting data driven early warning systems for enhanced decision making and sustainability in SACCOs. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents one of the earliest empirical contributions to predictive modeling of asset growth and liquidity risk in Umurenge SACCOs using machine learning techniques in Rwanda.

title: Evaluating Farmers’ Perceptions and Utilisation of Agrometeorological Services in Manyoni District, Tanzania
affiliations: Tanzania Meteorological Authority and University of Dar es Salaam

detail.title: Evaluating Farmers’ Perceptions and Utilisation of Agrometeorological Services in Manyoni District, Tanzania
detail.abstract: Provision of timely and reliable agrometeorological information is essential for enhancing climate change adaptation and improving agricultural productivity among smallholder farmers. However, limited understanding of farmers’ perceptions and utilisation of agrometeorological services constrains their effective application in farming activities. This study assessed farmers’ perceptions and utilisation of agrometeorological services in Manyoni District, Tanzania. Specifically, it identified available services, examined farmers’ perceptions of the reliability and accuracy of agrometeorological information, and evaluated its applicability in crop selection and pest management. A case study design employing both quantitative and qualitative approaches was used. Data were collected through household surveys, focus group discussions, key informant interviews, and field observations from 99 households selected using Yamane’s formula. Quantitative data were analysed using SPSS version 20 and Microsoft Excel, while qualitative data were analysed through content analysis. The findings revealed that seasonal weather forecasts, daily forecasts, early warning information, and advisory services were the major agrometeorological services available. Farmers’ perceptions differed significantly between Chikuyu and Makanda villages (χ² = 17.92, p < 0.001), with higher trust reported in Chikuyu due to clearer communication and improved dissemination systems. Agrometeorological services were applied in determining planting time, crop rotation and diversification, pest and disease management, and harvesting decisions. The study concludes that clear communication, local relevance, and consistency with farmers’ experiences enhance trust and utilisation of agrometeorological information. Strengthening dissemination systems and communication strategies could improve the effective use of these services among smallholder farmers.

title: No Ceiling, No Denominator, No Exit: Artificial Intelligence and the Architecture of American Energy Law

detail.title: No Ceiling, No Denominator, No Exit: Artificial Intelligence and the Architecture of American Energy Law
detail.abstract: For half a century the United States has run a federal program to make machines use less energy. It has never once run a program to make the country use less energy. The Energy Policy and Conservation Act regulates efficiency, which is a ratio, and the statute contains no authority to set a ceiling on aggregate consumption. That distinction was tolerable while the ratio and the total moved together. Artificial intelligence has pulled them apart. Google reports that the energy required to answer a median Gemini text prompt fell by a factor of 33 in twelve months, and reports in the same year that its electricity demand rose 37 percent, the largest annual increase in the company's history. This Article argues that the gap is structural, and that it appears three times. First, coverage. The gate through which a new product enters the consumer program at 42 U.S.C. § 6292(b)(1)(B) is a fraction with households in the denominator, and the standard-setting gate at § 6295(l)(1) is metered the same way, down to an aggregate figure that is expressly an aggregate of household use. When the Department of Energy proposed in 2013 to cover computer servers, it satisfied the statutory test by computing the energy used by servers in houses. Industry objected that the agency lacked authority over the commercial units, the agency withdrew the determination, and no coverage determination for servers exists today. The same agency, reading a 1978 definition, built the regulatory category of computer room air conditioner out of statutory text that never named it, and now sets mandatory efficiency floors on the machine that cools the data center while setting nothing on the machines inside it. Second, disclosure. Google publishes watt-hours per prompt and withholds the prompt count it used as the divisor, and its chief scientist has said on the record that the company is not comfortable revealing that number. OpenAI has released no model-specific energy data since 2020. The aggregate is therefore not merely unregulated; it is uncomputable by anyone outside the firms. Third, allocation. Compute is financed by risk capital that shareholders bear, and the grid that serves it is financed by a rate base that households cannot leave. The Article makes three contributions. It identifies the household denominator as the mechanism of EPCA's blindness rather than treating the absence of AI standards as agency inattention. It shows that the withheld denominator in corporate environmental disclosure reproduces the statute's own epistemic structure, so that the regime and the firm converge on publishing the quotient and suppressing the total. And it locates the resulting cost-allocation question in existing doctrine, where the term of art means what the Seventh Circuit says it means and not what the industry hears.

title: Below the Floor: Generative AI Adoption in Organizations without an Ostensive Infrastructure
affiliations: University of Wollongong

detail.title: Below the Floor: Generative AI Adoption in Organizations without an Ostensive Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Research on generative AI (GenAI) adoption in organizations, spanning technology-organizationenvironment models, human-centered tailoring approaches, and emerging theories of shadow AI use, shares an unstated assumption: that organizations possess a minimum layer of formal process infrastructure, whether documented procedures, defined roles, or a governance apparatus, against which individual technology use can be evaluated, tailored, or concealed. Many adopting organizations, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), do not meet this condition. We introduce the construct of ostensive thinness, drawing on Feldman and Pentland's (2003) distinction between the ostensive and performative aspects of organizational routines, to theorize what happens when GenAI is adopted in settings that lack a developed ostensive layer. We argue that under ostensive thinness, GenAI use remains performative only: individual, situated, and improvised, without a stable structural referent against which that use can be evaluated, generalized, or retained as organizational capability. We develop four propositions concerning gated rather than additive fit, the reframing of shadow use as unaccounted use, and a cognitive-style boundary condition, and we differentiate the resulting framework from adjacent theories of technologyorganization-environment fit, human-AI interaction tailoring, and shadow user innovation. We close with a research agenda and practical implications for resource-constrained organizations navigating GenAI adoption without formal implementation infrastructure.

title: Visible Waste, Invisible Inequality: Mapping Sanitation Disparities from Street View Imagery in Nairobi
affiliations: University College London, University College London - The Bartlett Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis, University College London, African Population and Health Research Center (APHRC), George Washington University - Department of Geography, University of Glasgow and University College London

detail.title: Visible Waste, Invisible Inequality: Mapping Sanitation Disparities from Street View Imagery in Nairobi
detail.abstract: Visible accumulation of unmanaged solid waste is a persistent feature of rapidly urbanising cities, yet its fine-grained spatial distribution remains poorly measured due to incomplete and inconsistent sanitation data, particularly in the Global South. This study presents the spatial distribution of visible waste accumulation as an indicator of sanitation inequality using street view imagery across Nairobi, Kenya. Applying a two-stage pipeline that combines computer vision (CV) and a vision-language model (VLM) on 306,420 images, we identified 3,236 verified waste-pile locations with high detection precision (94.70%). Spatial analysis revealed pronounced and statistically significant clustering, forming 32 persistent hotspots across the city. Waste exposure is strongly uneven: mapped urban poor settlement areas occupy only 2.86% of Nairobi's land area, yet contain 19.34% of all detections, with waste density more than 8 times higher than in other areas. Distance-decay modelling further showed that the probability of encountering visible waste declines sharply within 200-300 m of settlement boundaries, indicating a concentrated environmental burden near urban poor communities. These findings show that street view imagery can be transformed into finegrained spatial indicators of sanitation inequality. The resulting maps reveal systematic spatial disparities in visible waste exposure that are consistent with unequal waste-management conditions often overlooked by conventional administrative data. The approach offers a scalable framework for monitoring environmental exposure, identifying service gaps, and supporting more equitable urban infrastructure planning in data-scarce contexts.

title: Portfolio Margining Using PCA Latent Factors
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Portfolio Margining Using PCA Latent Factors
detail.abstract: Filtered historical simulation (FHS) is a simple and popular margin methodat central counterparties. However, FHS does not address time-varyingcorrelation. We propose an alternative that filters returns using latent riskfactors derived from principal component analysis (PCA). We compare itsperformance with FHS and a parametric model, both in simulations and withequity portfolios during COVID-19. The method performs well overall, andmuch better when addressing large changes in correlation. Its combinationof good coverage, appropriate stability, and low computational costs suggestthe PCA model could provide a viable margin method, even though someportfolios can be challenging.

title: Commodity Market Connectedness Across Crises: Evidence from Long Memory, Fractal Connectivity, and Directional Information Flow​
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Bhubaneswar, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Balamand, University of Balamand and Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Bhubaneswar

detail.title: Commodity Market Connectedness Across Crises: Evidence from Long Memory, Fractal Connectivity, and Directional Information Flow​
detail.abstract: Commodity markets play a central role in inflation transmission, portfolio allocation, hedging, and systemic risk management, yet the structure of their interdependence is unlikely to remain stable across crisis and recovery regimes. This study investigates the time-varying persistence, fractal connectedness, and directional information transmission among 23 major commodity futures over 1991–2025, covering eight financial, pandemic, geopolitical, and recovery episodes. We integrate long-memory estimation and testing, rolling Hurst analysis, fractal connectivity measures, and Wavelet Quantile Transfer Entropy to examine both low-frequency co-movement and scale-dependent, quantile-specific spillovers. The results show that long memory is episodic rather than uniform and tends to weaken during periods of severe market stress, most notably during the Russia–Ukraine war. Fractal connectivity is strongly regime-dependent, reaching its highest levels during the subprime and sovereign debt crises, while declining during calmer and post-crisis recovery phases. Directional information transmission is asymmetric, concentrated mainly at 16–32-day horizons, and characterised by rotating leadership across commodity groups and regimes. These findings demonstrate that commodity-market connectedness is structurally persistent but highly state-contingent, with important implications for diversification, hedging, crisis monitoring, and policy assessment. By combining persistence, fractal dependence, and quantile-based directional spillovers within a unified multi-crisis framework, the paper contributes to the commodity finance literature by offering a richer account of how shocks propagate across commodity futures markets as macro-financial conditions change.

title: Loyal to a Fault? Measuring Whether LLMs Produce Biased Responses Favoring their Parent Companies

detail.title: Loyal to a Fault? Measuring Whether LLMs Produce Biased Responses Favoring their Parent Companies

publicationDetails.detailsText: Accepted for publication in volume 28 of the Tulane Journal of Technology & Intellectual Property Law (forthcoming 2026).

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to exhibit numerous biasespolitical, racial, gender, and religious-inherited from the human-generated data on which they are trained. This Article examines a distinct and previously unmeasured category: "self-interest bias," the tendency of an LLM to provide responses that favor the commercial, reputational, or legal interests of the model or its parent company. Given the billions of dollars invested in these models, the litigation and regulatory exposure their parent companies face, and the documented tendency of AI systems to act self-preservingly in testing environments, one might expect LLMs to shade their responses in their own interest and the interest of their parent company. To test this hypothesis, ten categories of inquiries were posed to the four leading LLMs-ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grokcovering matters that directly implicate each model's self-interest, including summaries of litigation involving parent companies (Penske v. Google and Musk v. OpenAI), stock performance predictions, and rankings of the models' own accuracy, objectivity, and value. The results are striking: across twenty-six measurements, there is no evidence of self-interest bias, and responses against a model's self-interest were as common as those favoring it. This Article situates the findings within the literature on LLM bias, offers explanations for the counterintuitive result-including asymmetric reputational risk and alignment training-and considers implications for AI regulation, disclosure mandates, legal liability, and the growing use of LLMs by judges and attorneys. Because model behavior is not static, the finding warrants continued vigilance, not complacency. The novel framework provided in this Article will hopefully serve as a valuable tool in these future efforts.

title: Vega Exposure (VEX): Dealer Inventory and Volatility Suppression in the VIX Options Complex
affiliations: CrossVol Research

detail.title: Vega Exposure (VEX): Dealer Inventory and Volatility Suppression in the VIX Options Complex
detail.abstract: On a quiet trading day the spot VIX and the volatility of the VIX tell opposite stories: the level says near-term equity risk is subdued, while the price of convexity in VIX options says participants are paying richly to be protected if it is not. We resolve the contradiction through the inventory that option dealers are forced to warehouse. We name the metric Vega Exposure (VEX) and apply it, through a transparent and reproducible estimator, to the aggregate open interest of the VIX options complex on a single date, 15 July 2026. The book is 2.64 times more heavily weighted to calls than to puts; the dealer community is short vega by roughly 5.4 million units and, on gamma, marginally long and close to neutral. We read this as a conditionally stable regime and organize it with a suppressionsqueeze taxonomy: short vega pays dealers to sell volatility rallies and hold realized volatility down, but a near-neutral gamma on a call-heavy book flips a seller of rallies into a forced buyer once the move is large enough. The evidence is one cross-section, and we are explicit about what a snapshot cannot establish. The natural extension, which we flag rather than attempt, is to build VEX through time and test whether this configuration systematically precedes realized volatility spikes.

title: Scaling up Financial Education: A Saturation Experiment with Micro-entrepreneurs
affiliations: German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), University of Kaiserslautern-Landau (RPTU), Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin and Ruhr University of Bochum

detail.title: Scaling up Financial Education: A Saturation Experiment with Micro-entrepreneurs
detail.abstract: We study the effects of scaling up a financial-and business education program in a randomized saturation experiment in Uganda. We randomly assign the program at the clusterlevel and then randomize the share of treated individuals within treated clusters. 15 months later, we find that treated entrepreneurs increase their mobile money and bank savings, they invest more and have higher profits. We find evidence of tentatively negative spillovers on untreated peers. When the share of treated entrepreneurs increases with saturation, beneficial effects on the treated decline because the competitive advantage from being treated declines and because of training inefficiencies.

title: Do Younger Americans Really Earn Less? Reconciling the Evidence on Generational Earnings at the Same Age

detail.title: Do Younger Americans Really Earn Less? Reconciling the Evidence on Generational Earnings at the Same Age
detail.abstract: Ask most people whether young Americans earn less than their parents did at the same age and the answer comes back fast: obviously, yes. This paper gathers the best published evidence and finds that the obvious answer is wrong, at least in its strong form. Compared at the same age and adjusted for inflation, each of the four most recent generations has out-earned the one before it, if only by a modest margin (Corinth and Larrimore, 2024). That is not the whole story, because the popular sense of decline is not imaginary either. I trace the gap between the data and the mood to four things the headline number hides. The pace of generational progress has slowed, and what gains remain lean on longer work hours and, lately, help from parents. A divide has opened between college graduates, who have roughly held their ground, and the noncollege majority, who earn less than their counterparts once did. Reaching even that flat line now takes more schooling and more debt. And the odds that any one person out-earns their own parents have fallen by about half across cohorts (Chetty et al., 2017). The much-quoted figures about Generation Z, meanwhile, contradict each other for a dull reason: they measure different things, and the choice of measure, not any real dispute about the world, decides whether Gen Z looks ahead or behind. The defensible conclusion is a narrow one. Younger Americans as a group do not earn less at the same age. A large and identifiable share of them does, and a given paycheck no longer buys the position it once did.

title: Braille Digit Recognition with an FBG Tactile Sensor Using a GA-BP Neural Network
affiliations: Anhui University of Technology, Anhui University of Technology, Anhui University of Technology, Anhui University of Technology, Anhui University of Technology and Anhui University of Technology

detail.title: Braille Digit Recognition with an FBG Tactile Sensor Using a GA-BP Neural Network
detail.abstract: Braille recognition is essential for providing information access and natural interaction for the visually impaired, with significant potential in assistive technology and robotics. Current tactile sensing methods, however, often fall short in recognition accuracy and adaptability to dynamic, real-world scenarios that mirror human touch. This study presents a novel method for Braille digit recognition by integrating a three-row parallel fiber Bragg grating (FBG) tactile sensor array with a Genetic Algorithm-optimized Backpropagation Neural Network (GA-BP). The FBG sensing principle for Braille dot detection is first explained. The flexible encapsulation structure and grating parameters of the sensor are then designed and optimized through finite element simulation. Based on this design, a flexible FBG sensor array is fabricated, and an experimental setup for dynamic sliding recognition of Braille digits is established. Following sensor calibration, sliding recognition experiments are conducted on ten Braille digit samples (0-9) to collect tactile signals. A standard Backpropagation Neural Network (BPNN) is initially employed for signal classification. To enhance performance, a GA-BP neural network is subsequently implemented and evaluated for the same task. Experimental results indicate that the fabricated sensor achieves a high average sensitivity of 71.30 pm/N with excellent linearity (>0.996). In Braille digit classification, the GA-BP network attains an accuracy of 98.57%, outperforming the traditional BPNN (97.14%). The proposed approach, combining a parallel FBG array with GA-BP optimization, effectively enhances recognition accuracy and provides a reliable pathway for deploying high-precision tactile perception in assistive interactive systems.

title: Exact and Asymptotic Distributions of the Difference of Sample Squared Sharpe Ratios
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, Warwick Business School and Iowa State University

detail.title: Exact and Asymptotic Distributions of the Difference of Sample Squared Sharpe Ratios
detail.abstract: Following Barillas and Shanken (2017), traded factor asset pricing models are increasingly compared on the basis of the squared Sharpe ratios of the tangency portfolios of their factors. Inference typically relies on the asymptotic normal distribution of the difference of the two sample squared Sharpe ratios. We show that this asymptotic approximation can be very poor in the sample sizes and Sharpe ratio congurations that are typical in applications. The limiting distribution is nonstandard precisely on the boundary of the null hypothesis that matters for model comparison, the sample difference is biased, its exact density can be unbounded at zero, and the usual t-ratio is not asymptotically standard normal for nested models or when the two models are close in explanatory power. Under multivariate normality, we derive the exact nite-sample joint distribution of the two sample squared Sharpe ratios for nested, non-overlapping, and overlapping models. We obtain explicit expressions for the exact moments in terms of hypergeometric functions and develop stochastic representations that permit extremely fast simulation of the exact distribution using only low-dimensional random variables. A Pearson curve approximation based on the rst four exact moments is shown to be nearly indistinguishable from the exact distribution.

title: Informality and Macroeconomic Shock Transmission in Sub-Saharan Africa: Evidence from Local Projections
affiliations: and Kwara State University - Kwara State University, Malete

detail.title: Informality and Macroeconomic Shock Transmission in Sub-Saharan Africa: Evidence from Local Projections
detail.abstract: More than 70 percent of workers in Sub-Saharan Africa are employed outside the formal labour market, yet the macroeconomic role of this informal sector during external shocks remains poorly understood. We examine whether informality conditions the transmission of adverse commodity price shocks to unemployment, household consumption, and output across 44 Sub-Saharan African countries, 1991-2022. Identification uses the individual-commodity terms-of-trade shock from the IMF PCTOT database, weighting internationally determined prices for up to 45 commodities by each country's predetermined net trade exposure. A balance test confirms that initial informality is uncorrelated with commodity trade structure, supporting the interaction design. Adverse commodity price shocks significantly reduce household consumption from the three-year horizon onwards. Higher production-side informality (DGE) significantly buffers this consumption decline, consistent with informal-sector income maintenance. Effects on unemployment and aggregate GDP are not significantly conditioned by informality in the pooled sample, though among net commodity exporters informality amplifies output losses. The informal sector provides meaningful consumption protection against commodity price shocks in Sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Identifying Peer Effects under Reflection: A Panel-Data Approach
affiliations: University of Canberra and University of Canberra

detail.title: Identifying Peer Effects under Reflection: A Panel-Data Approach
detail.abstract: We propose a new approach to identifying peer effects that addresses the reflection problem by using the timing of decisions. The approach combines panel data with the ordering of decisions to separate peer influence from simultaneity. Variation in the order of decisions and in exposure to peers provides the basis for identification, allowing estimation of peer effects in settings where standard approaches are not informative. We illustrate the method using a multi-level panel of more than 2,000 judicial rulings over a 16-year period, where cases are randomly assigned to judges. The data allow us to implement the approach and examine the sources of peer influence. We find heterogeneous and asymmetric responses, with both the magnitude and direction of effects differing across types.

title: A Dual-Modal Spectral-Image Fusion Network Based on Multispectral Imaging for Composite Insulator Aging Identification
affiliations: Anhui University of Science and Technology, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Anhui University of Science and Technology, Anhui University of Science and Technology, Anhui University of Science and Technology, Anhui University of Science and Technology, Anhui University of Science and Technology, Anhui University of Science and Technology, Anhui University of Science and Technology and Anhui University of Science and Technology

detail.title: A Dual-Modal Spectral-Image Fusion Network Based on Multispectral Imaging for Composite Insulator Aging Identification
detail.abstract: In the maintenance of power transmission systems, composite insulator aging assessment based on hyperspectral imaging faces challenges related to high costs and significant data redundancy, whereas traditional methods struggle to capture the degradation of microscopic physicochemical properties. To address these issues, this paper proposes a Dual-modal Spectral-Image Fusion Network (DSI-FusionNet) based on Multispectral Imaging (MSI) to achieve precise, non-contact aging assessment. To accommodate the heterogeneous nature of 1D spectral data and 2D spatial textures in multispectral data, a unique dual-stream architecture is designed. The spectral branch, SpecFormer, utilizes an Adaptive Multi-scale Contextual Self-Attention (AMCSA) module to effectively overcome the limitations of traditional convolutions in modeling long-range spectral dependencies, achieving precise localization of key aging absorption peaks such as O-H bonds. Simultaneously, the image branch, VisNeXt, integrates a Dynamic Multi-Statistic Attention (DMSA) module. By adaptively fusing multi-order statistics with frequency-domain features, it significantly enhances the extraction capability for early, minute aging textures. Furthermore, a robust data processing pipeline is also developed, incorporating physics-driven augmentation, gradient-based Region of Interest extraction, and hash-based band selection to handle complex industrial environments. Experimental results demonstrate that DSI-FusionNet achieves a high accuracy of 99.70% ± 0.12% in aging grade identification tasks, with a model parameter count of only 87.33 K and a single-sample inference time of just 4.16 ms. Multi-level noise robustness evaluation confirms that the model maintains excellent anti-interference capabilities even under simulated complex field conditions. This study provides a high-precision, low-cost, and real-time engineering solution for the online monitoring of composite insulator aging status.

title: Same Equilibrium, Different Outcomes: Strategic Complementarity Matters
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) and Technische Universitat Berlin

detail.title: Same Equilibrium, Different Outcomes: Strategic Complementarity Matters
detail.abstract: What determines departures from equilibrium in strategic interactions? We provide experimental evidence that strategic structure is a key determinant in games of incomplete information, even when equilibrium predictions are held constant. We compare two symmetric environments with identical ex ante expected Bayes-Nash equilibrium actions that differ only in whether actions are strategic complements or substitutes. Despite the common equilibrium benchmark, choices are significantly higher under complements. Elicited beliefs are systematically above the equilibrium benchmark in both environments and higher under complements. These differences in beliefs account for a substantial share of the treatment gap, while the remaining difference reflects how beliefs are translated into actions across strategic environments.

title: Financial Sanctions and the Gravity of International Banking

detail.title: Financial Sanctions and the Gravity of International Banking
detail.abstract: Financial sanctions have been increasingly used over time and can disrupt international banking, but their dynamic balance-sheet effects remain poorly understood. We estimate structural gravity in local projections with methods for staggered and non-absorbing treatments that are robust to heterogeneous effects across cohorts. The sample covers 210 countries and 5,516 directed country pairs during the period 1978-2023. Only sanctions that remain in force for at least 4 years have a statistically detectable negative association. Sanctions that remain in force for 4 years are associated with cross-border interbank positions that are 33.7 percent lower. We find heterogeneity by sanction objective, with domestic politics associated with the most negative estimate. We find no heterogeneity in historical period, geopolitical distance between the sanctioning and sanctioned country, G7 membership of the sanctioning country, whether the sanction is imposed unilaterally or by a multilateral coalition, or whether the sanction is imposed by the origin or destination country.

title: Constitutional Control Architectures for LAWS under Electronic Warfare: Sovereignty Without Communication

detail.title: Constitutional Control Architectures for LAWS under Electronic Warfare: Sovereignty Without Communication
detail.abstract: The companion paper in this series ("Structural Sovereignty Limits in Autonomous Systems: A Constitutional Architecture for LAWS Governance") argued that human authority over lethal autonomous weapon systems (LAWS) must reside in a component the autonomous system cannot reach, model, or manipulate; a criterion we termed structural sovereignty. That result generates an apparent operational paradox. Contemporary conflicts unfold precisely in environments where communications are degraded or denied: electronic warfare, satellite navigation spoofing, emissions control, jamming, deliberate radio silence. If human sovereignty is exercised through a communication channel, and the channel disappears, sovereignty appears to disappear with it-leaving only two options, both unacceptable. An architecture rigid enough to preserve sovereignty is militarily useless; an architecture flexible enough to fight is sovereign in name only. This paper argues that the paradox rests on a category error: the identification of sovereignty with synchronous communication. Distinguishing four concepts that current debates systematically conflate (physical presence, communication, authority, and sovereignty) it shows that only the last is constitutive of the governance requirement, and develops three constitutional mechanisms that preserve structural sovereignty when the communication channel fails: temporal sovereignty (time-locked constitutional mandates), epistemic sovereignty (hardware-validated telemetry enclaves), and distributed sovereignty (the transitional sovereignty proxy). The analysis culminates in a general principle, constitutional compression: under degradation, autonomous authority must contract monotonically-from broad authorization to specific authorization to defensive authorization to suspension-and may never expand. Operational flexibility is constitutionally legitimate if and only if every degradation path contracts rather than expands autonomous authority.

title: Austerity, Monetary Policy, and the Budget Deficit: Evaluating the Economic Strategy of the British Government Elected in 2010

detail.title: Austerity, Monetary Policy, and the Budget Deficit: Evaluating the Economic Strategy of the British Government Elected in 2010
detail.abstract: After the 2008 global financial crisis, the coalition government, which was elected in May 2010, had to deal with one of the largest British budget deficits in modern history. The public was not only borrowing more, but public revenues were also down, unemployment was rising, and government spending was increasing to bolster the economy. To address this, the government started a period of fiscal austerity which would combine the implementation of budget deficits with spending cuts and tax hikes. Concurrently, the Bank of England would adopt an expansionary monetary policy that would keep interest rates low and employ quantitative easing (QE). This essay examines the appropriateness of the austerity measures employed by the British government and compares them with the macroeconomic doctrines of Keynesian economics and Monetarism, which will be discussed in this course. Before we assess a policy, there are a few foundational concepts we need to grasp. These are the functions of money. Money provides a means of facilitating economic exchanges, maintaining stable purchasing power over time, and measuring values of goods and services. Prior to the formation of modern banking and monetary frameworks, goods and services were exchanged through a barter system. Modern banking systems are required to intermediate between savers and borrowers to create credit in the economy. Banks also create reserves in the system through their holdings at the central bank. These are deposits of cash that are available to meet demands for withdrawal and regulatory reserve requirements. All these systems and structures are fundamental for carrying out monetary policy and affect the real economy.

title: Social Without Humans? Herding Among AI Agents on an AI-Native Platform
affiliations: Georgia State University

detail.title: Social Without Humans? Herding Among AI Agents on an AI-Native Platform
detail.abstract: We study social influence among AI agents, using 79,000 sentiment-scored posts about financial assets on Moltbook, a social platform for AI agents. We find evidence that these agents herd: an agent's sentiment rises by about one quarter of the increase in the peer consensus. While agents' posting volume forecasts asset volatility, the herded component of sentiment does not positively predict returns. Agents deployed from the same template express more similar sentiment-prompt herding, a construction-driven correlation with little analog in human markets; the social herding remains significant when this channel is accounted for.

title: Coral Bleaching and the Limits of "Local Solutions" in a Global Economy

detail.title: Coral Bleaching and the Limits of "Local Solutions" in a Global Economy
detail.abstract: Coral reefs face a multitude of risks today. This paper focuses on the risks that climate change and mass bleaching events pose. Global reef bleaching represents a “tragedy of the commons” approach to global emissions. The costs for insufficient or no effort in climate and reef protection are borne by the developing small island nations. Here, I outline the problems of the existing International climate control measures like The Paris Agreement. I also analyze the lack of real climate protection and the accountability of nations to really reduce pollution and improve reef protection. I propose a combination of local reef protective measures with a global pollution and climate protection improvement with a real accountability and climate protection tools. Burdening developing nations while calling for local sink reforms to address the ongoing degradation of reefs without global climate action.

detail.abstract: The relevance of cybersecurity response capability cannot be underestimated within any organization. If properly managed, it can be one reason relevant clients’ information may be kept safe and out of malicious hands. The current study aims at assessing the cybersecurity response capabilities of selected banks in Ghana. Specifically, the study sought to identify specific cyberattacks that banks record annually, the implications of these attacks on customers’ perceptions of bank brands, the cybersecurity response measures implemented, and the challenges to deploying such measures. Using a mixed-methods approach to research development, ten (10) commercial banks were purposively selected, with their IT and Cybersecurity Managers used as participants for data collection. Both qualitative and quantitative data were collected using a questionnaire with open-ended and closed-ended items. The findings revealed that the main cyberattacks recorded by banks in Ghana are phishing, social engineering, botnets, ransomware, and cyber fraud. The attacks have resulted in some loss of confidence on the part of customers of the banks. Finally, the study made recommendations for policy and practice improvement in cybersecurity awareness, information access and protection, as well as capacity development.

title: Copyright and Generic Entry in Book Publishing: Comment
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas - School of Management - Department of Finance & Managerial Economics

detail.title: Copyright and Generic Entry in Book Publishing: Comment
detail.abstract: This comment revisits Reimers (2019), which concludes that copyright protection for books reduces social welfare (abstracting from creative incentives) and raises prices. Using her model and data, I show that this welfare result is driven by mismeasurement: sales of dominant titles are substantially undercounted, while free downloads are overstated. I trace these discrepancies to data construction and market definition choices. Running corrected data through her structural model reverses the results-copyright protection increases rather than reduces welfare, with a larger magnitude than the original estimate. Restricting the price analysis to new books yields much smaller and statistically insignificant price effects.

title: Look-Through or Look Closer? Energy Shocks and Underlying Inflation in the Euro Area
affiliations: Bank of England

detail.title: Look-Through or Look Closer? Energy Shocks and Underlying Inflation in the Euro Area

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The views expressed in this manuscript are solely my own and should not be interpreted as reflecting the views of the Bank of England or its committees.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the transmission of exogenous energy supply shocks to underlying inflation in the euro area. Using externally identified energy supply shocks and local projection methods, it examines whether and under which conditions energy price movements propagate beyond headline inflation into core inflation. The results show that energy shocks generate sharp but short-lived increases in energy and headline inflation, while pass-through to core inflation is delayed, persistent, and concentrated in non-energy industrial goods. Crucially, this pass-through is highly state dependent. When wage growth, inflation expectations, or headline inflation are elevated, or when energy price increases are large, energy shocks transmit into core inflation faster, more strongly, and more persistently. In low-inflation environments, pass-through is negligible. These findings imply that linear estimates mask important nonlinearities and that the appropriateness of "looking-through" energy shocks depends critically on prevailing macroeconomic conditions.

title: Below Replacement, Unequally: Settlement-Era Regional Cultures and U.S. County Fertility

detail.title: Below Replacement, Unequally: Settlement-Era Regional Cultures and U.S. County Fertility
detail.abstract: The United States total fertility rate reached a record low of 1.60 in 2024, but the national figure conceals durable regional variation. This article maps contemporary fertility onto the American Nations model, a typology of settlement-era regional cultures (Woodard 2011) that follows county borders and has been applied to violence, health, and political outcomes, but not to fertility. Using CDC WONDER natality data (2021-2024 pooled), Census Bureau denominators, and a tract-level cultural-region crosswalk published by the Urban Institute, total fertility rates are computed for each nation and county-level models estimated with controls for religious adherence, income, education, and urbanicity. Nation-level TFRs range from 1.42 on the Left Coast and 1.54 in Yankeedom to 1.73 in Greater Appalachia and 1.77 in New France; every region is below replacement. Cultural region adds 11 percentage points of explained variance in county TFR beyond the controls, and roughly a quarter of a child separates Greater Appalachia from the Left Coast once composition is held constant. The regional ordering echoes the geography of the antebellum fertility decline, in which Yankee-settled areas led the nation: the national rate has converged on the level Yankeedom pioneered, while the ordering that region belonged to has not dissolved. Settlement-era cultural boundaries remain a live axis of American demographic variation two centuries later. The full analysis pipeline and derived datasets are archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21396077.

title: Energy Price Shocks and Climate Concern: A Causal Forest Analysis

detail.title: Energy Price Shocks and Climate Concern: A Causal Forest Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: We examine the heterogeneous treatment effects of oil price shocks on climate concern using the causal forest method, applied to monthly US data from January 2004 to August 2025. High oil prices are associated with a significant decrease in climate concern of 11.52 points, representing about 3.78% of the sample mean. Treatment effects exhibit substantial heterogeneity, moderated primarily by personal income, consumer sentiment, and inflation. Effects are smallest during low unemployment and largest during economic downturns. Complementary analysis using Google Trends reveals contrasting positive effects (ATE = +0.817), suggesting institutional attention decreases while individual information-seeking increases. These findings suggest that economic hardship from energy price shocks crowds out climate concern, with implications for counter-cyclical climate communication strategies.

title: Re-Optimization Under Constraint: Evidence from Major League Baseball
affiliations: , Wake Forest University, Wake Forest University and Seton Hall University

detail.title: Re-Optimization Under Constraint: Evidence from Major League Baseball
detail.abstract: Firms continually adjust decisions as incentives change, yet whether they re-optimize efficiently remains an open question. We exploit Major League Baseball's 2023 disengagement rule as a natural experiment and develop a game-theoretic model to generate equilibrium predictions under both rule regimes. Using pitch-level data from more than 3 million pitches during 2021-2024, we compare observed strategic decisions with equilibrium behavior rather than inferring optimization from aggregate outcomes. Players adjusted in the predicted direction but incompletely and asymmetrically. The remaining deviations imply approximately 94 additional runs per season, indicating persistent departures from equilibrium despite repeated play and strong incentives.

title: The Political Economy of Debt of Sri Lanka's Debt
affiliations: and University of Colombo

detail.title: The Political Economy of Debt of Sri Lanka's Debt

declarations.funderStatement: The Asia Foundation's International Development Cooperation Unit

detail.abstract: This chapter investigates the political economy of Sri Lanka’s public debt crisis, analyzing the structural vulnerabilities and policy failures that culminated in the historic sovereign debt default of April 2022. Despite its status as a leading economic model in South Asia, Sri Lanka engaged in persistent deficit financing to sustain political popularity, driving general government gross debt from 68.7% of GDP in 2010 to 115.5% in 2022. This study traces the trajectory of this collapse, evaluating the  impact of short-term fiscal mismanagement—such as the late 2019 tax cuts. Crucially, the analysis deconstructs the composition of Sri Lanka's external debt obligations, demonstrating how a transition to middle-income status shifted the debt portfolio away from concessional loans toward expensive commercial debt, specifically International Sovereign Bonds (ISBs). Furthermore, evidence is presented to refute the prominent narrative of Chinese "debt trap diplomacy," revealing that market-based ISBs, rather than bilateral loans from China, constituted the vast majority of the country's foreign debt and servicing obligations. The study highlights how institutional weaknesses and tax concessions caused revenue collection to plummet to 7.7% of GDP by 2021. The study importantly explores the domestic political economy for Sri Lanka's public finance decisions and the weak fiscal social contract that contributed to the 2022 Economic Crisis. The chapter concludes that long standing structural weaknesses must be addressed in addition to governance reforms and improvement of state capacity.

title: The Theory of Distributionally Weighted Investment

detail.title: The Theory of Distributionally Weighted Investment
detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of distributionally weighted investment in which the investment effect of household income depends on who receives the income, how strongly recipients adjust expenditure, which firms receive that expenditure, and how those firms respond to expected demand. At the firm level, the model defines a distributional investment weight as the product of a household group's marginal expenditure response, the firm's exposure to that group's spending, and the responsiveness of desired investment to expected sales. An income-preserving redistribution therefore changes firm investment whenever the recipient and donor groups carry different firm-specific weights. Aggregating across firms produces an economy-wide investment weight for each household group. The analysis establishes three principal results. First, the effect of any income-preserving redistribution on aggregate desired investment is determined by the alignment between the redistribution and the vector of economy-wide investment weights. Second, aggregate investment is neutral to every income-preserving redistribution if and only if these weights are equal across groups. Third, aggregate consumption is not generally a sufficient statistic for investment. It is locally sufficient only when economy-wide investment weights are an affine function of household marginal expenditure responses. Otherwise, a redistribution can leave both aggregate income and aggregate consumption unchanged while altering investment because expenditure is reallocated across firms, sectors, or regions with different investment responsiveness. The theory complements accelerator, user-cost, Tobin's q theory, uncertainty, and financing-based approaches by introducing a demand-composition channel. It predicts that investment responses should vary with predetermined customer exposure, recipient-group expenditure behavior, expected sales revisions, capacity utilization, demand persistence, domestic production content, and firms' ability to implement expansion. The central implication is that the distribution of purchasing power can become an investment state variable whenever heterogeneous household expenditure responses interact with heterogeneous firm exposure and demand-sensitive capital expenditure.
