detail.abstract: Responsive regulation's enforcement pyramid has been adopted widely across Australian regulation, but the published instruments that administer it operate an allocation logic the theory does not describe and its authors did not prescribe: the prosecution criteria of evidentiary sufficiency, seriousness and public interest, applied topdown across the enforcement system rather than only at its apex. This paper tests that claim across three layers of evidence and one theoretical confrontation. The doctrinal layer shows that corporate-attribution doctrine makes the apex conditional on questions-whose acts and whose fault count as the company's-that the prosecution policies never answer, and that the constraint produces size-regressive enforcement, harm-based filtering of risk-based offences, and a hollow apex. The documentary layer, a structured scan of twenty-five current Australian instruments (with two United Kingdom comparators), finds the evidentiary filter stated (seventeen of twenty-five) and its selectivity-defendant selection and corporate-fault theory-close to unstated (five and one respectively). The theory-engagement section establishes that the instruments' seriousness-sorted, prosecution-apexed pyramids are departures from responsive regulation measured against its authors' own texts, not a strawman of the theory. The paper argues the silence is complexity-driven but not justified by complexity, and that it is in part administratively fixable: defendant-selection criteria have been codified abroad and articulated judicially at home.

title:
The Car Did Not Change. The Price Did.
Why Electric Vehicles Depreciate Faster than ICE Vehicles, and Why the Gap is more Complicated than Battery Wear

detail.title:
The Car Did Not Change. The Price Did.
Why Electric Vehicles Depreciate Faster than ICE Vehicles, and Why the Gap is more Complicated than Battery Wear
detail.abstract: In this paper, the author attempts to find out the reasons for the faster depreciation of electric vehicles (EVs) compared to internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles and test whether the physical decay is sufficient for explaining such depreciation. In the previous research, the author managed to observe higher depreciation rates for EVs, but the explanation of the issue that was provided, including mechanical reliability problems and battery degradation, cannot fully explain the drop in market value of such vehicles. Contemporary electric vehicles' engines include fewer moving parts, and less maintenance is required compared to ICE vehicles. Moreover, the data obtained from large batteries suggest that most EVs have 95 percent of their initial range left after five years of operation. In this paper, the author investigates the issue of depreciation as both a physical and market phenomenon. The factors examined by the author include vehicle age, mileage, battery condition, technological progress, reduction in the price of new cars, incentives to buy EVs, prices of energy, access to charging stations, and used-vehicle supply. It is possible to show that technological improvement of EVs, price reduction for new vehicles, and changes in supply can cause the decrease in the value of existing vehicles despite their physical condition.

title: From AI Assistance to Responsible Academic Agency: A Human-centered Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education
affiliations: University of the Cumberlands (formerly Cumberland College)

detail.title: From AI Assistance to Responsible Academic Agency: A Human-centered Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known financial, personal, professional, or organizational relationships that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, the preparation of this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this conceptual article did not involve human participants, patient data, interviews, surveys, experiments, or identifiable personal information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any public, commercial, or nonprofit funding organization.

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has moved from a peripheral educational technology to an ordinary part of university study, writing, research, and assessment. Existing scholarship has documented substantial opportunities in personalized support, accessibility, feedback, and productivity, while also identifying persistent concerns involving misinformation, academic misconduct, privacy, bias, inequitable access, and cognitive dependence. However, the debate is too often organized around a narrow question: whether artificial intelligence should be allowed or prohibited. This conceptual article argues that the more consequential question is whether students retain responsible academic agency when artificial intelligence participates in their learning. Drawing on research in artificial intelligence in education, self-regulated learning, academic integrity, human-centered artificial intelligence, and institutional governance, the article develops a Responsible Academic Agency Framework. The framework integrates six interdependent domains: purpose and learning alignment; cognitive ownership and human judgment; epistemic verification; transparency and attribution; equity and privacy; and institutional governance and assessment validity. The central proposition is that artificial intelligence contributes to education only when it strengthens rather than substitutes the learner's capacity to set goals, evaluate evidence, make decisions, explain conclusions, and accept responsibility for academic work. The framework provides practical guidance for students, educators, university leaders, and technology providers, and offers a research agenda for evaluating learning quality rather than focusing solely on adoption. The article contributes to the literature by shifting the discussion from tool access and rule compliance toward the preservation, demonstration, and development of human agency within artificial intelligence-mediated higher education.

title: Relational Degradation: The Reconfiguration of the Relational Subject - Discussion I

detail.title: Relational Degradation: The Reconfiguration of the Relational Subject - Discussion I
detail.abstract:
Problem. A class of relational deformations resists the vocabulary in which relational harm is ordinarily described. Some have no identifiable perpetrator, some proceed without malice, and some are assembled entirely from judgments no party was wrong to make. The vocabulary of act, intention, and fault has nothing to attach to in such cases, and this is argued to be a consequence of a premise it carries without stating: that the subject is prior to the relation.

Approach. The paper proceeds deductively from the ontology of generative relational being, on which the subject is not an entity standing in relations but is what is generated within them. A consequence follows by definition rather than by inference: any degradation of a relation is a change in the conditions under which subjects are generated. Seven cases are examined, not as evidence for the thesis but as exhibitions of the paths by which the alteration transmits.

Findings. Two corrections cut against the natural formulation. Degradation does not diminish the subject's dynamics but reconfigures them, and the reconfigured dynamics are frequently the more intense. And the reconstitution of subjects cannot be the wrong, since every relation reconstitutes its participants. A criterion is therefore required, and it cannot be framed in terms of generativity without collapsing into the utilitarian norm the framework exists to displace. The criterion the ontology entails is revisability: degradation is present when the reconfiguration forecloses the possibility that the conditions of generation be further revised through common experience.

Contribution. Revisability is proposed as the sixth principle of the ethics of relational reproduction, and as a meta-principle rather than a further virtue: it governs not relations but the five principles themselves, since any principle that has lost its revisability may degenerate into an instrument of the party it was framed to constrain. A second result concerns distributive justice, shown to be limited in principle, and not merely in execution, with respect to abandonment.

title: Where Does the Strait of Hormuz Crisis Lead? Forecasting the Future of Middle East Energy Security Post-2026
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Where Does the Strait of Hormuz Crisis Lead? Forecasting the Future of Middle East Energy Security Post-2026
detail.abstract: On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran, triggering a five-week war that culminated in the death of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and, more consequentially for the global economy, the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz the chokepoint through which roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil and a fifth of global liquefied natural gas (LNG) normally transit. Although a memorandum of understanding signed on June 17, 2026 was intended to end the conflict within sixty days, renewed U.S.-Iran strikes in mid-July 2026 over transit rights and tolls demonstrate that the crisis remains unresolved. This paper synthesizes open-source reporting, U.S. Congressional Research Service analysis, and energymarket data to construct three forward-looking scenarios for Middle East energy security through 2027-2030: (1) a fragile normalization in which prewar shipping patterns gradually resume; (2) a persistent low-intensity blockade in which Iran selectively tolls or bans vessels; and (3) a structural bypass scenario in which importing nations and Gulf producers permanently reduce dependence on the Strait through overland pipelines, alternative suppliers, and strategic reserves. The paper argues that even under the most optimistic resolution, the 2026 crisis has already produced durable shifts accelerated pipeline investment (notably Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline), renewed interest in the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), and faster adoption of renewable energy and electric vehicles that will outlast the conflict itself. The paper concludes with policy implications for oil-importing states, particularly in South and Southeast Asia, and identifies avenues for further empirical research once higher-frequency shipping and price data become available.

title: Strangled or Strengthened? Innovation in Chinese Technology Firms Targeted by U.S. Sanctions
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE), University of Maryland - R.H. Smith School of Business, University of International Business and Economics, University of International Business and Economics, University of Texas at Dallas and University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: Strangled or Strengthened? Innovation in Chinese Technology Firms Targeted by U.S. Sanctions
detail.abstract: Economic sanctions have become a prominent instrument of geopolitical competition, yet their consequences for firm innovation remain poorly understood. Existing research has focused mainly on innovation quantity, with less attention to innovation quality, underlying mechanisms, and firms' adaptive responses. We examine U.S. export-control sanctions imposed on Chinese technology firms using a panel of publicly listed high-technology firms from 2013 to 2025. Comparing 122 sanctioned firms with 548 comparable same-industry high-technology firms, we use a staggered difference-indifferences design based on the Callaway and Sant'Anna estimator to estimate sanction effects under conditional parallel-trends assumptions. We find no strong evidence that sanctions change innovation quantity, measured by patent applications. However, sanctioned firms experience substantial post-sanction declines in innovation quality, reflected in lower technological impact, commercial value, economic value, and novelty of patents. Heterogeneity analyses suggest that these declines are most pronounced among firms operating in technology domains more dependent on U.S.-origin knowledge, while financial exposure plays a secondary role. Government support and innovation-oriented managerial resources help sustain patenting activity but do not appear to offset declines in patent quality. We further document patterns consistent with adaptive reconfiguration: sanctioned firms increase references to Chinese and European prior art and shift patenting toward less sanction-exposed technological domains. Firms making stronger adjustments experience smaller quality declines, although these adjustments do not eliminate the overall quality penalty. Our findings inform understanding of organizational adaptation and innovation under geopolitical fragmentation.

title: Aggregation Failure in Stochastic OLG Economies with Production ⋆
affiliations: Central Reserve Bank of Peru

detail.title: Aggregation Failure in Stochastic OLG Economies with Production ⋆
detail.abstract: We study whether aggregate macroeconomic dynamics in stochastic overlapping generations economies with production can be summarized by a lowdimensional state. In a three-period OLG economy with state-contingent returns, we show that aggregation fails generically: even when aggregate capital arises endogenously, it does not summarize the payoff-relevant distributional information required for asset pricing. We derive cross-cohort Euler compatibility restrictions implied by such representations and show that they are generically violated. Consequently, no low-dimensional aggregate-state representation is consistent with equilibrium; equilibrium must be recursive with additional endogenous states. This implies sequential market incompleteness and potential inefficiency. Benchmark cases clarify that aggregation fails due to multi-period lifetimes, state-contingent returns, and post-shock portfolio rebalancing.

title: From Maps to Meadows: Ecologically Literate Zoning and the Regeneration of Wildlife Habitats
affiliations: Albany Law School

detail.title: From Maps to Meadows: Ecologically Literate Zoning and the Regeneration of Wildlife Habitats
detail.abstract: For more than a century, zoning has shaped the American landscape, often at the expense of wildlife and ecosystems. Rooted in legal doctrines that treated animals as property and nature as a raw material, zoning codes have fragmented habitats, erased migration corridors, and accelerated biodiversity loss. At the same time, federal protections are narrowing, leaving critical gaps in environmental governance. This Article argues that local governments possess both the authority and the obligation to respond. By embedding ecological principles into zoning—through conservation districts, wildlife corridor protections, wetland buffers, pollinator protections, dark skies, wildlife fencing, habitat restoration, and others—municipalities can transform land use law from a tool of exploitation into one of regeneration. Drawing on the framework of “insider environmental law,” this Article highlights place-based strategies that align community priorities with ecological needs. In doing so, it demonstrates how ecologically literate zoning can foster resilience, protect biodiversity, and ensure that land-use planning sustains all species.

title: Aid Sanctions and Hybrid Regimes
affiliations: Singapore Management University and Banque de France

detail.title: Aid Sanctions and Hybrid Regimes

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banque de France Working Paper No. Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Banque de France Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Recent advances combining sanctions scholarship and the study of authoritarianism relate sanctions effectiveness to regime type. These studies generally conclude that economic sanctions tend to be more effective on democracies than on autocracies, but also on weakly institutionalised autocracies rather than on other authoritarian types. This literature at the intersection between international relations and comparative politics focuses on the democracy-autocracy dichotomy, or the categorization of autocratic types, to the detriment of the exploration of 'hybrid' regime types. Equally importantly, it has neglected examining the impact of aid suspensions as a subcategory of sanctions. We address these deficits by investigating whether (i) the autocratic type or the level of democratic openness of the target better predicts sanctions effectiveness, (ii) whether hybrid regimes behave like closed autocracies or like democracies under sanctions, and (iii) whether aid suspensions perform similarly than other sanctions in terms of effectiveness. The hypotheses are tested on an original dataset rich in aid sanctions.

title: From International Experience to Local Performance: The Specific Return Generation Logic and Formation Mechanism of Chinese Public REITs

detail.title: From International Experience to Local Performance: The Specific Return Generation Logic and Formation Mechanism of Chinese Public REITs
detail.abstract: The return sources of public REITs are not fully studied under China's unique institutional arrangement and complex property rights system. This paper compares the return models of REITs in mature markets such as the United States, Singapore and Japan and combines this analysis with the institutional characteristics of China's pilot phase. We find three distinct forces that support the pricing logic of Chinese REITs: (1) a scarcity premium due to policy restrictions, (2) a governance premium due to the dual-tier structure of "public funds + asset-backed securities (ABS schemes)", and (3) a green valuation premium due to the "dual carbon" targets. Conversely, the two binding constraints are the mandatory high dividend payout ratio and incomplete property rights, which, respectively, suppress the potential return from the dimensions of growth and asset appreciation. Based on the above, we build a "institution-market-asset" three-layer analytical framework, and empirically verify three key policy events through event study methodology (under full-market inclusion principle: Event 1, N = 12; Event 2, N = 24; Event 3, N = 32; Bootstrap tests show robustness). The results indicate that the market is sensitive to policy events and the direction of the reaction depends on the type of policy. For supply-contracting policy (establishment of the follow-on offering mechanism), the reaction is significantly positive (ACAR = 1.48%, p < 0.01). For supply-expanding policy (inclusion of consumer infrastructure), there is no significant short-term reaction but a significantly negative medium-to-long-term reaction (ACAR =-1.65%, p < 0.01). For institutionalization policy (normalized issuance), the reaction is robustly positive (ACAR = 0.74%, p < 0.01). This paper helps investors to understand the unique operation logic of the Chinese REITs market, and provides a reference for regulators to improve the institutional design.

title: Quality Scoring with ESG Adjustments and REIT Returns: A Framework for Australian REITs

detail.title: Quality Scoring with ESG Adjustments and REIT Returns: A Framework for Australian REITs
detail.abstract: We propose a new scoring framework, the ESG-Adjusted REIT Quality Score (E-REQS), which integrates sustainability and carbon transition dimensions into a Piotroski-style quality assessment for Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs). Score-based investing has consistently outperformed equity markets, however, no research has systematically combined quality scoring and ESG integration for REITs. The E-REQS is built on the classical F-score framework, augmented by 13 binary signals across three categories: financial quality, operational efficiency, and ESG/carbon transition quality. The split of the score into a Traditional Quality Score (TQS) and an ESG Incremental Score (EIS) permits direct tests of whether sustainability signals add value beyond conventional financial metrics. We outline a research design to examine whether higher E-REQS scores are associated with improved risk-adjusted returns using portfolio sorts and panel regressions with Australian A-REITs in the period 2015-2025. We expect that this framework will add to the score-based investing literature and the ESG-REITs debate, and offer institutional investors a transparent and replicable screening tool for sustainable real estate investment.

detail.abstract: Global legal artificial-intelligence platforms sell two things: access and speed. For civil law jurisdictions, neither is the real problem. The real problem is the accountability of reasoning: how a legal proposition produced by a machine can be answered for — to the client, to the court, and to the ethical rules of the profession. This paper proceeds from two findings that reinforce each other. First, the preregistered empirical finding that the "hallucination-free" claim of leading AI legal research tools does not survive testing: those tools still err on roughly one in six to one in three queries. Second, the textual finding that official discourse within the Supreme Court of the Republic of Indonesia — the civil law jurisdiction in which the author practices — has not yet named hallucination as a challenge at all. Against that double gap, this paper proposes a standard that can be promised honestly: not a machine that never errs, but reasoning that can be audited. It sets out an architecture of three separations that the author has practiced and published in Indonesia — a separation of roles, a four-point verification gate, and a disciplined audit trail — together with a new category of examination for the civil law family: Nasab Norma, the lineage record of a norm measured at four points, demonstrated in full on the lineage chart of a family statute in force since 1974. The paper closes with a limit of claims stated openly: traceability is not material truth, and precisely for that reason a named human remains the decider. This is the author's English version of a preprint first posted in Indonesian: "Penalaran Hukum Teraudit bagi Yurisdiksi Civil Law: Arsitektur Seorang Praktisi dari Indonesia" (Zenodo, 2026), doi: 10.5281/zenodo.21633646.

title: Hiding in the Mean: The Two Margins of AI's Employment Effect
affiliations: and Liminal Capital

detail.title: Hiding in the Mean: The Two Margins of AI's Employment Effect
detail.abstract: Estimates of AI's employment effect disagree in sign. We argue the disagreement is built into the measurement: AI substitutes for some of an occupation's tasks and complements others, so one exposure number nets two opposing forces before estimation begins. We classify every O*NET task by what its workflow requires of a human, giving each occupation a substitution mass S, a complement mass C, and an inert remainder, conserved rather than averaged. In OEWS data on 705 occupations, employment growth after 2021 loads negative on S and positive on C in the same regressions, and published exposure indices lose their coefficients once composition is entered beside them. The substitution gradient runs from-0.056 per year against a 2019-2021 baseline to-0.021 against occupations' own pre-COVID trends, significant under family clustering (p = 0.042) but not under a wild-cluster bootstrap, and it operates through hiring rather than separations, binding on entrants aged 22 to 25. The complement gradient is positive and concave, carried by real-time interpersonal delivery rather than sign-off work: +0.034 per year (p = 0.017) on post-2021 growth, surviving a battery built against the post-pandemic care-demand alternative, though its family-wise adjusted values sit at the ten percent boundary. We grade the complement result robust in sign, and the substitution effect consistent with AI rather than established.

title: Double-Peak Splitting: The Hidden Structure of Finite-Lattice Phase Transitions in the 3D Ising Model --Verification of the Factor Hierarchy Law on an NP-Complete System: Double-Peak Splitting, Transition Regime, Piecewise Control Function, and Multi-Regime State Decoupling Algorithm
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Double-Peak Splitting: The Hidden Structure of Finite-Lattice Phase Transitions in the 3D Ising Model --Verification of the Factor Hierarchy Law on an NP-Complete System: Double-Peak Splitting, Transition Regime, Piecewise Control Function, and Multi-Regime State Decoupling Algorithm
detail.abstract: On the L=64 lattice of the 3D Ising model-an NP-complete problem rigorously proven to have no analytical solution-the six functional dimensions of the Testability Norms were applied, achieving the detection and classification of the ferromagnetic-paramagnetic phase transition with a statistical confidence of p = 3.33×10⁻⁷⁰. Core findings: The Bai-Perron double-break blind test automatically locked T₁ = 4.39 and T₂ = 4.49 (F = 285.7, significantly outperforming the single-break F = 238.3), precisely aligned with the M_sp switch (4.40, F = 1524) and the U₄ switch (4.50, F = 2335), with deviations of 0.01 and 0.01 respectively. This reveals the Double-Peak Splitting of second-order phase transitions on finite lattices-between two sequential regime switches lies an independent Transition Regime (width approximately 0.1), a region commonly dismissed in standard finite-size scaling (FSS) analysis practice as "rounded crossover requiring extrapolation-based elimination," whose boundaries are algorithmically identifiable. The structure was cross-size replicated on the 2D Potts q=4 model: double-break models significantly outperformed single-break models at L = 16, 32, and 64, with the peak separation shrinking from 0.260 at L = 64 to 0.180 at L = 128, evolving according to scaling laws. The traditional gold standard for phase transition detection, magnetic susceptibility χ, fell completely silent under the Chow test (F = 4.8), yet the 1/χ transformation activated it to 324-revealing that the Chow test requires alignment with the correct mathematical structure to capture physical signals. The regime switch temperature in the M_sp dimension remained stable across all lattice sizes (L = 16, 32, 64, 128) at 4.40-4.46, showing no convergence toward the thermodynamic limit Tc = 4.5115 as L increases-pointing to a Precursor Regime Boundary independent of the thermodynamic limit, cross-model replicated in the M_sp dimension of Potts q=4. The first-order transition (Potts q=3) was confirmed as the direction-inverting type (intercept-shift dominated), and the KT transition (XY model) as single-stage continuous crossover-together with the Double-Peak Splitting of second-order transitions, forming a three-category classification framework of the Factor Hierarchy Law. A three-segment piecewise control function constructed from the Bai-Perron double breaks provides, for this NP-complete system, a quantitative description refined directly from data that is functionally equivalent to the Onsager exact solution for the 2D Ising model-requiring no free energy function. The two 2 inflection points of this function were automatically identified by the Bai-Perron algorithm, without relying on any a priori definition of free energy or order parameter, directly demonstrating the capacity of the Testability Norms to extract physical laws from data. Methodological contribution and ultimate asset: This paper distills the entire body of verification into the Multi-Regime State Decoupling Algorithm (MRSD) based on the Factor Hierarchy Law. Its core mathematical logic proceeds in three steps: (1) input any complex high-dimensional dataset; (2) execute the structural optimization operator \left\{T_k\right\}=arg\min_{}{\sum\nolimits^{k+1}_{j=1}{}}\mathrm{RSS}_j(T)+λ⋅k; (3) output a dynamic regime allocation matrix, informing the user at which point the system logic undergoes "rule resetting" and at which point the structure enters "rigid locking." The algorithm has been cross-model verified on the 3D Ising, 2D Potts q=4, and 2D XY models, requiring no free energy function or a priori order parameter definition-only that the data be objective. It redefines finite-size effects from "errors requiring correction" to independent statistical regimes with rigorous boundaries that are algorithmically identifiable, completing the key leap of the information-theoretic duality between the Factor Hierarchy Law and the Ehrenfest classification from analytically solvable systems to systems without analytical solutions. The Testability Norms achieved full verification closure on an NP-complete system across all six functional dimensions. Leave-one-out cross-validation (Tc range [4.47, 4.48], standard deviation 0.0021), Bootstrap threshold regression (95% CI [4.44, 4.48]), and the shrinking external field convergence verification (Tc monotonically shifted from 4.48 to 4.50) jointly confirm the high robustness of the conclusions.

title: Data Sovereignty: From the Digital Silk Road to the Return of the State
affiliations: Georgetown University Law Center and The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Data Sovereignty: From the Digital Silk Road to the Return of the State

publicationDetails.detailsText: Georgetown University Law Center Research Paper

detail.abstract: Digital sovereignty—the exercise of control over the Internet—is the ambition of the world’s leaders, from Australia to Zimbabwe, a bulwark against both foreign state and foreign corporation. Governments have resoundingly answered first-generation Internet law questions of who if anyone should regulate the Internet—they all will. The second-generation question to confront is not whether, but how to regulate the Internet. This volume features new theoretical perspectives on digital sovereignty and explores cutting-edge issues associated with it. Drawing mainly on various theories concerning political economy, international law, human rights, and data protection, it presents thought-provoking ideas about the nature and scope of digital sovereignty. It also examines the extent to which new technological developments in sectors, such as artificial intelligence, e-commerce, and sharing economy, have posed challenges to assertion of digital sovereignty, and considers how to deal with such challenges. In particular, the volume discusses the promise and pitfalls of digital sovereignty in the process of trade liberalization, data localization, and human rights protection.

title: Detecting Critical Junctures as They Unfold: Foundations, Measurement, and Applications from 120 Years of Reporting
affiliations: London School of Economics, , London School of Economics, University of California, Berkeley and London School of Economics

detail.title: Detecting Critical Junctures as They Unfold: Foundations, Measurement, and Applications from 120 Years of Reporting
detail.abstract: Explaining why some countries grow rich while others remain poor requires knowing how — and when — institutions change. A large body of research argues that institutional change often occurs at critical junctures: moments when multiple institutional futures are possible, including a return to the status quo. Yet most empirical work examines critical junctures only in retrospect, risking the omission of pivotal moments when institutions were in flux but ultimately remained unchanged. We develop a new empirical approach to detect critical junctures as they unfold. Our key insight is to understand critical junctures as moments of uncertainty about institutions, which provides a text classifier with a theoretically motivated object to detect in contemporaneous discourse. In this chapter, we apply this idea to the study of historical critical junctures using newspaper text as a rich source of information regarding contemporary beliefs about institutional uncertainty. We translate this insight into a measurement strategy by training a large language model-based classifier, which we apply to the Times of London archive — 11.95 million articles spanning 1800 to 2019 — while focusing our main empirical analysis on 120 years of reporting from 1900 to 2019. This produces the first long-run, text-based measure of institutional uncertainty grounded in the concept of critical junctures. Compared to established indices of geopolitical and economic risk, our measure innovates on several fronts: (i) it captures high uncertainty even in periods without formal institutional change, consistent with ex-ante definitions of critical junctures; (ii) it provides earlier signals of major global convulsions, such as World War I; (iii) it evaluates candidate critical junctures using a common ex ante measure; and (iv) it opens new avenues for studying how critical junctures shape institutions and long-run development. Today, our Times-based index suggests that institutional uncertainty in the US and UK is as elevated as it was in the early 1940s — a signal missed by other leading measures of risk.

title: Following the Talent: Analyst Coverage Decisions and Inventor Mobility
affiliations: Purdue University, University of Alberta - Department of Accounting, Operations &  Information Systems, University of Alberta - School of Business and University of Alberta - Department of Accounting, Operations &  Information Systems

detail.title: Following the Talent: Analyst Coverage Decisions and Inventor Mobility
detail.abstract: We examine whether sell-side equity analysts' relationships with inventors affect analysts' coverage decisions following inventors' job moves. We find that after an inventor relocates from an origin firm to a destination firm, analysts who covered the origin firm prior to the move are 45% more likely to co-migrate by initiating coverage of the destination firm than the unconditional mean probability of initiating coverage. Cross-sectional tests show that co-migration is stronger when analysts exhibit greater incentives and have more opportunities to form and maintain relationships with inventors, proxied by conference-call engagement, prior employment overlaps, and geographic proximity. The pattern is also stronger when innovation-related information is more valuable to the analyst, both when the moving inventors are positioned to carry more valuable proprietary knowledge and when the destination firm's environment places greater weight on innovation-related information. Finally, compared to other analysts covering the same destination firm, co-migrating analysts issue more accurate earnings forecasts, generate stronger market reactions to their forecasts and recommendations, and are more likely to issue long-term forecasts. Overall, our findings highlight analyst-inventor relationships as portable informational capital that shapes analysts' coverage decisions and capital-market information production.

title: Cryptocurrency Kiosks: Geography, Fraud Risk, and the U.S. Regulatory Response
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: Cryptocurrency Kiosks: Geography, Fraud Risk, and the U.S. Regulatory Response
detail.abstract:
Cryptocurrency kiosks and tellers are an understudied piece of consumer financial infrastructure in the United States. This study makes three contributions. First, it constructs a nationwide location-level census that captures both physical kiosks and counter-service cash-to-crypto locations. Second, it connects the distribution and design of these services to consumer harms, particularly those experienced by older adults. Third, it provides a comparative account of the rapidly changing litigation and regulatory response through mid-2026. 

We identified 42,587 service locations in the first half of 2025, 36% more than the 31,143 reported by Coin ATM Radar, the industry-standard public aggregator. This suggests that public sources under count the installed base, particularly when counter service teller locations are included. Services are concentrated in cash-intensive, lightly supervised retail locations: gas stations (38%), convenience stores (25%), and grocery stores (19%). California, Texas, Florida, and Illinois together host roughly a third of all identified locations. 

Consumer risks are substantial. Transactions are generally irreversible, carry high fees, and require little verification. Reported losses in scams involving crypto kiosks exceeded $388 million in 2025, with older adults bearing a large share of this. Additional operational and counterparty risks include breaches exposing customer data, loss of operator reserves, and operator insolvency. 

31 states have crypto kiosk legislation, with Indiana, Tennessee, Minnesota, and Vermont adopting statewide bans. The findings show that cash-to-crypto services occupy a significant consumer-protection gap: they are presented like familiar retail financial services but expose users, especially older adults, to high-cost losses without strong safeguards.

title: Modeling Coase Theorem Worlds: Why the History of Economic Analysis Matters for the History of (Economic) Science
affiliations: Duke University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Modeling Coase Theorem Worlds: Why the History of Economic Analysis Matters for the History of (Economic) Science
detail.abstract: This paper uses the two-decade controversy over the Coase theorem's long-run validity to highlight the importance of the history of economic analysis for understanding and writing the history of (economic) science. The argument is that in many instances a reasonably accurate understanding of why economic ideas evolved as they did and thus of particulars of what passes for economic knowledge at any given point in time, requires grappling with the theoretical (or empirical) nitty-gritty. In short, the minutia of the analysis itself is part of, and often a key element of, the knowledge production function.

title: The Moral Logic of Blame for Civilian Casualties: Evidence from Iraq
affiliations: University of Oxford  and

detail.title: The Moral Logic of Blame for Civilian Casualties: Evidence from Iraq

publicationDetails.detailsText: Duke Law School Public Law & Legal Theory Series Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Duke Law School Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: A large literature holds that civilian casualties are strategically costly because conflict-affected populations punish whoever harms them. Punishment implies moral judgment, but whether moral principles resonate with conflict-affected populations and how they allocate blame has not been rigorously tested. We do so with two conjoint experiments in a household survey of 1,520 residents of Mosul, Iraq, who survived ISIS's harsh rule and the devastating battle that ended it, complemented by interviews and focus groups. Respondents do not simply count bodies: they penalize the intentional killing of five civilians more than the unintentional killing of 125, reward operational success, but withdraw the support that success earns as human costs rise. Contrary to the prevailing theory, blame is not zero-sum. Respondents blame multiple actors for the same death, including, in nearly half of responses, the civilian victim. These findings have implications for counterinsurgency doctrine, civilian protection, and post-conflict reconciliation.

title: It Adds Up: The Cumulative Impact of Police Deployments
affiliations: Texas Tech University,  and Universidad de Costa Rica

detail.title: It Adds Up: The Cumulative Impact of Police Deployments
detail.abstract: Do policing effects accumulate? We study Costa Rica's Megaoperativos-high-intensity mobile police deployments sustained from 2018 to 2022-using weekly district-level data. Separating cumulative from instantaneous exposure, we isolate behavioral deterrence from mechanical detection. Cumulative exposure produces large and persistent crime reductions, with spillovers as strong as direct effects; instantaneous effects are small or positive, consistent with short-run reporting. Aggregated over the policy, we estimate roughly 19,000 prevented crimes. A simple framework linking perceived apprehension to repeated and neighboring enforcement rationalizes the patterns. Deterrence here is cumulative, additive, and geographically diffusive-not a single-operation shock.

title: Determinants of Municipal Housing Price Change: Supply, Demand, and Spatial Spillovers

detail.title: Determinants of Municipal Housing Price Change: Supply, Demand, and Spatial Spillovers

detail.abstract: Housing affordability has become a central policy concern across North America. This study estimates the relationships between municipal housing supply, demand, and price outcomes using a SAR-Error spatial regression model applied to 94 Canadian municipalities between 2016 and 2021, with housing price change measured by a Laspeyres composition-standardized index and supply measured as bedrooms per effective demand unit. Both relative supply growth and income growth were statistically significant predictors (p < .001). A 5% increase in relative housing supply was associated with approximately 12.3% lower home prices (95% CI: 6.8% to 17.5%), and a 5% income increase with approximately 6.2% higher prices (95% CI: 4.0% to 8.5%). Supply and income changes in neighbouring municipalities had spillover effects of similar magnitude. Findings offer a novel empirical framework for projecting municipal housing supply needs based on targeted price outcomes, extending North American housing needs assessment frameworks.

title: Arbitrage Bounds and Kelly-Optimal Hedging in Fixed-Odds Sports Betting Markets: A Fee-Adjusted, Time-Indexed Approach

detail.title: Arbitrage Bounds and Kelly-Optimal Hedging in Fixed-Odds Sports Betting Markets: A Fee-Adjusted, Time-Indexed Approach
detail.abstract: We develop a formal framework for arbitrage and hedging in twooutcome, fixed-odds sports betting markets, motivated by a practical hedging problem arising in soccer wagering. We derive a fee-adjusted, time-indexed arbitrage condition showing that a guaranteed-profit position is structurally unavailable within a single bookmaker's simultaneous quote, due to the bookmaker's built-in margin, but occasionally attainable across two points in time as quoted odds drift. We then extend the single-bet Kelly criterion to the two-outcome hedged case under a symmetric proportional fee, deriving a closed-form optimal hedge fraction that reduces to the standard Kelly formula in the absence of a prior position. This framework resolves an apparent tension between expectedprofit maximisation and risk minimisation by showing both to be special cases of a single expected-log-growth-maximising calculation. A preliminary check against five seasons of English Premier League data illustrates the arbitrage condition in practice, finding that it is satisfied in a modest but non-trivial fraction of matches, and we discuss the distinction between the existence of such windows and their practical exploitability as a direction for future empirical work.

title: Divergent Responses to Voluntary Sustainability Disclosure: Evidence from Domestic and Foreign Institutional Investors

detail.title: Divergent Responses to Voluntary Sustainability Disclosure: Evidence from Domestic and Foreign Institutional Investors
detail.abstract: This study investigates how voluntary sustainability disclosure influences institutional investment decisions in an emerging market, using the Thai stock market as the empirical setting. Drawing on signaling and institutional theory, the study predicts that sustainability disclosure has differential effects across investor types and that these effects vary with the strength of home-country institutional environments. Using investor-level data from 2011 to 2018, with sustainability disclosure proxied by inclusion in the Thailand Sustainability Investment (THSI) list, the analysis employs staggered difference-indifferences approaches. The findings reveal a clear divergence in institutional investor behavior. Voluntary sustainability disclosure attracts greater investment from foreign institutional investors but reduces investment by domestic institutional investors. Further analyses show that institutional investors from countries with strong governance quality and environmental social norms respond more positively to sustainability disclosure. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of investor heterogeneity and home-country institutional environments in shaping ESG-related investment decisions in emerging markets.

title: The Citizens Standard: Bounded Citizen Ownership and the Transactional-Money Locus — Price Determination and the Limits of Structural Ownership under Rules-Based Money Creation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Citizens Standard: Bounded Citizen Ownership and the Transactional-Money Locus — Price Determination and the Limits of Structural Ownership under Rules-Based Money Creation
detail.abstract: This paper derives the price-level and ownership consequences of rules-based money creation in a two-circuit monetary system, in which newly issued money is routed between a transactional circuit that prices goods and an asset circuit that holds claims on the productive economy. Inflation and citizen ownership are treated not as free parameters but as outputs of the issuance rule. Three results follow. First, price stability under a standing citizen dividend is a locus rather than a coincidence: for a given real growth rate the transactional circuit admits exactly one growth-matched expansion, which on the United States calibration is g·M^T ≈ $229.7B. Issuance beyond it is absorbed by the asset circuit, where it raises claims values rather than goods prices; issuance below it is deflationary. The four channels (K1, K2, K3, KI) are therefore a single budget under a constraint, not four free dials. Second, structural citizen ownership is bounded above by c/g — the ratio of the equity absorption flow to the growth rate — and cannot run to the whole market. The issuing authority is a permanent gross buyer with a demographically lagged gross seller attached: floors accumulate over a working life and are liquidated in retirement. The no-decumulation counterfactual diverges; the decumulating system converges. Universal ownership is thus self-limiting by construction, and the common-ownership concerns raised against large passive holders bear on a bounded share rather than on literal universal ownership. Third, the fixed-supply limit sits inside the model rather than outside it: setting every creation channel to zero yields a mildly deflationary hard-money regime as a special case, which makes the architecture a dial rather than a commitment to expansion. The paper then treats the four points at which the structure is most exposed — the M^T decomposition, the asset-to-goods spillover, the market-capitalization assumptions, and the governance of the constitutional parameters — and reports how far each conclusion moves under plausible calibration error. In each case the contested quantities are empirical inputs with stated identification strategies and bounded effects rather than load-bearing constants. Replication code for every quantity reported is cited in the references.

detail.abstract: The article is devoted to analyzes the experience of European countries in the field of anti-forestalling regulation. It was found that anti-forestalling measures are divided into four types, such as: cap on tax stamps, cap on release for consumption, sell-by date, paying the tax difference. It has been found that in some countries of the EU optimal antiforestalling regulation has been achieved over a period of time, in several stages and through the introduction of several measures at the same time. Determined that the rapid increase of excise tax rates on tobacco products in Ukraine also caused the problem of forestalling. Estimated that due to this the loss of tax revenues in 2015-2017 amounted to €2.9 to 4.5 million. It has been proved that current anti-forestalling regulation was not sufficiently effective for counteracting the accumulation of tobacco product stocks. In view of this, the article proposes a new anti-forestalling regulation in Ukraine, by improving the existing measure and introducing an additional term for the circulation of tobacco products in wholesale and retail trade with tax stamps purchased in the previous year to three months.

detail.abstract:
Institutional year-ahead outlooks anchor board discussions and investment-committee memoranda. They are almost never checked. This paper checks them. Fifteen institutions are graded across the 2024, 2025, and 2026 half-year cycles against an answer key of events that materially moved global markets, under a rubric crediting only calls specific on actor, mechanism, direction, and time window. Two further tiers extend the sample: eight banks on their published S&P 500 year-end targets, 2021 through 2026, and Eurasia Group and the World Economic Forum across a full decade.

The cross-section earns between roughly 1 and 7.5 of 45 available credits per cycle, and no call in any cycle earns full credit. The street's flagship call missed direction in consecutive opposite years, a median target of 4,825 ahead of the 19 percent decline of 2022 and 4,000 ahead of the 24 percent rally of 2023, with targets revised intra-year to follow realized prices. Confident anti-predictions fail symmetrically at both ends of the decade: the 2016 report dismissed the US presidential election as a red herring, and the 2026 report dismissed "Sell America" in the half-year official gold holdings overtook foreign-held Treasuries. The instrument transmitting each cycle's largest repricing appears on no published list. The record's strong calls share one feature, each described an already-formed present condition rather than predicting a discontinuity.

All grading tables are published for replication. A rescore with a second independent coder is pre-registered for December 31, 2026

detail.title: A biofunctional memristor with machine learning and neuromorphic biosensing for intelligent detection of adenoviruses
detail.abstract: Adenovirus (AdVs) infection of the central nervous system (CNS) often leads to disorders of consciousness, paralysis, and even death. However, accurate and timely detection of AdVs infection in the CNS remains a clinical gap. Herein, we prepared an Ag/βCD-G/Ta2O5/FTO memristor, where the β-cyclodextrin-gelatin (βCD-G) interfacial layer can selectively capture and enrich AdVs, while the Ta2O5 layer converts the binding event into a stable and quantifiable resistance switching. Upon AdVs exposure, the memristor exhibits a concentration-dependent suppression of the resistance window above 105 VP·mL-1 across physiologically relevant matrices, including artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF). Specifically, by coupling memristor-derived electrical responses with an XGBoost classifier, these subtle perturbation-encoded signals can be robustly decoded without external signal preprocessing, achieving an aggregated ROC AUC of 0.962, an aggregated PR average precision of 0.992, and an overall classification accuracy of 0.956. In addition, circuit simulation verified that the device can perform in-sensor logic gate operations, highlighting its potential in edge computing diagnostics. Furthermore, it demonstrates excellent biocompatibility without histopathological abnormalities or behavioral deficits by a 14-day intracranial implantation in mice. Therefore, this work provides a rapid strategy for real-time intelligent pathogen detection, paving the way for the neuromorphic memristive-sensor in the applications of neuroscience.

title: Effective Legal Remedies without Courts? The Role of Supervisory Authorities in EU Digital Regulation

detail.title: Effective Legal Remedies without Courts? The Role of Supervisory Authorities in EU Digital Regulation
detail.abstract: EU digital regulation increasingly relies on supervisory authorities not only to enforce regulatory obligations, but also to provide effective remedies for individuals. This reflects a broader shift from a court-centred model of rights protection, towards a more pluralistic system in which administrative authorities play a central role in safeguarding fundamental rights. This paper examines that development by analysing the complaint mechanisms established across the EU digital acquis, including, amongst others, the General Data Protection Regulation, Digital Services Act, Artificial Intelligence Act and the Data Act. It argues that, although these complaint procedures are increasingly framed as administrative remedies, their procedural design remains rooted in the logic of public enforcement. Drawing on the experience of complaint handling under the GDPR, the paper demonstrates a structural misalignment between the remedial function assigned to supervisory authorities and the enforcement-oriented procedures through which complaints are handled. It further argues that arguments such as accessibility and efficiency, commonly invoked to justify the shift towards administrative remedies, derive from the authorities' public enforcement mandate and do not readily support their emerging adjudicative role. The paper concludes that the growing reliance on supervisory authorities to resolve disputes between two parties raises a broader constitutional question: under what conditions can administrative authorities legitimately perform functions traditionally associated with courts? It argues that, if complaint procedures are to constitute genuine alternatives to judicial remedies, they must be accompanied by procedural guarantees and institutional safeguards appropriate to the adjudication of individual rights.

title: The Citizens Standard: Constitutional Vulnerability of a Rules-Based Monetary Statute — Nondelegation, Takings, and the Limits of Entrenchment
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Citizens Standard: Constitutional Vulnerability of a Rules-Based Monetary Statute — Nondelegation, Takings, and the Limits of Entrenchment
detail.abstract: Proposals to place money creation under a binding rule have, with few exceptions, sought the constitutional route and failed there. This paper asks the prior question. Can a rules-based, citizen-anchored monetary architecture be enacted by ordinary statute and survive constitutional review — and if so, where is it most exposed? The answer developed here inverts the usual framing: the authority is not seriously in doubt, but the durability is. Congress's power to coin money and regulate its value, read broadly in the Legal Tender Cases (1871) and confirmed in peacetime in Juilliard v. Greenman (1884), is the constitutional basis of the modern dollar; a statute issuing money under the same authority requires no new grant of power. The genuinely novel element is distributional — routing new issuance to citizens as vested accounts — and it is that element, not the money power, that carries the litigation risk. The paper maps four vulnerabilities against current doctrine and rates each. Nondelegation is the least exposed, not the most. A formula that runs automatically from published inputs delegates almost nothing, and it satisfies each prong of the test Justice Gorsuch set out in dissent in Gundy v. United States (2019); Loper Bright (2024), by withdrawing deference from agency construction, further favours a power written explicitly into the statute over one left to an agency to fill in. Separation of powers is moderate and turns on whether the issuing authority's certification function is a report or a veto — the distinction Bowsher v. Synar (1986) makes dispositive. Takings is moderate and depends on a drafting choice: accounts vested as individually owned private property at the citizen event fall outside the Flemming v. Nestor (1960) line that treats social insurance as revocable, and inside the Fifth Amendment. Entrenchment is the hardest, and this paper does not claim to solve it. The supermajority repeal threshold on which the design relies is precisely the device Roberts and Chemerinsky (2003) argue is impermissible — a rule preventing a present majority from undoing a predecessor's choice — even as Posner and Vermeule (2002) contend the anti-entrenchment rule has no sound foundation at all. We do not resolve that debate. We concede the legal point and relocate the claim: a statute's durability rests not on the threshold that guards it but on the constituency it creates. Vesting a compounding property interest in every citizen is entrenchment by functional alternative in the sense of Levinson and Sachs (2015) — it does not make repeal unlawful, it makes repeal expensive. That is a weaker claim than the constitutional version of the architecture, and it is the strongest one ordinary legislation can support.

title: A Unified Neuroeconomic Model of Decision-Making: Expected Utility, Evidence Accumulation, and Homo ADM
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Unified Neuroeconomic Model of Decision-Making: Expected Utility, Evidence Accumulation, and Homo ADM
detail.abstract: Economics often works with rational-agent frameworks, particularly Expected Utility Theory (EUT), and increasingly incorporates process-based models such as the Drift Diffusion Model (DDM). With the development of neuroeconomics and critical perspectives in economic methodology, the rational-agent framework and several assumptions underlying econometric modelling have been increasingly questioned and re-evaluated. This article presents a modified integration of EUT and DDM, synthesised with contemporary developments in neuroeconomics. The article also examines the limitations of economic equations, or more precisely, a rethinking of critiques of both the rational agent and economic modelling more broadly, as well as the possibility of complementing agent-centred approaches with alternative perspectives. Furthermore, it introduces Homo ADM (Automaticus-Deliberativus-Meta) as a multilayered cognitive architecture integrating automatic, deliberative, and metacognitive processes.

title: Tipping, Coexistence, and Protected Niches: A Microfounded Dynamic Duopoly Taxonomy of Standards Wars
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Tipping, Coexistence, and Protected Niches: A Microfounded Dynamic Duopoly Taxonomy of Standards Wars
detail.abstract: We provide a microeconomic foundation for the differential-equation models long used to describe technological substitution, and use it to build a taxonomy of standards wars. Two firms selling incompatible technologies maximize profits against a kinked inverse demand, in which the cross externality is symmetric across technologies and demand derives from a representative consumer whose utility generates the system exactly on the economically active region; the resulting best-response dynamics coincide, up to a positive time rescaling, with profit-gradient adjustment, and a representative-consumer potential replicates the demand system exactly on the economically active region. Quantity data identify a reduced-form parameter vector whose two dimensionless combinations classify the entire Nash equilibrium set: a tipping index 𝜅 1 𝜅 2 and a differentiation ratio √ 𝜇 1 /𝑅 1. When both firms' rivals exceed level-based annihilation thresholds, the game has three equilibriatwo stable dominance outcomes and an interior saddleand history selects among them; otherwise a unique stable equilibrium obtains, ranging from symmetric coexistence to drive-through annihilation. We calibrate one and the same eight-parameter model to six standards wars: Betamax-VHS, Android-iOS, e-readerstablets, cassette-vinyl, CD-cassette, and the live NACS-CCS-CHAdeMO charging-connector contest. The model reproduces each trajectory (𝑅 2 between 0.86 and 0.99), dates the VHS tipping event to 1984 with a bootstrap confidence interval, shows that a Betamax-victory equilibrium existed, finds that cassettes would never have killed vinyl, that the CD annihilated the cassette without any equilibrium multiplicity, that the smartphone duopoly sits statistically on the tipping boundary, and that the e-reader industry survives in closed form off its differentiation parameter. Welfare is set-identifiedthe unobservable split of demand curvature from cost convexity enters every surplus object affinelyyielding sharp bounds and ranking results across all five calibrated wars: the VHS-monopoly equilibrium dominates the Betamax alternative on 89 percent of the admissible split space, the CD transition was welfare-improving on 90 percent of it, vinyl's incremental social value was approximately zero, and the smartphone market's decade-long interior state is welfare-dominated by either tipping outcome at the point estimates. A nested installed-base extension cannot be distinguished from flow rivalry in these data, and all substantive conclusions are invariant to the choice.

title: The Financial Layer as Measuring Instrument: The Pricing of Time in the Global Flow System

detail.title: The Financial Layer as Measuring Instrument: The Pricing of Time in the Global Flow System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an independent geostrategic theorist with no institutional, commercial, or financial relationship bearing on this study. The author declares no competing interests. The analysis is the author's own independent scholarly work and does not represent the position of any institution.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a theoretical and analytical study in geostrategy and international political economy. It involves no human or animal participants, no clinical or experimental data, and no personal data. Ethics approval is therefore not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or funding from any agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. It was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the global financial system as the measuring layer of a wider flow system, the structure through which disturbances in energy, logistics, information, and industrial capacity resolve into a single priced dimension: the price of time. The argument proceeds historically and structurally. It traces the flow system's genesis from prehistoric exchange through the Bronze Age, classical antiquity, the Industrial Revolution, and Bretton Woods, to establish that the financial layer's measuring function is a historical formation rather than a fixed property of money. It then maps the contemporary financial layer across its constituent strata: the dollar-centered foundational layer of central banks and reserves; the payments infrastructure of CHIPS, Fedwire, SWIFT, and their emerging alternatives (CIPS, SPFS, mBridge); capital markets and the derivatives complex; currency and commodity markets; marine and war-risk insurance; shadow banking and institutional investors; and the digital infrastructure of stablecoins and central bank digital currencies. A dedicated analytical frame, the price of system capacity, is developed to distinguish transactional pricing from the price of mobilizing an entire system under stress, illustrated through a military case (a 2026 combat search-and-rescue mission in Iran) and applied to central bank balance-sheet capacity. A case study of the United Arab Emirates during the first half of 2026 documents how an acute financial vortex can convert into a durable, multi-quarter crisis state. A further section maps the financial layer's algorithmic substrate, where trading now runs on a microsecond timescale outside human decision rhythm, producing a new class of self-generated vortex. The paper's central claim is that by 2026 the global financial space has bifurcated into two parallel, selectively connected systems, a Western dollar-centered space and a parallel gold-renminbi-CIPS space, coordinated not through alliance but through direct, capital-level settlement among the United States, China, and Russia. The Strait of Hormuz functions as the operational intersection of that coordination. The paper concludes that the financial layer's twofold function, as both measure and amplifier of systemic tension, points beyond its own analytical boundary toward the question of compute and the extension of flow beyond the terrestrial system, addressed in a separate analysis.

title: Equity, Private Ordering, and Corporate Law
affiliations: The University of Mississippi School of Law

detail.title: Equity, Private Ordering, and Corporate Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: The University of Mississippi School of Law Summer Scholarship Grant

detail.abstract:
Equity, private ordering, and law are the cornerstones of corporate governance.  Courts and scholars regularly hold forth on the interaction between them, drawing the lines separating them ever more finely.  According to most scholars and judges, fundamental tensions beset these interactions.  Among them: Contractarian theory cannot account for mandatory rules of corporate law.  Private ordering must yield when it conflicts with judicial authority to make sound public policy.  Equitable features of corporate doctrine are in tension with private ordering.  Because of this, corporate governance is left to muddle along with no complete theory, forever locked in a battle where law, equity, and private ordering conflict.

The result in Delaware has been the development of a corporate law that is, frustratingly, both inconsistent and rigid.  In turn, recent cases spurred a flurry of blunt legislative changes as a rearguard effort to fix it.  All this for a corporate law canon where the selling points are supposed to be stability, clarity, and expertise.

      This Article proposes a new theory to help resolve the tension: The Corporate Bargain Model.  The Corporate Bargain Model reveals that, contrary to the oft-recited tension between them, mandatory corporate law, equitable doctrines, and private ordering are in fact harmonious.  Indeed, every corporation, of every shape and size, consists of a unique corporate bargain, which contains all aspects of the parties’ relationships over time.  Sound equitable reasoning facilitates private ordering, specifically and importantly, of the tacit or relational kind, by inquiring carefully into the entire terms of that corporate bargain – not just expressly chosen terms, default rules of law, or even curated principles of equity.

title: Policy Design and Strategic Compliance: Incentives of Crypto Exchanges under EU's MiCA Framework
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Policy Design and Strategic Compliance: Incentives of Crypto Exchanges under EU's MiCA Framework
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of cryptocurrency markets has positioned exchanges as core infrastructure in the digital asset ecosystem. Episodes of exchange collapse have exposed systemic vulnerabilities arising from weak governance, insufficient transparency, inadequate risk management, and cybersecurity weaknesses, prompting regulators to adopt more comprehensive oversight frameworks. This paper asks whether regulatory compliance can function as a coordination mechanism that aligns profit-seeking exchange behavior with long-term market stability. Focusing on the European Union's Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) framework, the study examines how exchanges respond strategically to regulatory constraints and how alternative compliance outcomes affect welfare. The methodological approach draws primarily from game theory, supplemented by institutional analysis from communications and financial regulation. The paper develops a multiplayer game in which cryptocurrency exchanges choose among alternative compliance strategies within MiCA. These include capital safeguards, governance standards, cybersecurity obligations, and disclosure rules, modeled as strategic policy choices rather than purely exogenous constraints. Exchanges select their policy set once and interact repeatedly over time, allowing reputation effects and long-term incentives to influence outcomes. Each policy is evaluated using a scoring framework capturing its expected impact on market capitalization, investor trust, exchange security, and compliance costs. The framework is informed by historical developments, including major incidents such as the Mt. Gox Hack (2014) and the Bybit Hack (2025), incorporating lessons from past failures and subsequent security improvements. We analyze the outcome of the game through computational simulations exploring equilibria, payoff structures, and aggregate welfare under different configurations. The analysis suggests two possible equilibria. In the first, exchanges adopt full MiCA compliance, resulting in higher aggregate welfare due to increased trust and reduced systemic risk. In the second, exchanges converge on cost-minimizing partial compliance. While individually rational, this outcome generates lower collective payoffs due to reduced investor confidence, illustrating a coordination problem. We further evaluate efficiency using the Price of Anarchy and the Price of Stability; in our model, the latter equals one, indicating that the socially optimal outcome can be sustained as an equilibrium. These findings suggest that regulatory design has a significant impact on exchange incentives. Rather than serving only as an external constraint, compliance may facilitate coordination toward higher-trust market outcomes. This contributes to debates in digital market policy by linking regulatory architecture to strategic behavior in crypto-asset markets, highlighting the importance of minimizing regulatory arbitrage and ensuring consistent enforcement.

title: From State Security to Self-security: The Individualization of Security in Digital Society
affiliations: and University of Dhaka

detail.title: From State Security to Self-security: The Individualization of Security in Digital Society
detail.abstract: Digital technology has produced a real shift in where security threats come from and who is responsible for facing them. Security studies has long treated security as protection of the state, built around armies, treaties, and borders. That picture has changed. A person today can be harmed through a data breach, identity theft, or covert data harvesting without any state or army being involved at all. Drawing on securitization theory and the concept of human security, the argument here is that the individual has become a security actor in their own right, exposed to threats that states are often slow to recognize and even slower to take necessary action. The main categories of digital threats individuals face are surveyed, along with the uneven distribution of responsibility across governments, companies, and individuals themselves, using the Cambridge Analytica case as a concrete illustration. The conclusion is that this individualization of security is not a temporary side effect of new technology but a lasting shift in where risk sits, one that both policy and security studies as a field need to catch up to.

title: How Important is Internal Information Asymmetry for Firm-Level Productivity?
affiliations: University of Connecticut,  and University of Connecticut - Department of Accounting

detail.title: How Important is Internal Information Asymmetry for Firm-Level Productivity?

keywords: internal capital markets JEL Codes: G23

detail.abstract: Theoretical research suggests internal information asymmetry (IIA) between top managers and divisional managers can reduce productivity by distorting internal resource allocation. The net effect, however, is unclear because IIA also reflects valuable private information within divisions, and empirical evidence is limited due to the unobservability of managers' private information sets. Using a measure of IIA that exploits differences in returns to insider trading by top and divisional managers, we find that higher IIA is associated with lower total factor productivity. A one standard deviation increase in IIA corresponds to a 2.6% decrease in productivity relative to industry peers. This effect is comparable in magnitude to other important internal informational frictions, such as internal control weaknesses, and is distinct from internal information quality (IIQ). Cross-sectional analyses indicate that the negative association is stronger when curative measures are limited and when agency conflicts between top managers and shareholders are greater. Mechanism tests indicate that IIA reduces internal capital market efficiency and increases underinvestment. Finally, using brokerage mergers and closures as a plausibly exogenous shock, we find that increases in IIA lead to declines in productivity. Overall, we provide empirical evidence that IIA is an economically important determinant of firm-level productivity.

title: Accounting and the Informal Economy: A Review and Discussion

detail.title: Accounting and the Informal Economy: A Review and Discussion

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Accounting and Economics, Forthcoming

detail.abstract: This paper discusses Aguilar, Lind, and Ramesh's study of accounting practices in the informal economy. Using survey data from the International Labour Organization (ILO), the authors document that a substantial fraction of informal microenterprises in Central America voluntarily maintain accounting records, and that accounting quality is associated with owner characteristics, financing choices, access to credit, and business expansion plans. I situate these findings within the broader literature on informality and on the role of accounting in economic development, and argue that the paper opens up a promising agenda for accounting research in developing economies. I also outline directions for future work, including the need for research that can identify the causal effect of accounting on economic development.

title: A Currency Premium Puzzle
affiliations: , Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco and Boston University

detail.title: A Currency Premium Puzzle

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The views expressed here are solely those of the authors and do not necessarily represent those of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco or the Federal Reserve System. We thank John Campbell, Mikhail Chernov, Riccardo Colacito, Max Croce, Xiang Fang, Federico Gavazzoni, Valentin Haddad, Jonathan Heathcote, Oleg Itskhoki, Rohan Kekre, Robert Kollmann, Moritz Lenel, Pierre De Leo, Pierlauro Lopez, Hanno Lustig, Matteo Maggiori, Andreas Stathopoulos, Adrien Verdelhan, Rosen Valchev, and seminar participants at the University of Southern California, SUFE, PKU NSD, Macro Finance Society, WFA 2024, CFRC 2024, NBER SI 2024, NBER Asset Pricing 2024, AFA 2025, and 3rd International Finance/Macro/Trade Conference for helpful comments.

detail.abstract: We show that quantitative asset pricing models, built to address the equity premium and risk-free rate puzzles, systematically fail when applied to open economies: they cannot generate the large and persistent interest rate differentials we observe between risky and safe currencies. This failure stems from the key mechanism that produces their success in matching both closed-economy puzzles: In these models, the mean of the stochastic discount factor offsets its variance nearly one-for-one, which immobilizes interest rates-so that differences in expected currency returns across countries must arise almost exclusively from predictable changes in exchange rates, at odds with the data. We prove this result in a broad class of models that allows for market incompleteness and exchange rate disconnect, requiring only that each country's risk-free asset is priced by investors who demand compensation for risk in line with observed risk premia. We argue this tension between canonical asset pricing and international macroeconomic models is a key reason researchers have struggled to reconcile the observed behavior of exchange rates, interest rates, and capital flows across countries. * The views expressed here are solely those of the authors and do not necessarily represent those of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco or the Federal Reserve System.

title: The Gender Preference Gap: Evidence from Two Decades of Experimental Research
affiliations: University of Lausanne and University of Sydney

detail.title: The Gender Preference Gap: Evidence from Two Decades of Experimental Research
detail.abstract: This paper presents a large-scale meta-analysis of gender differences in economic preferences, drawing on individual-level data from 255 samples across 188 experimental economics studies and comprising more than 140,000 participants. We examine differences in both means and variances across time, risk, competition, honesty, and social preferences. Our analysis reveals systematic gender differences in both central tendencies and variability. Mean differences are largest for competitive preferences and smallest for social preferences. Across nearly all measures, men exhibit greater variability than women. We compare these effect sizes with gender differences in labor market outcomes. Mean differences in risk preferences are comparable in magnitude to the gender wage gap, whereas mean differences in competitive preferences are substantially larger. Among the most risk-tolerant participants, the male-to-female ratio is close to 2:1, while among those with the strongest competitive preferences it is approximately 5:1-a ratio comparable to the current gender composition of corporate boards of directors.

title: An Integrated, Name-Attributed Geospatial Dataset of Natural Park Regulatory Zones in Gifu Prefecture
