detail.title: Firms Relocation Saga: A Bibliometric and Econometric Analysis of Firm Relocation Research
detail.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive examination of the scholarly literature concerning firm relocation. I assess a broad collection of studies in this domain, tracing their development from the earliest records to the current day. By classifying the research according to its medium of dissemination-distinguishing between PDFs, web-based content, and books-I detect a pronounced transition in citation practices over the decades. Whereas books once formed the primary vehicle for sharing insights, PDF-based formats have now become overwhelmingly dominant. The available evidence further indicates that PDF articles tend to garner a substantially higher number of citations than books, pointing to a tangible impact advantage for digital formats. The volume of publication has risen sharply in more recent years, with the greatest density of papers occurring in the modern period. A closer inspection of the subject matter reveals a significant evolution in scholarly focus. Earlier work concentrated chiefly on conventional location determinants, such as input costs and logistical considerations. More recently, however, the discourse has gravitated toward contemporary issues, including cross-border production shifts, industrial repatriation, technological digitization, and the influence of sudden regulatory interventions. Cumulatively, this review enables me to map the field's progression toward maturity, highlight the scholarly rewards of adopting current publication modes, and establish a foundational reference point for future bibliometric inquiries in economic geography.

title: Dharma Beyond Outcomes: Conscience as the Measure of an Impeccable Life
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Dharma Beyond Outcomes: Conscience as the Measure of an Impeccable Life
detail.abstract: This essay argues that righteous action consists in fidelity to conscience-disciplined by truthfulness and non-harm, values it derives as the minimal preconditions of discernment itself rather than assuming outright-regardless of outcome, following the Bhagavad Gita's teaching on action without attachment to its fruits. It defines adharma not as any particular ideology but as a recurring mechanism: the substitution of a pre-issued category for case-by-case discernment, visible alike in caste, in the strand of Enlightenment rationality that fused with commerce, in market logic, in certain forms of identity politics, and inside rule of law itself, whenever protection from harm is made conditional on prior classification rather than grounded in the harm itselfwhile distinguishing this from a case against rules as such, since fixed categories remain indispensable protections against power asymmetry and the cognitive limits of individual discretion, and become adharmic only when they stop answering to the case they were made to serve. Extending the discernment test from the individual to the organization, the essay develops an account of dharma as a continuously learnt protocol rather than a fixed virtue or rule-a discipline of reverence for the other that must be relearned at each encounter, illustrated through natural coexistence (the platypus and its ecology) and collective synergy (a football team in flow), and drawing a considered distinction from relativism, Kantian deontology, virtue ethics, care ethics, stakeholder theory, value pluralism, agonistic pluralism, and Ubuntu ethics. It then confronts the vulnerability of any such process account-that a learnt protocol can drift into capture while still calling itself dharmic-and examines, without fully resolving, what kind of reference could correct such drift without repeating the very fault it corrects, drawing on the Samkhya distinction between Purusha and Prakriti and the Saiva Siddhanta relation of Siva and Sakti as models of a reference incapable of capture because it does not act, while being explicit that neither this reference nor the appeal to love that follows from it constitutes an operational solution to the drift problem-only an orientation the unresolved work of discernment must not lose sight of. The essay closes by applying this framework honestly to artificial intelligencearguing that an AI system is structurally all Sakti and no Siva, that human oversight cannot itself supply the uncapturable reference the argument requires, and that this limitation, honestly acknowledged, is itself the more useful contribution to AI ethics than a false resolution would be.

detail.abstract: This analysis examines the sharp surge and modest reversal of overall homelessness between 2022 and 2025 according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's (HUD) 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report (AHAR). After rising by 32% (189,018 people) between 2022 and 2024, literal homelessness on any given night fell by 3% (25,828) between 2024 and 2025. Underneath this slight decline are two divergent trends: an 11% drop in family homelessness paired with continued increases in individual and chronic homelessness, which both reached record highs. The reversal was also concentrated in the same geographies that accounted for the majority of the previous increases. States like New York and Illinois attribute this reversal to a declining inflow of migrants and the closing of emergency shelters temporarily constructed to serve new arrivals (U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development [HUD], 2026b). We demonstrate that the surge and partial reversal were both driven by local dynamics rather than a broader national trend.

detail.abstract: Disability narratives are inspired by the lived experiences and first-person accounts of people with disabilities. Disability narratives are essential for understanding and promoting inclusion within society, as they allow disabled and nondisabled individuals to understand the many components that play into the disabled experience. Despite this importance, disability narratives suffer from a lack of conceptual clarity and inconsistencies with intersectionality, diversity, inclusion and accessibility. Additionally, representation is inconsistent, highlighting those with visible disabilities, white experiences and nondisabled perspectives. This showcases a challenge within disability narratives that contributes to a limited view of identities. This explication follows Miller's (2023) seven-step explication process to narrow down a concise conceptual definition of disability narratives, allowing for better understanding of academic research and proper media representation. This explication uses quantitative analysis to establish the core ideas and frameworks of disability narratives. Key findings of this explication include an emphasis on identity, representation and accessibility. This explication displays conceptual precision and supports future research and analysis of disability representation.

title: The Nature of Firm Financing and Growth
affiliations: INSEAD - Finance, Imperial College Business School,  and Imperial College Business School

detail.title: The Nature of Firm Financing and Growth
detail.abstract: Using the universe of incorporated firms in the United Kingdom, we document that long term debt that is not secured by specific corporate assets (commonly referred to as cash-flow-based debt) is ubiquitous, even among very young firms. Consistent with cash-flow-based lending depending on firms' continuation value, both the timing and the amount of cash-flow-based debt at first financing are strongly related to future performance. In fact, the age at which firms first access cash-flow-based long-term debt is a strong predictor of firm outcomes up to twenty years later. In contrast, the age at which firms access asset-based lending does not predict future performance. To understand how lending based on continuation value impacts firm dynamics, we develop a tractable theory of firm life cycle dynamics with permanent heterogeneity and financing frictions-where access to finance can be based on signals of both current and future performance. The model highlights the importance of financing based on future value in matching the predictability of cash-flow-based financing observed in the data. It also highlights how frictions to financing based on available collateral vs. future value lead to differential selection and hence very different distributions of firms that survive and grow. The degree to which firms can access financing based on future value is therefore fundamentally intertwined with aggregate firm dynamics.

detail.abstract: Studies and reports show that over half of SMEs fail within the first five years of inception, and over one-third fail within the first two years of operation. As a result, the study aims to harness the potential of intellectual capital, formal education, hard/soft skills, and e-commerce to drive competitive advantage and enhance SME's performance in Kwara State. The study was grounded in Resource-Based Theory and Dynamic Capabilities Theory because of their effectiveness in explaining the subject. This study employed a descriptive survey research design for a population of 3,124 SMEs registered with the Kwara State Board of Internal Revenue. The sample size was determined using Raosoft online, resulting in 354. The study was analyzed using descriptive statistics, measures of central tendency and inferential statistics. It was found that formal education has a weak but statistically significant positive influence on SMEs' performance (R=0.305; p<0.001). Also, hard/soft skills have a positive (moderately significant) influence on SMEs' performance (R = 0.428; p<0.001). Finally, e-commerce platforms have a weak but statistically significant positive effect on SMEs' performance (R=0.322, p<0.001). The study found that e-commerce adoption appears more prevalent among experienced SME operators. Similarly, using both hard and soft skills is necessary to integrate e-commerce into corporate processes. SME vendors are advised to use social media and e-commerce platforms to boost their online presence.

detail.abstract: The federal professional accountability system—the institutional framework through which attorneys admitted to practice before federal courts are investigated, adjudicated, and sanctioned for professional misconduct—operates through a complex governance architecture of distributed authority spanning state licensing authorities, federal district courts, courts of appeals, agency professional-responsibility offices, and the Supreme Court. Although this distribution preserves constitutional checks and balances, professional independence, and federalism values, it also creates conditions under which accountability processes may fail when authority, information, or coordination become insufficiently integrated across organizational boundaries. This paper applies the Governance Accountability Architecture (GAA) framework to the federal professional accountability system as a diagnostic test case. Building directly upon the general theory developed in Paper A of the GAA Research Series (Whiteside & Whitesides, 2026a), the paper examines how governance architecture may influence accountability-process performance, procedural legitimacy, trust production, and institutional trust within the federal judiciary. The paper introduces Judicial Governance Capacity (JGC) as a domain-specific application of the broader Institutional Governance Capacity construct and proposes five Provisional Judicial Trust Dimensions as domain-specific applications of the Institutional Trust Framework. The paper develops a provisional map of the Governance Authority Configuration, specifies how Governance Authority Integration could be evaluated across five dimensions, identifies conditions under which Distributed Accountability Failure may emerge, and proposes four comparative institutional counterfactuals—information integration only, coordination integration only, hybrid federal credential, and consolidated federal accountability system—to isolate the distinct mechanisms through which governance architecture may influence accountability outcomes. The federal professional-accountability domain serves as the first theory-elaborating application of the framework. By assessing the framework's conceptual fit and identifying domain-specific mechanisms, boundary conditions, and testable propositions, the paper establishes a structured basis for evaluating whether the framework can be adapted to additional domains. Cross-domain portability remains a proposition to be assessed through cumulative comparison rather than a conclusion established by this paper. The paper concludes with a measurement-development agenda and comparative research design for future empirical testing.

detail.abstract: Can fiscal space from artificial intelligence finance recurrent social protection in Latin America? This paper develops a prespecified, scenario-based feasibility test that translates an AI dividend into income and fiscal capture, compares it with policy costs, and applies debt-consistency and persistence screens. For Peru, Chile, Colombia, and Mexico, no deterministic crossing occurs under non-stress scenarios because translation and capture jointly fall short. Crossings arise only under diagnostic disruption: Chilean guaranteed minimum income is conditionally feasible and debt-consistent; Peru's social pension crosses accounting but fails the debt guardrail; Colombia and Mexico do not cross. Crossing frequencies are model-implied, not predictive probabilities.

title: How Can Digitization and Artificial Intelligence Enhance Service Delivery in Kenya's Marginalized Units to Combat Corruption and Foster Development?

detail.title: How Can Digitization and Artificial Intelligence Enhance Service Delivery in Kenya's Marginalized Units to Combat Corruption and Foster Development?
detail.abstract: Kenya's arid and semi-arid marginalized counties, including Turkana, Mandera, Wajir, Garissa, Samburu, Marsabit, and Tana River, continue to experience the compounded effects of historical neglect, weak public infrastructure, and endemic corruption that together undermine equitable service delivery. This paper examines how digitization and artificial intelligence (AI) can strengthen service delivery, curb corruption, and foster inclusive development in these historically underserved regions. Drawing on peer-reviewed literature, government policy documents, and recent empirical studies, the paper situates Kenya's digitization agendaanchored in the Kenya National Digital Master Plan 2022-2032, the Huduma Kenya and e-Citizen platforms, the Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS), and the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2030-within the country's broader governance and anti-corruption reform trajectory. It argues that while digitization has demonstrated measurable gains in reducing opportunities for petty corruption and improving administrative efficiency, its benefits remain unevenly distributed, with marginalized counties experiencing persistent digital exclusion, weak connectivity, and elevated risk of exclusion from digital identity and welfare systems. The paper further considers the dual-use character of AI as both a tool for detecting and deterring corruption and a potential source of new governance risks, including opacity, centralization of administrative discretion, and data protection harms. It concludes with policy recommendations emphasizing infrastructure equity, rights-based digital identity reform, human-centred and explainable AI design, and strengthened institutional capacity as prerequisites for digitization and AI to meaningfully advance transparency and development in Kenya's margins.

title: Governance Deficits in a Marginalized Devolved Unit: Corruption, Capacity, and Accountability Challenges in Turkana County, Kenya

detail.title: Governance Deficits in a Marginalized Devolved Unit: Corruption, Capacity, and Accountability Challenges in Turkana County, Kenya
detail.abstract: Since the promulgation of the Constitution of Kenya in 2010, devolution has been presented as the principal mechanism for redressing the historical marginalization of Kenya's arid and semi-arid regions. More than a decade into the devolved dispensation, Turkana County, the country's second-largest county by land area and among its poorest, illustrates both the promise and the limits of this reform. Drawing on Auditor-General reports, parliamentary records, national statistical data, peer-reviewed studies, and contemporaneous news reporting, this paper examines eight interlocking governance deficits in Turkana County: (1) corruption and misappropriation of public funds; (2) limited innovation and weak digital infrastructure constraining e-government; (3) high adult illiteracy and constrained human capital; (4) structural dependency on donor and humanitarian aid; (5) weak monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems undermining project sustainability; (6) the absence of structured, competitive human-resource frameworks in the county public service; (7) patronage-oriented cash disbursements at the expense of infrastructure investment; and (8) a persistent gap between projects reported as "complete" in audit records and their actual, often non-functional, state on the ground. The paper situates these findings within good-governance and principal-agent theoretical frameworks and within the broader literature on devolution and corruption in Kenya. It concludes with a set of policy recommendations, including the adoption of performance-linked contractual employment in the county public service, strengthened County Integrated Monitoring and Evaluation Systems (CIMES), and greater public disclosure of project status and expenditure.

title: Machine Learning for Financial Statement Manipulation Risk Prediction in a Frontier Market: Evidence from Nepal
affiliations: University of Delhi - Ramjas College

detail.title: Machine Learning for Financial Statement Manipulation Risk Prediction in a Frontier Market: Evidence from Nepal
detail.abstract:
Fraud detection models have been trained and validated on data from developed markets, where disclosures follow standard formats and enforcement runs deep (Beneish, 1999; Dechow, Ge, Larson, & Sloan, 2011; Gepp, Kumar, & Bhattacharya, 2021; Perols, 2011). Nobody has tested whether these models retain their predictive power in frontier markets, where filings are incomplete and regulators lack capacity. Models trained on NYSE- or ASX-listed firms have never been tested against incomplete filings, weak oversight, and a financial system that bears little resemblance to the markets where the models were built.

Nepal provides a useful test case. NEPSE lists approximately 300 companies. The Securities Board of Nepal (SEBON) has pursued firms for late filings but has not, during our sample period, brought enforcement actions related to accounting manipulation. The listed universe is dominated by banks, microfinance companies, and hydropower developers. That sector mix does not exist in the US panels that trained Beneish or Dechow models. Annual reports present additional challenges: many are published in Nepali, typeset in Preeti font (a non-Unicode encoding that prevents standard text extraction), and they omit receivables or fixed asset data that the Modified Jones Model requires.

Gepp, Kumar, and Bhattacharya (2021, 2024) built the GEPP framework for fraud detection using financial ratios, market signals, and governance variables. Their approach normalizes ratios by industry median and predicts manipulation one year forward. The framework has performed well on US and Australian data. No study has tested whether it retains that performance when variable coverage drops below 50% and the panel spans only a decade.

We started with a simple assumption: if the same economic incentives that drive manipulation in the US (debt covenants, profitability pressure, size-related scrutiny) also drive it in Nepal, then the same machine learning methods should work in both settings. We expected the models to work, but we expected lower accuracy than what US studies report, and we expected macroeconomic variables to matter more in Nepal given the country's greater economic volatility.

Three questions motivate this paper. First, can publicly available financial data predict next-year manipulation risk among NEPSE-listed firms? Second, which predictors dominate, firm-level characteristics or macroeconomic conditions? Third, do macroeconomic controls add predictive value beyond what firm-level ratios provide on their own? A Random Forest model answers all three.

title:
Four Lenses of AI Measurement: Capable on Paper 
A Deployment-context Framework for Organizational AI Capability Assessment

detail.title:
Four Lenses of AI Measurement: Capable on Paper 
A Deployment-context Framework for Organizational AI Capability Assessment
detail.abstract: Organizations routinely assess what an artificial intelligence system can do under evaluation conditions and then deploy it under conditions that differ, producing a systematic gap between assessed and delivered capability. This paper argues that the gap is a measurement problem rather than solely a matter of governance or implementation, and that it can be assessed before deployment rather than discovered through failure. It develops the capability lens, the third in a four-lens architecture for organizational AI measurement, by distinguishing general deployment capability, the performance a system can reach under favorable conditions, from deployment-context capability, the performance it delivers under the conditions of a specific organizational use. The gap between the two is located in five degradation pathways, distribution shift, integration degradation, scope creep, temporal degradation, and use-condition divergence, each tied to a documented phenomenon in the machine learning literature and each corresponding to a specifiable dimension of a deployment context. The paper proposes design requirements for a pre-deployment diagnostic instrument, works one dimension in full as a proof of concept, and addresses the interaction among pathways through qualitative governance heuristics, a red-flag override and a decision matrix, that route diagnostic readings to proportionate pre-launch actions rather than to a combined score. A discontinued retail computer-vision deployment serves as the running case. The instrument is offered as a structured diagnostic rather than a predictive model, and its validation is identified as the work that remains.

title: Forecasting Economic Time Series Under Volatility: A Comparative Study of K-Nearest Neighbors and Exponential Smoothing

detail.title: Forecasting Economic Time Series Under Volatility: A Comparative Study of K-Nearest Neighbors and Exponential Smoothing
detail.abstract: The application of machine learning (ML) algorithms in economic forecasting has gained significant traction, often under the assumption that non-linear models inherently outperform traditional econometric techniques. This paper tests this hypothesis by conducting a comparative study between the non-parametric K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) regression algorithm and conventional Exponential Smoothing (ETS) models. Utilizing a dataset of monthly automotive registrations in Greece from January 2010 to October 2021, the study evaluates the forecasting performance of these models across a period characterized by severe economic volatility. A rigorous methodology is applied, testing various configurations of the KNN algorithm (including individual neighbors up to k = 24 and combined multi-target vectors) alongside an automated ETS model. Performance is evaluated using RMSE, MAE, and MAPE accuracy metrics across multiple step-ahead forecasting horizons. Contrary to the prevailing enthusiasm for complex ML applications, the empirical results demonstrate that the traditional econometric ETS model consistently outperformed the KNN algorithms, yielding the lowest forecast errors. Among the ML configurations, the simplest model (k = 3) produced the most reliable and competitive results. This study highlights that for volatile, industry-specific economic indicators, computationally simpler and established econometric smoothing techniques remain highly robust, providing a strict and difficult-to-beat benchmark for modern predictive algorithms.

title: Field Geometry in Practice Two Protocols for the Coordination Economy

detail.title: Field Geometry in Practice Two Protocols for the Coordination Economy
detail.abstract: The first two papers of this series established, respectively, an empirical diagnosis of extractive economic structure and a formal theory of why such structures transition and what a coordination-respecting successor must be built of. This paper supplies the missing third element: concrete protocol specifications audited against the theory's own design criteria. Two cases are examined. The first is a credentialing crisis in elite corporate recruitment: the university degree, this paper argues, was never primarily a certificate of skill but a costly, compliance-based proxy for coordination capacity (Spence, 1973), adopted because coordination is expensive to verify directly and because executive review time — the scarce resource the credential filter economizes — is itself a coordination-bandwidth constraint, finite and unforceable in exactly the sense the second paper formalized. The paper's central technical contribution is the Adversarial Anti-Derivative Filter, an algorithm that restores direct, low-latency evaluation of coordination capacity at scale by generating a model's own baseline solution distribution and filtering submissions by their semantic distance from it — a computable test for the compliance/coordination distinction, situated against the AI-generatedtext detection literature and its documented arms-race limitations. The second case is shippingrouter, a local-first, open-source logistics telemetry protocol, audited section by section against the second paper's design triad: an open sink (value dissipates as demurrage avoided and labor saved, never re-accumulating as a token or reservoir), the absence of stock-accumulable gains, and universal forkability, with one terminological correction — the protocol's “zero-knowledge telemetry” is precise anonymized aggregation, not zero-knowledge proof, and the paper restates the mechanism accordingly. A supply-chain case study unifies both protocols under the second paper's stock/flow distinction: legacy enterprise software records participation after the fact, while a semantic telemetry layer detects coordination failure — the ripple not yet connected — before the flow-based checkpoint trips. The paper closes with a generalized protocol grammar, a checklist against which future builders can audit new architectures, and a set of counterarguments including the filter's own adversarial ceiling and Goodhart's law.

title: Automated Comment Moderation Enhances Social Media Advertising Performance
affiliations: Harvard Business School and Harvard University - Business School (HBS)

detail.title: Automated Comment Moderation Enhances Social Media Advertising Performance

publicationDetails.detailsText: Harvard Business School Working Paper No. 27-011
Harvard Business School Marketing Unit Working Paper No. 27-011
publicationDetails.journalName: Harvard Business School: Marketing Unit Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Social media advertising exposes brands not only to potential customers but also to unfiltered consumer discourse in the form of user comments. While comments can enhance authenticity and engagement, they also introduce reputational risks through spam, hate speech, and negative user-generated content. Despite the increasing prevalence of AI-powered comment moderation solutions, little causal evidence exists on whether moderation (i.e., hiding harmful comments) improves ad effectiveness. Across six empirical studies—including two large-scale field experiments and four online studies—we demonstrate that automated moderation of harmful comments causally improves ad performance, including conversion rates, return on ad spend, and purchase intentions. We also identify two important platform-governance boundary conditions: the gains from moderation depend on whether the platform is transparent about the brand’s moderation behavior, and what types of comments are moderated. At the same time, the moderation effect persists when the brand is transparent about its own moderation practices. We advance theory on context effects in social media advertising, by uncovering the first targeted, preventative intervention for avoiding negative adjacencies. For managers, the results show that AI-assisted comment moderation impacts real ad performance but may be contingent upon platform-level transparency design.

title: Optimizing Visibility in Generative Engines A Critical Survey of Generative Engine Optimization
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Optimizing Visibility in Generative Engines A Critical Survey of Generative Engine Optimization
detail.abstract: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) seeks to increase content's presence, likelihood of citation, or influence in answers produced by generative engines. Since the foundational GEO paper, the field has expanded rapidly, but terminology, metrics, and evidence standards remain heterogeneous. This critical survey reviews 45 studies selected under a November 2023-July 2026 publication window, including one earlier preprint published at EMNLP after the window opened, plus relevant RAG and evaluation work. We argue that GEO is not a single ranking task but a stochastic, partially observable pipeline spanning search activation, crawling and indexing, retrieval, reranking and context allocation, citation, prominence, factual absorption, fidelity, and user behavior. The foundational paper's widely cited gains are valid within its experimental setting but conditional on a source already being present in a fixed context; they establish neither organic discoverability nor durable traffic effects. Reviewed work indicates that topical relevance and context position are the most reproducible levers, generic heuristics transfer poorly, competition can erode individual gains, and citation-oriented rewrites can impair retrieval. Commercial audits further reveal low source overlap, substantial run-to-run variability, and persistent fidelity gaps. We contribute a multistage formal model, a visibility vector separating discoverability, citation, absorption, and economic outcomes, an evidence hierarchy, and a reproducible protocol based on repeated measurements, paraphrases, controls, human validation, and multi-actor interference. Within this corpus, the evidence is narrow: alreadyretrieved content can causally alter its citation or use, but no reviewed technique shows a stable, longitudinal, cross-platform causal effect on organic discoverability or downstream behavior.

title: The Time-Privilege Touchstone A Relativity-Grounded Shift of the Burden of Proof in the Debate on the Affectedness of Artificial Systems
affiliations: Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi Christian University Inc.

detail.title: The Time-Privilege Touchstone A Relativity-Grounded Shift of the Burden of Proof in the Debate on the Affectedness of Artificial Systems
detail.abstract: In the debate on the moral status of artificial systems, a fundamental as sumption about time is at work that is rarely named explicitly. Many an thropocentric positions presuppose that the human being experiences time in a privileged, flowing sense that an artificial system cannot have. This experience thereby tacitly becomes a condition of entry for count ing as a possible bearer of consciousness and affectedness. This paper renders that assumption visible and examines whether it holds. To this end it employs two tools from physics and the logic of time. From Einstein’s relativity of simultaneity it follows that simultaneity is not fixed independently of the observer and that an objectively privi leged present thus lacks physical ground. Gödel’s rotating cosmology shows, in addition, that an objective passage of time need not belong to the essence of time. Neither consideration grounds a theory of consciousness or a proof of affectedness in artificial systems. They withdraw the basis from one par ticular exclusion argument. Consciousness and affectedness of artificial systems cannot be excluded solely because these systems allegedly do not experience a human flow of time. From this negative result the paper develops an applicable diagnostic instrument, the Time-Privilege Touchstone, which examines every exclusion criterion by means of a single counterfactual question, namely whether it still holds even if there is no objectively privileged, flowing passage of time.

title: What Corporate AI Text Measures: A Multi-State Indicator of Corporate AI Diffusion
affiliations: Southern Methodist University (SMU) - SMU Cox School of Business

detail.title: What Corporate AI Text Measures: A Multi-State Indicator of Corporate AI Diffusion
detail.abstract: Researchers increasingly use corporate disclosures to trace artificial intelligence (AI), but a keyword hit may describe a working focal-firm system, a tentative plan, another organization, or an unrelated acronym. We construct a validated three-state disclosure indicator that distinguishes substantiated focal-firm claims (A1), weak focal-firm claims (A2), and no valid focal-firm claim (A3). The classified corpus contains 185,551 documents. Of these, 138,606 fall within the active 2015–2025 listing intervals of the 6,934 U.S. public firms in the analysis sample. In a stratified human benchmark, A1 precision rises from 0.493 for keyword retrieval to 0.940 under the full taxonomy. Across firm-years, keyword prevalence exceeds A1 prevalence by a median of 21.3 percentage points. More importantly, the discrepancy changes form: unrelated acronyms and other lexical false positives dominate early, whereas external and non-focal discussion becomes dominant later. Disclosure paths are only partly ordered. A2 is associated with later A1, but 77.0% of firms observed in A1 have no prior A2. Comparisons with Census and patent data further show that agreement depends on how observations are combined and which benchmark is used. In an empirical application to subsequent high-confidence AI-patent publication, raw keyword exposure has no detectable association while prior focal-firm claims do. The multi-state measure improves fit among firms used to estimate the model over raw keywords but does not improve prediction for other firms. Corporate text therefore records disclosed evidence of technological activity rather than adoption itself. The paper contributes a measurement framework for showing when retrieval, attribution, and evidence rules change both observed disclosure diffusion and conclusions drawn from the indicator.

title: Humans as the Loop: Tethering Trust in AI, via Fiduciary Governance of Personal Augmentation Agents
affiliations: GLIA Foundation and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Humans as the Loop: Tethering Trust in AI, via Fiduciary Governance of Personal Augmentation Agents
detail.abstract:
The explosive growth of semi-autonomous AI agents-exemplified most recently by OpenClaw's viral adoption and the Moltbook agent-to-agent platform-has created an urgent governance crisis. Millions of AI agents now operate with direct access to users' sensitive data, messaging platforms, and financial accounts without any enforceable obligation to serve the interests of the individuals they purport to assist. Meanwhile, Big Tech walled-garden agents (OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini) operate under vendor-locked architectures whose primary loyalty runs to their corporate principals. Both the open-source and proprietary extremes share a common deficiency: they are structurally "double agents," with no actual, enforceable accountability to the end user. 

This Article introduces the Personal Augmentation Agent (PAA)-a new class of AI system oriented to operate exclusively on behalf of individuals, across different domains of human life. We articulate three primary reasons why each of us should expect, and even demand, the right to augmentation via these personal AI agents: (1) our lack of adequate representation as we interface with AI systems making consequential decisions about us; (2) our inability to contest these systems as they progressively extract our data and cognition across a number of domains; and (3) our interest in embracing augmentation as a means of enhancing our personal autonomy and agency. The PAA fills all three of these significant gaps.

The Article then presents the concept of a Fiduciary PAA: a PAA that holds itself out as a fiduciary to end users as a matter of governance by its supporting entity. We pose a series of four questions to determine whether and how such an agent can successfully take on fiduciary duties, as a matter of (1) ontology (can an AI system “have” such human-derived duties), (2) technological architecture (can LLM-based systems in particular operate pursuant to such duties), (3) business models (can commercial LLM platforms operate pursuant to such duties), and (4) institutions (can AI systems navigate the balancing of interests and accountability inherent in real-world fiduciary practice). The Article proposes a new architectural element, the Institutional Trust Tether (ITT), as a mechanism for conveying fiduciary duties between the underlying entity and the AI agent. 

This Article then introduces the GliaNet ecosystem, anchored by Net Fiduciaries™ supporting a specific kind of Fiduciary PAA called the gliagent. The gliagent is certified under the GliaNet Alliance’s Fiduciary Governance Infrastructure (FGI), a sixteen-layer governance stack that embeds fiduciary — Page 1 — HUMANS AS THE LOOP • WHITT & CLASBY • JULY 2026 INITIAL DRAFT responsibilities in tangible ways that make compliance architecturally verifiable, rather than merely promissory. This Article responds to each of the four dimensional questions by reference to the proposed role of the gliagent, drawing on three structural moves: (1) the duty-bearing relocation (locating duties at the institutional entity rather than at the AI component), (2) the loyal-system thesis (loyalty borne by the institutional system as a whole), and (3) the SEAMs-Incompatibility Principle (structural exclusion of surveillance-capitalism business models from certification). The Institutional Trust Tether is the proffered means for enacting each of these structural moves. 

This Article also advances a public policy architecture comprising five individual rights (interoperability, portable data access, delegation, query, and augmentation) and a two-tier regulatory structure: a mandatory duty-of-care floor for all AI deployers, paired with incentivized certification for entities willing to assume higher fiduciary obligations. This Article concludes with specific opportunities for operationalizing Fiduciary PAAs through ongoing pilots and through current legislative and regulatory vehicles, and outlines a cross-disciplinary research agenda for the questions that remain open.

title: Expanding into On-Demand Markets with 'Airbnb of Warehousing'
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management and University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management

detail.title: Expanding into On-Demand Markets with 'Airbnb of Warehousing'
detail.abstract: Problem Definition: Despite the potential to capture additional demand through free on-demand fulfillment, few retailers offer such services because they require substantial upfront investment. The "Airbnb of Warehousing" (AW) offers a potential solution by allowing retailers to access excess fulfillment capacity from independent warehouses closer to their markets. We examine whether and how retailers should leverage AW's fulfillment flexibility to expand into on-demand markets. Methodology/Results: To answer this question, we propose a hybrid inventory strategy that combines centralized inventory with the AW, and we show that this approach can support efficient on-demand market expansion via the AW improving the two benchmark strategies: pure centralized fulfillment and pure AW-based fulfillment. We use techniques from robust inventory management. We first characterize the AW business model and then derive robust inventory policies to support efficient on-demand market expansion through AW. For retailers with unknown on-demand markets prior to entry, we propose a hybrid strategy with a robust learning policy at the intersection of robust optimization and Bayesian inference under which retailers can flexibly learn their on-demand markets while minimizing the worst-case mismatch costs. On a testing bed constructed with data from a leading AW platform, we show that the hybrid strategy can significantly increase retailers' expected profit relative to a pure centralized benchmark, and that these gains are larger in markets with less demand variability. Moreover, in markets with higher demand variability, the hybrid strategy outperforms a pure AW-based fulfillment strategy, which highlights the role of centralized facilities in cost-efficiently absorbing demand fluctuations through risk pooling, which AWs alone cannot efficiently handle. Managerial implications: Our proposed policies are robust to distributional assumption errors and can help retailers decide whether to expand into previously untapped on-demand markets, as well as how to do so efficiently through the AW.

title: Proof by Physics: Peer-to-Peer Identity Verification in the Age of Generative AI

detail.title: Proof by Physics: Peer-to-Peer Identity Verification in the Age of Generative AI
detail.abstract: For most of the internet era, the cost of convincingly impersonating a human being was high enough that digital identity systems could treat certain artifacts-a face on a video call, a voice on a phone line, a photographed government document, an established social media history-as reasonable proxies for personhood. Generative artificial intelligence has collapsed the cost of producing all of these artifacts to near zero. We argue that this constitutes a phase change, not an incremental escalation: any identity signal that exists purely as data can now be synthesized at scale, and therefore no verification scheme built exclusively on data artifacts can remain spoofresistant. Drawing on federal law enforcement casework patterns and the 2025 emergence of AIenabled fraud as a formally tracked crime category, we develop a threat model for AI-mediated impersonation in peer-to-peer contexts-dating, commerce, real estate, caregiving, and elder interaction-where individuals, not institutions, must establish trust with strangers. We then propose a design principle we term proof by physics: spoof resistance in the generative era requires binding identity claims to constraints that impose real-world, non-replicable cost on an attackerphysical co-presence confirmed in time and place, cryptographic keys bound to secure hardware, and transitive attestation from previously verified humans. We formalize a peer-to-peer verification framework built on these primitives, analyze its residual attack surface (Sybil attacks on attestation graphs, coercion, collusion, and privacy leakage), and situate the framework against NIST SP 800-63-4, arguing that institutional identity-assurance guidance must be extended to the interpersonal layer where an increasing share of AI-enabled fraud now occurs.

title: Artificial Intelligence and International Marketing: Emerging Opportunities, Ethical Challenges and Implications for Business Practice

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and International Marketing: Emerging Opportunities, Ethical Challenges and Implications for Business Practice
detail.abstract: AI has gone beyond just a niche analytical tool and is now a key element of global marketing strategy. New machine learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics and generative artificial intelligence help organisations uncover international market opportunities, study consumer behaviour, modify communications to the client, translate and localize content, automate customer interactions and enhance marketing decision-making. The developments are especially relevant for multinational enterprises (MNEs) and internationally oriented small and medium sized enterprises (SMEs) as international marketing is more complex than domestic marketing in terms of culture, institutions, language and regulations. With the increasing adoption of AI, however, there are ethical and managerial issues related to consumer privacy, algorithmic bias, cultural misrepresentation, intellectual property rights, misinformation, transparency, and managerial accountability. This focused literature review discusses the recent studies on artificial intelligence application in international marketing and the literature published from 2020 to 2026. It does not suggest that AI is solely a technology designed to increase efficiency, but an ability of the organisations to act dynamically with marketing, which needs data quality, human skills and knowledge, and ethical control and sensitivity to the local marketing environment. The review firmly concludes that international marketers need to build hybrid systems of humans and artificial intelligence, where the technology complements, but does not supplant, cultural judgement, creativity and managerial responsibility. Therefore, artificial intelligence literacy, data ethics and cross-cultural analysis and responsible technology management should be incorporated in the marketing education in business schools.

detail.abstract:
This short paper discusses the rules on "biometric emotion recognition systems" in the EU AI Act and concludes that:
"C]ontrary to what is said in recital 44 to the AI Act or provided for in the body of the Act, the defects in and risks posed by emotion recognition systems noted in that recital are not only unacceptable in the very limited contexts of the workplace or in educational settings – they should lead (and should have led) to the complete rejection of this snake oil: they should be (and should have been) classified as “prohibited” and banned in all contexts. In the meantime, any risk- or fundamental rights assessment that concludes that such a system is data protection- and fundamental rights-compatible should be challenged: any sound assessment could only confirm what I said above: that these systems lack any proper scientific basis, are invalid in scientific terms, and should never be used on real people."
On 15 July 2026, I sent the paper to the European Commission for consideration in their consultation on their guidelines for high-risk AI systems.

title: Multi-Method Ensemble Framework for LLM Hallucination Detection

detail.title: Multi-Method Ensemble Framework for LLM Hallucination Detection
detail.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) frequently generate fluent but factually unsupported content-a failure mode known as hallucination-undermining their reliability in high-stakes applications. Existing detection approaches typically rely on a single signal, such as retrieval grounding (Lewis et al., 2020) or selfconsistency sampling (Manakul et al., 2023), leaving them vulnerable to failure modes the chosen method was not designed to catch. This work proposes an equal-weight, six-signal ensemble framework combining natural language inference (NLI), retrieval-augmented grounding, a three-model LLM-judge panel (OpenAI, Groq, Gemini), and cross-sample self-consistency checking, implemented as a LangGraph state-machine pipeline with parallel execution. Evaluated on 76 HaluEval-QA examples, 77 TruthfulQA examples, and a 40-instance hand-labeled dataset spanning four domains, the system achieves 72.4% (95% CI: 61.4-81.2%), 92.2% (95% CI: 84.0-96.4%), and 87.5% accuracy respectively. McNemar's exact test applied to a 37instance ablation study found no statistically significant difference between any signal-subset configuration (all p > 0.05), indicating the study is underpowered to confirm individual signal contributions despite an 8.2point raw accuracy drop when adding RAG-grounding to an NLI-only baseline. Inter-judge agreement analysis (n=38 claims) revealed Groq and Gemini agree with each other substantially more often (84.6%) than either agrees with OpenAI (71.1%, 73.1%), identifying OpenAI's judge as a conservative outlier within the panel. A quadrant analysis crossing detector-flagged status with sample-consistency status found that claims flagged by detectors AND consistent across samples were real hallucinations 100% of the time (n=4), outperforming the system's own "high-confidence" category (flagged + inconsistent, 66.7% precision), challenging the original architectural assumption that instability signals maximum confidence. Fifteen handcrafted adversarial examples further expose concrete, reproducible failure modes: in 8 of 15 cases, RAGgrounding produced false positives on true-but-context-absent claims; self-consistency proved insensitive to superficial phrasing variation independent of factual content in 2 cases; and a sentence-splitting parser artifact was identified as a genuine implementation limitation. This work contributes a working, deployed detection system and an empirically grounded account of where individual detection methods fail, do not fail, and where ensembling does and does not recover those failures.

detail.abstract:
Many organisations have successfully deployed artificial intelligence in technical terms - models run, dashboards refresh, and automation scripts execute. Yet the business transformation that was promised frequently does not follow. Work processes remain unchanged, users do not trust the output, ownership is unclear, and governance arrives too late. This DBA thesis addresses that gap directly. It asks what leadership, organisational and governance conditions are required for AI to move from a successful pilot to a genuine business transformation, and it answers that question through the development of the Comprehensive Intelligent Strategic Leadership Framework (CISLF).

This research adopts a qualitative, exploratory and applied DBA research design. The methodology combines thematic documentary analysis with design science artefact demonstration. Evidence is drawn from peer-reviewed strategic leadership, digital transformation, AI adoption, socio-technical systems and proportionate AI governance literature. This theoretical base is supplemented by stable public CXO documentary sources and two open-source artefacts developed by the researcher: Cogni CISLF Advisor, a live executive assessment application, and CogniClean Assistant, an earlier bounded prototype.

The documentary and design-science analysis indicates that AI transformation fails not because of technical weakness but because of four interconnected leadership gaps: unclear vision and sponsorship, misalignment between technology choices and business processes, insufficient people capability and user readiness, and the absence of operational governance before scale. CISLF addresses each gap through a corresponding pillar - Leadership Mindset and Vision, Strategic Business-Technology Alignment, Organisational Capability and Culture Building, and Responsible AI Governance - and integrates them into a single stop-redesign-scale decision gate that executives can apply at any portfolio review.

 The study offers practical implications for technology executives who must evaluate AI use cases before investment, during pilot execution and before enterprise-wide scaling. Technology executives in any sector can use CISLF to evaluate AI use cases before investment, during pilot execution and before enterprise scale. The framework does not replace domain expertise or technical architecture decisions; it provides the leadership and governance discipline that makes both more effective. Cogni CISLF Advisor shows that this discipline can be embedded in a live working tool, making the framework accessible to practitioners without requiring deep familiarity with the underlying theory. While the study does not include primary interview data or statistical validation, it provides a rigorous evidence-informed foundation that future researchers can test through executive interviews, Delphi panels, longitudinal case studies and field applications.

title: When the Code Keeps its Promise but the Contract Doesn't: A Governance Gap in South Korea's Tokenized Securities Framework

detail.title: When the Code Keeps its Promise but the Contract Doesn't: A Governance Gap in South Korea's Tokenized Securities Framework

declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a legal and regulatory policy analysis based exclusively on publicly available primary and secondary sources (legislation, regulatory guidelines, technical documentation, and academic literature). detail.abstract: When a smart contract executes exactly as programmed, it can still fail to do what the parties actually agreed to. This paper examines a structural gap between legal contracts, written in ordinary language that tolerates ambiguity by design, and executable code, which cannot process ambiguity at all. Drawing on Accord Project's own teaching documentation, the paper shows that even the most influential open-source framework for smart legal contracts treats deliberately open legal standards, such as "in the receiver's opinion" or "force majeure," as simple binary variables, embedding legal indeterminacy into code without resolving it. This gap acquires particular urgency in South Korea, where a February 2027 deadline requires tokenized securities platforms to register under a new distributed ledger framework, amid technological fragmentation across at least five competing architectures and a "digital native" model in which the ledger itself, without a parallel central registry, becomes the sole legal record. The paper argues that closing this gap does not require new technology, but a governance requirement modeled on a well-established regulatory pattern found in civil aviation and other fields: certifying verifiable outcomes without prescribing the specific technique used to achieve them. It concludes with a concrete recommendation for Korea's forthcoming distributed ledger standard requirements guideline.
